#8308. “We Used FFS and Were Targeting Big Bass.” Angler Breaks 76-Year-Old Smallmouth Bass Record

Published Nov 4, 2026 4:14 PM EST

The hottest fishing news, tips, and tactics

On the morning of October 30 Austin Schiefer and his fishing buddy Ted Johnson launched their bass boat into Green Bay, a huge Wisconsin portion of Lake Michigan. They started about 7:30 working a reef area in 18 feet of water about two miles from shore. Before long, they’d go on to break a 76-year-old fishing record.

“It was a spot we’d fished previously and caught nice smallmouths on,” Schiefer tells Outdoor Life. “We used forward-facing sonar and were targeting big bass.”

The morning started windy, ideal conditions for clear water bass on Green Bay. The duo was catching bass, but about mid-day the wind died and the water got calm.

“That’s not the best conditions for Green Bay,” says Schiefer, who works for UPS when he’s not producing his own line of soft plastic lures (Schief’s Custom Baits). “There were plenty of bass on the reef, but they were finicky and wouldn’t take the lures I was casting.”

Johnson, however, was catching bass using a different type of soft plastic. He suggested to Schiefer that he try one of the lures he was doing well with, and to go lighter with his tackle.

“The bite was light and deep, so I changed to the setup that Ted suggested,” says Schiefer, from Menasha, Wisconsin.

Schiefer changed over to a Deps Sakamata Shad Soft Jerkbait, which is a 5-inch lure, and the productive hue was “champagne-pepper.”

He threaded the lure onto a 3/32nd-ounce jighead and made a long cast with the lightest 7-foot spinning rod he owns. His reel was spooled with 8-pound test Power Pro braided line with a 10-pound test fluorocarbon leader.

“I wanted to make a long cast and sort of swim the lure back as it sank, a pendulum like retrieve,” says Schiefer. “We could see fish on bottom with sonar, but they’d rise up to take lures. Except they were refusing my lures just before they’d hit – until I cast that Deps Jerkbait.”

It was about 2 p.m. and as Schiefer’s lure sank he felt a hit. But the fish didn’t fight like a smallmouth. The battle wasn’t fast and furious and there were no jumps. Just a couple minutes of it taking drag, and rugged deep pulling and rolling – so much so that Schiefer thought perhaps he’d hooked a freshwater drum.

“But as I worked it to the surface I got a look at it in that clear water about 10 feet down, and I saw that it was a huge smallmouth,” he says. “I knew it was a monster, and when I got it to the boat Ted netted it.

“I got lucky, because the hook was bent when I took the lure out of its mouth.”

Schiefer had caught big smallmouths previously, but nothing over 7 pounds, so he knew his catch was important. They put the lunker bass in their boat livewell and tried to contact Wisconsin’s Department of Natural Resources. But it was Friday afternoon before Halloween, and no one from the DNR was available.

The anglers quit fishing and trailered their boat to a grocery store where the bass was weighed at 9 pounds, 11ounces on certified scales. It measured 23.75 inches long. The smallmouth easily topped the 1950 Wisconsin record smallie weighing 9 pounds, 1 ounce. That fish was caught by Leon Stefonek in Oneida County’s Indian Lake.

To qualify as a state record bass, the DNR required the fish to be weighed and examined by state biologists. That didn’t happen until the next day, when DNR fisheries staff weighed and inspected the fish.

They discovered the bass was a male, not a female – which usually are the larger of the two fish genders. Additionally, Schiefer’s 9.70-pound smallmouth had nothing in its stomach, again unusual as most bass in autumn are feeding heavily for the coming winter.

Schiefer will have a skin mount made of his smallmouth bass record, which he says has been officially recognized by DNR as Wisconsin’s heaviest bronzeback of all time. He’s also considering having replica mounts made of the fish.

Read Next: 7 Forward Facing Sonar Tips: Settings, Mounting, and Techniques Explained

“I think a replica mount of the bass would be nice for the National Freshwater Fishing Hall of Fame in their Hayward museum, and maybe one for Bass Pro Shops, too,” he says.

“My only regret in all of this is I didn’t release the fish alive. I couldn’t with the DNR requirements for weighing and inspecting the fish for the record… I’ve had some sleepless nights because of that. I did everything in my power to keep from killing that bass.”

#8306. Floating Alone Down the Brahmaputra on a Bamboo Raft

Indian mountaineer and adventurer Shekhar Bordoloi has just started a solo expedition down the Brahmaputra River. He set off on a homemade on a bamboo raft from the Dhola–Sadiya Bridge on November 1 and aims to finish at Dhubri, 891km later. The route covers the entire Brahmaputra within India and should take 22 to 25 days in all. The river begins in Tibet and continues beyond India into Bangladesh, covering 2,900km in all.

This won’t be Bordoloi’s first time down the river. In 2020, he and two friends took a similar bamboo raft down a 400km section of the Brahmaputra. Earlier, in 2015, Bordoloi was one of 11 who tackled another part of the river over 11 days under the auspices of the Assam Mountaineering Association. This expedition, however, will test his endurance, pitting him against river conditions for longer, and with less support, than ever before.

Bordoloi on a previous raft expedition on the Brahmaputra. This raft took Bordoloi and friends from the world’s largest river island, Umananda, to its smallest, Majuli. Photo: Shekhar Bordoloi/Instagram

Bordoloi’s raft was hand-built from bamboo poles carefully lashed together over several days. Such craft are a traditional way of navigating rivers across the region, and are still used by local communities for fishing and transportation.

Though the river can be temperamental, Bordoloi’s first two days have been relatively calm, taking him down the Lohit, one of the Brahmaputra’s many tributaries and channels. Navigating the complex river system alone will be a challenge. The Brahmaputra is one of the largest river systems in India, the ninth-largest in the world by discharge, and is prone to flooding and powerful currents.

But according to Bordoloi, those obscure, winding corridors are at the heart of this project. Many sections of the river remain underexplored, and he believes there is hidden potential for the people in his home region of Assam. If he can map routes for river tourism and model environmentally responsible river navigation through those routes, he hopes to draw attention to this important riverine ecosystem and the economic opportunities for the people living along it.

The logistical challenges of a long expedition will further complicate progress. On previous expeditions, Bordoloi traveled with minimal supplies or no food at all, relying entirely on foraging and knowledge of the natural landscape. But this adventure will take over twice as long and may put those skills to their limits.

Bordoloi is documenting his daily progress on Facebook and Instagram.

Lou Bodenhemier holds an MA in History from the University of Limerick and a BA in Creative Writing from the University of Arizona. He’s interested in maritime and disaster history as well as criminal history, and his dissertation focused on the werewolf trials of early modern Europe. At the present moment he can most likely be found perusing records of shipboard crime and punishment during the Age of Sail, or failing that, writing historical fiction horror stories. He lives in Dublin and hates the sun.

#8303. Details, Video of Jugal II First Ascent

The Spanish team is back in Kathmandu after their first ascent of Jugal II via a highly difficult 2,000m route. Yet, the climbers insist that the best part of the experience was climbing part of the route with Italians Nives Meroi and Romano Benet. Jugal II was Plan B for the Italian pair after flooding washed out access to their primary target, Tilicho Peak in the Annapurna region.

The peak, northeast of Kathmandu on the Nepal-Tibet border, has been a coveted goal since it opened to climbing teams in 2023. In the end, it was the skill and smart strategy of Mikel Zabalza, Ruben Perez, and Mikel Saez de Urabain that put them on the unclimbed 6,518m summit after an alpine-style push via the east-southeast face.

Route topo, including a special mention of Nives Meroi and Romano Benet.

The team said that the greatest technical difficulties came high on the route. “From the upper bivouac, the climb goes on pretty vertical mixed terrain, with sections of poor-quality rock,” Zabalza explained. “It’s sustained M5 with some even harder sections, until 6,450m. Then the rest of the way to the summit follows along a 55˚-60˚snow slope.”

A tough, vertical mixed section. Photo: Mikel Zabalza

They reached the summit on October 29, at 4:00 pm. The weather was clear but very cold, with some evening humidity.

“We made three bivouacs on the route, two on the way up and one more on descent, and all of them were rather precarious,” Mikel Zabalza told ExplorersWeb from Kathmandu. “Luckily, we had a tarp to enlarge them.”

One of the climbers on the summit of Jugal II. Photo: Mikel Zabalza

The Spanish team, all highly experienced alpinists, had been studying the route for months. This was key to their success.

The situation was different for Benet and Meroi of Italy. Since they had not planned to do Jugal II, their approach to the route was more improvisational. They had no previous information about what they would find. To make matters worse, the third member of the team, Tine Cuder of Slovenia, had to abandon the expedition due to health problems.

One of the Spanish team’s bivouacs, with a tiny ledge enlarged by a fabric tarp. Photo: Romano Benet

There was no competition between the two teams, who happily joined forces for the summit push. However, the Spaniards’ strategy proved essential on the highly steep ramps covered with unstable snow.

Nivel Meroi loaded with bivy gear on highly steep mixed ramps on Jugal II. Photo: Romano Benet

“We set off on an adventure, having never seen the mountain before and not knowing what kind of ascent awaited us, but we gave it a try,” Romano Benet reported from Kathmandu. “We decided to turn back to avoid a third bivouac. ”

The two teams joined forces and were in good spirits on the route. Photo: Romano Benet

Benet explained that they lacked the necessary gear (specifically, a tarp like Zabalza’s group) to pitch bivvies “on this type of face, where it’s impossible to carve out a ledge.”

Otherwise, the two groups returned as friends. “Nives and Romano are exceptional people,” Zabalza said.

“We are back from the mountain with new experiences and ideas but, most of all, with three new fantastic friends with whom, hopefully, we will share more adventures in the future,” Romano Benet concluded.

#8302. These Are the 13 Tactics Expert Whitetail Hunters Actually Use to Tag Mature Bucks

Published Nov 4, 2026 5:13 PM EST

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

The best deer hunters in the nation (known and unknown) all share a common thread. They are students of deer and the woods, and they never stop learning. As such, they continually experiment with new and advanced deer hunting tactics.

In order to learn some of these secrets (and to share them with you), I called a handful of the best deer hunters I know. Here’s how they find success season after season.

Mark Drury of Drury Outdoors has bagged more big deer than most. His approach is proven, and the process he uses includes saving and analyzing a lot of trail camera data, especially historical information. He has kept every single trail cam pic of a racked buck since 2007.

“Save trail monitoring pictures in an organized fashion for easy review in future years,” Drury says. “Bucks are incredibly habitual from year to year. Study your pics year-round to formulate patterns with individual bucks or areas. [Over time you’ll build] a database that helps lead to patterns in future years, as crop rotations, weather, and moon in future seasons mirror conditions that occurred in the past. It takes a lot of time to assemble and study but saves time in future seasons.”

Grant Woods of Growing Deer TV is one of the most renowned deer scientists in the country. He seems to get inside the mind of whitetails and understands what they do and why they do it. To that point, he stresses making hunting decisions based on what deer do, and not what we think they should do.

“An issue I’ve seen is hunters making setup and tactical decisions based on human thoughts,” Woods says. “The hunters I know that have repeated success filling tags in all types of conditions and habitats always think like a deer. They consider what deer need that day, and what will deer avoid.”

As Paul Beasley, co-host of “Canada in the Rough” TV, says, hunters are creatures of habit. “The longer we hunt a piece of ground, the more established our hunting setups and entry/access/travel points become,” he says. “We tend to rely more on what has worked before, and while deer in general also tend to gravitate to the same trails, food sources, and pinch points, it has been my experience that mature bucks need to be treated as individuals and hunted accordingly.

“The buck I shot this year helps illustrate my point. We have hunted this same 100-acre property for over 10 years, and have always taken deer off of it in the same 50-yard-by-80-yard area. Throughout the spring and into summer, this buck was working that area perfectly, but as hunting season approached, his behavior changed. His appearances on camera began to fall off. So, I scrambled to put up more cameras and found that he hadn’t gone anywhere. He was just using different parts of the property.”

Beasley killed that buck on the second afternoon of the season. He arrowed from a setup that his crew had never harvested a buck from before.

“It was through paying attention to this individual buck’s behavior, and not just doing the same old thing that has always worked, that allowed me to put my tag on him,” Beasley says.

Oftentimes deer hunters do things without thinking. We react, rather than making decisions based on logic. HeadHunters TV’s Nate Hosie agrees, and says we should hunt smarter and not harder.

“Growing up, I used to think the more I was out there the better my chances,” he says. “It’s not completely wrong, but as I’ve grown as a hunter, I’ve learned to pick my moments for when to strike. Wind, temperature, time of year, trail cam intel, [and more] now go into my hunt. The less I’m in and out, and the higher probability my attempts are, the more success I find.”

Rick White is a longtime staple in the outdoor industry and he suggests that hunters go all or nothing with scent management.

“One of the biggest things I try to instill in people is always going to the woods as scent-free as possible,” he says. “Always play the wind. Never intentionally hunt a stand on a bad wind. But also know that deer don’t always come in from where we want them to. So, if you’re not going to follow every step with scent elimination, then save your money.”

Read Next: 15 Scent Control Strategies That Actually Work

It sounds like rudimentary advice, but even experienced hunters make blunders that lead to being seen, heard, and smelled by deer. It’s something we must continually keep at the forefront of our mind. Will this entry route cause bedded deer to see me? Will this exit route blow scent into a bedding area?

Bone Collector Co-Host Nick Mundt knows deer hunting as well as anyone. As a former deer hunting guide and current big deer killer, he stresses the importance of going undetected when getting in and out of your hunting spots.

“Never think the wind will just work,” he says. “Always know that they’ll bust you if the wind is wrong. It dictates every sit.”

Aaron Gaines of Ani-Logics advises hunters to kill a target buck as early as possible. The early season and pre-rut offer opportunities to hunt consistent bucks.

“This is when he’s on a pattern and most predictable,” Gaines says. “To do this, I utilize most recent information from cameras. I’m very disciplined on hunting the right wind. If he’s daylighting, and I’ve got the right wind, things usually work out well.”

Read Next: Why the Last Week of October Is the Best Time to Kill a Big Buck

During the rut, whitetail bucks seem to travel via loops. That’s not hearsay or some hokey hack from your grandaddy’s hunting journal. That’s straight from a deer biologist. More specifically, former CEO of the Quality Deer Management Association and current HuntStand biologist, Brian Murphy.

“The biggest piece of advice I’ve learned over the years is to develop a plan and then stick with it long enough for it to have a reasonable chance of success,” Murphy says. “In other words, informed optimism. The hunters who have done their homework and keep a positive attitude, often after multiple dismal outings, are ultimately the most successful. Knowing from research that bucks often take a few days to complete loops within their home range, it’s not surprising that it takes persistence to increase the odds you will get an opportunity.”

Nathan Mrnak, COO of Base Camp Leasing, is a diehard deer hunter. He spends many days in the field each year. He stresses that it’s OK to move off your original plan and make a move.

“Picking out a stand location can be one of the toughest decisions while setting up on a mature whitetail,” he says. “I have had many first sits that ended with my target buck just out of bow range. Seeing his exact route provided the last bit of intel to moving a set just 50 yards to capitalize the next sit. This has worked time and time again in big timber.”

The most basic element of deer hunting is hunting deer where they are. To do that, you need current information.

Own the Season’s Art Helin knows this well. “Hunt where the bucks want to be during the correct phase of the season,” he says. “Food sources during early season, transition areas during the pre-rut (between field and bedding and staging areas), funnels and ridge edges during the rut (all day or mid-day sits especially), and back to food sources late season.”

During the rut, a lot of deer hunters choose to do all-day sits. Whitetail Properties Land Specialist Ben Harshyne does, too. However, he changes things up.

“I grew up hunting all-day sits in one stand,” he says. “Over time, I learned that deep timber and thick cover are action-packed in the morning and afternoon, yet often go cold by evening. In the afternoon, shift focus to hunting cover and edges near food sources or along travel lines leading to food. Not necessarily the actual food edge, but nearby. Does bed near food and still want to feed — and the bucks know it. Few stands are productive all day, so fine-tune your late-day move to target cover that relates to food.”

Big buck killer Jared Mills has arrowed a lot of big whitetails. He says don’t be afraid to be aggressive, but do it at the right time.

“I think most guys tend to be too conservative when hunting a target buck, staying on the fringes and only getting out when the conditions are perfect,” he says. “That’s fine if you have the entire season to hunt, and there’s little chance of him getting killed by a neighbor, but that’s a very rare scenario for most of us. While the windows of opportunity to encounter a target buck are already small enough, we make them even smaller by not getting in there after him. Be smart with your hunting, of course, but don’t sit around waiting for the absolute perfect time to move in, otherwise, you’ll likely miss a chance.”

Finally, just keep hunting. You won’t always kill a deer on opening day. It might just be closing day. So, keep hunting, and don’t give up.

“Have patience and persistence,” Helin concluded. “The entire season can change, and it can all happen in a short minute. Stay with it, and never give up, but also never get lazy. Always follow the same regimen from day No. 1 until the end.”

#8301. Te Araroa day 12: An exciting side-quest!

4.5km, Waitangi Holiday Park to Paihia Top 10

Last winter I did a week of maintenance on the tall ship R. Tucker Thompson, which is berthed in Opua. The crew told me to let them know when I was passing through on TA and they would help out how they could. I almost didn’t text, as I hate to ask for favours, but I figured maybe I could get my friends a tour of the ship and if I was really lucky perhaps I could sleep on board on the way through. I got a reply right away; they were sailing on Tuesday and did I want to join? How could I refuse that offer! Of course I said yes, so on Tuesday morning I found myself taking the ferry from Paihia over to Russell, where the trip would depart from.

A fun rainbow bench on the way to the ferry 🏳️‍🌈

Waiting in Russell for the ship to arrive

On the quay, I chatted to my fellow sailors a bit while we waited. As I boarded, I recognised the skipper Pete, because we had spent a day varnishing the fore mast together last winter. We set off from the quay, and I eagerly stepped up when they asked for volunteers to help set the sails. It was great to pull some ropes again! The plan was to engine sail to an island, where we would go ashore, have lunch, swim, and then sail back. Shortly after departing, the crew gave a safety briefing for climbing the rigging, and I got harnessed up.

One of the other passengers snapped some photos of me up the rigging

It’s been a while since I climbed the rigging on a ship under sail, and it was quite breezy. But I was pleased that I didn’t feel too scared, although I didn’t want to climb too high.

Once I got down from the rigging, other passengers started noticing dolphins close to the ship. They were swimming right alongside and leaping out of the water literally a metre from us. It was so cool to see that! I didn’t manage to get photos because I was scared to drop my phone over the side.

Soon we arrived at Motuarohia Island, which was a postcard-perfect Bay of Islands view. There was a track up to a lookout, which felt extremely easy for me without my pack for once – it felt like I was floating. The views were great and I stood up there for a while admiring them.

Some people were swimming in the bay, but unfortunately I hadn’t brought my towel across to the island with me. Eventually the crew brought the RIB back to pick us up and lunch was waiting on board. Most people were eating sausages, but the cook had prepared some falafels for me. I asked if there were any other veggies, and she said she didn’t think so. I left a couple of falafels just in case, and good thing I did! A German lady was in the next batch of passengers to come back from the island, and it seemed like she maybe hadn’t informed them in advance that she didn’t eat meat.

After eating lunch, some people swung off a rope from the rigging into the water. That was a bit much for me, but I was regretting not swimming earlier so I climbed down the ladder into the water. It was pretty chilly, but definitely refreshing.

Then we started heading back, and set all the sails – which of course meant pulling more ropes. All too soon, we were approaching Russell and taking down the sails. There was due to be a ferry back to Paihia shortly after arrival, which I just about managed to make. It was an awesome day out, and really cool to chat with all the crew, see the sights, and most importantly be under sail again! The weather was also much better than the forecast had made it sound.

Back in Paihia, I made a quick stop in the Four Square to grab a couple more snacks for the next section. There wouldn’t be a shop for a couple of days and I wanted to be sure I would have enough.

I hadn’t realised, but the next section of track was tidally dependant and the tide was now all the way in. I had to walk along the road instead, which did at least have a pavement but wasn’t the most scenic. After a bit of road walking, I reached some track which went through the bush above the shoreline. It was a nice walk, and felt easy after my restful day. Soon I arrived at the Paihia Top 10 holiday park, which has a special rate for TA hikers. I ended up between Georgia, who I met the previous night, and Harry, who I had last seen at the Krishna Sanctuary before Raetea Forest. It was a cool tent spot, right on the water, and I ate dinner, chatted a bit with Georgia, and went to bed.

Nice-coloured water heading out of Paihia

#8298. Huge Crowds Trek to Everest Base Camp

The image of an endless line of trekkers heading to Everest Base Camp this week seemed like deja vu. Why are conga lines similar to the infamous ones filmed every May on Everest’s Hillary Step, now repeating at the base of the mountain? We asked the local trekking guide who shot the video.

Ngima Sherpa of Osprey Adventure explained that this is not the norm, but the delay caused by Cyclone Anwar, which hit Nepal last weekend, has created a huge backlog.

“Even though there are always a lot of trekkers heading to Everest Base Camp, this kind of traffic is not usual,” Ngima Sherpa explained. “This video was shot on November 1, after three days of continuous snow and rain…During that time, all the trekkers were stuck in Dingboche, which is two trekking stages away from Everest Base Camp.”

When the weather finally cleared, all those trekkers set off for EBC at the same time, causing heavy traffic on the route from Dingboche to Gorakshep.

The recent cyclone is also the reason why the surroundings are so heavily covered in snow. Usually, the entire trail to Everest Base Camp is dry.

The fresh snow on Nepal’s peaks is having consequences for those planning to summit trekking peaks. Conditions on otherwise straightforward snow slopes have become problematic, as climbers sink into deep, heavy snow.

Satori Adventures had to retreat after swimming in snow on the flanks of Mera Peak, in the Khumbu. “Four to five feet of fresh snow made it impossible to move forward above high camp,” leader Furba Sherpa reported.

Ramesh Gurung noted today that he has retreated from an attempt on 6,119m Lobuche East, another popular Khumbu 6000’er. However, Gurung said he will try again with another group soon.

Conditions will change only as the snow transforms under the dimming sun and freezes in the approaching winter temperatures.

On Ama Dablam, Sherpa climbers struggled to reopen the route to Camp 1 on Tuesday but managed to complete it. The route above Camp 1 follows a steep, mixed ridge with less accumulated snow. Several teams are now on their summit rotations and expect to top out in the next few days.

Tenzing Sherpa of Gokyo Namaste Lodge has shared some useful information for trekkers who plan to cross the huge Ngozumpa Glacier between Gokyo and Dragnag. The recent snowfall makes the usual route less safe, and he recommends following local people along an easier route between Longbanga Tso (1st Lake) and Taujung Tso (2nd Lake). See Tenzing’s sketch of the route:

Alternative route between Gokyo Lakes, suggested by Gokyo Tenzing Sherpa.

Tenzing also noted that the route from Thame to Gokyo is open, as the Gokyo Lodge Association cleared and reopened the trail from the Gokyo side yesterday. However, conditions on the glacier may change quickly.

The route across Gokyo is one of the most popular side trips in the Khumbu, for those wanting to enrich their Everest Base Camp trek. The area features stunning scenery, with high mountain lakes, glaciers, and a view of the formidable South Face of Cho Oyu.

#8295. The Old-School Guide to Not Getting Lost in the Woods (Before We Had GPS)

Published Nov 5, 2026 9:30 AM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

The ridge I was on sloped gently down to a flat gap that spilled off into wide coves on either side. Through the spring and summer the forest in this mountain backcountry had been blessed with abundant rainfall and the wild creatures were busy reaping the berries, seeds and other browse. Deer tracks were everywhere and several trails crossed in the gap where deer had traveled along the ridge or moved between the high coves.

The ridge trail I followed was wet from recent rains and I pussy-footed almost without sound toward the top of a contour from which the slope pitched abruptly into the gap. I was following the general rule for a stalking deer hunter, which specifies that you walk for two counts, then pause, look and listen for four. I was in the second phase of this procedure when something moved just below me in the edge of the gap.

At first I thought I saw the haunches of a deer with its posterior toward me. But a closer look revealed a man, dressed in camouflage, on his hands and knees as though he were after doodlebugs. I moved cautiously toward him, keeping a tree trunk handy so that I could step behind it should the hunter suddenly detect or sense my presence and whirl on me with his gun, which leaned against a tree close beside him.

He was so engrossed that he did not see or hear me. I stopped a few yards away, scarcely believing my eyes. Spread out on the ground was a 6×6-foot map, with a compass propped up in its middle. He was intently studying one and then the other.

I cleared my throat. He gave a little start, straightened up and looked around.

“Oh, no,” he said and stood up. “I just wanted to see where I was going, to make sure I didn’t get lost.”

We exchanged introductions. His large-caliber rifle told me he was after big game—in this case a whitetail deer because it was the largest game animal around. I was curious about the map and compass and the way he was using them, yet I didn’t want to appear too nosey.

“Looks like you have your hunt pretty well organized,” I suggested mildly.

“Oh yes,” he said. “Then I always know where I am.”

“I’m interested,” I said. “If you don’t mind, please tell me how you do it.”

“Of course I don’t mind,” he said and smiled. “It might help you some time.”

He went back to his knees and I squatted beside him. He put his finger on a spot where he had made an X.

“Here is where I left my car,” he told me. “I took a bearing on this gap and followed a compass course to it. Didn’t miss it by more than a couple hundred yards.”

The map showed that the straight line he had followed between the two points crossed a deep cove, with steep sides. A much easier route would have been at a slight angle to his direct line, up a gentle slope to the ridge and then an almost level walk into the gap. I did not want to confuse him by pointing this out.

With his finger he traced another scope of country, then another, in a sort of rough triangle that would put him back in the vicinity of his car.

“You’ve probably seen plenty of deer sign,” I suggested, “tracks, scrapes, rubs and such.”

“Well, really I haven’t,” he admitted. “I was told this country is full of whitetails and I’m looking for a big buck.”

He stood up, folded his map, slid the rifle sling over his shoulder and looked at his compass.

“Good luck,” I said. “I hope you find him somewhere on your course.”

During many years of walking trails I have run into a number of hunters who concentrated so hard on map and compass reading that they forgot to hunt. This may be because there are many new hunters who either lack wilderness smarts or who have read articles in the magazines explaining how a man in the woods can find his way by taking bearings with a compass on top of a map. I’ve read a few of those articles and somehow got the impression that most of them were written by men who knew more about maps and compasses than they did about hunting. A man walking through the woods with a map in one hand and a compass in the other can’t devote much time to his reason for being there.

I’m not saying that a map and compass are not necessary. Both are. My old Western hunting buddy Jim Gay used to say that when a man needs a compass, it’s too late. I must disagree.

Months before I hunt any territory new to me, I write for maps. They are available from the U. S. Forest Service and a number of other federal agencies and from the states and provinces. Some maps show the trails and streams, others are contoured to indicate topography.

Everything is bordered by something. In the broadest sense of the term, North America lies generally between three oceans, the Gulf of Mexico and Canada.

Narrow this down to any segment of our vast land and you have rivers, creeks, swamps, ridges, roads and trails that surround your hunting territory, however large or small it might be. Fix those landmarks in your mind, with compass directions, and you can always come out on a road or trail that eventually leads you to where people are.

I was in Wyoming’s Thorofare wilderness with a hunter who had seen very little backcountry. One afternoon when we were moving our camp from one segment of this range to another, my friend somehow got ahead of the packstring and took the wrong trail. When night came he was very much lost. He was smart enough to stop and build a fire. In the morning he remembered what I’d told him: “Most of the Thorofare trails parallel streams, so if you get lost, go downhill until you find a creek and follow it. Eventually it will lead to a trail.”

We went looking for him after breakfast. We found where he’d branched off the main trail and we followed the tracks of his horse. They led to the remains of his fire and where he’d turned downhill to a creek that he followed to the main trail. Because we were tracking him and moving more slowly, he arrived in camp hours before we did.

Even though I think I know all the features, I normally carry a map in my backpack or saddle bags. And a number of times I have used it to help me choose the right ridge or valley.

A paper map with no backing for substance soon wears out from folding and unfolding or from hauling it around. Its life may be prolonged if you will glue it to some fabric such as sailcloth, very lightweight canvas or thin plastic. A coat of shellac helps keep it dry. Many outdoorsmen carry this type of reinforced map.

So before you hunt anywhere, get the lay of the land in mind, even if it’s only from a crudely drawn map done by someone who is familiar with the territory. It may save you from getting turned around.

I am convinced that a compass is a necessity. I often make the statement that I don’t go into the backyard at night for firewood without my compass. This may be a bit exaggerated but you can wager your last scrap of magnet that on any hunting trip I always have a compass with me. Over many years I’ve been turned around in the woods innumerable times. I’m sure that on a few of those occasions a compass kept me from getting hopelessly lost.

Once in Montana I followed a divide between two watersheds that cradled vast river systems. In the heavy timber, the crest of the divide made an awkward turn that I did not notice. When I reached this same place on my way back to camp, I discovered a ridge that branched off the one I followed. Thinking it was only a spur, I continued on. I knew something was wrong when I ran into a jumble of ridges, none of which bore any resemblance to the main divide.

I looked at my compass but it pointed in the wrong direction. I had no map with me, so I sat down, brushed away the leaves and pine needles and with a stick drew a crude map on the bare earth. I spent half an hour trying to correlate my map in the dirt, the compass, and the lay of the ridges. One of the toughest “lost” decisions I ever made was to backtrack myself to the “spur” ridge and follow that one.

An experienced woodsman subconsciously keeps track of himself by the sun, the direction of the wind and the features of the land. It’s only in a snowstorm, dense fog or on a cloudy night that he needs a compass and doesn’t hesitate to use it. A man new to wild country is not likely to think of these natural guides and sometimes not even his compass if he carries one. He makes a common and often serious mistake, when he is not on a trail or road, of trying to go out of the woods the way he came in. Without knowing it, he begins to walk in circles.

I have helped find a few lost hunters who stumbled for a day or two—or more—around in a circle. One was within a few hundred yards of a broad highway. If he had stopped long enough to listen, he would have heard the noise of cars passing. We found another staggering a few steps and falling, then getting up to stagger a few more steps. He had thrown away his gun, his clothes were torn and his face looked like he’d just come out of the heavyweight championship ring. He didn’t even recognize his friends.

Only two of the men we found had accepted the fact that they were lost and calmly built a fire to wait it out. One had responded to calls from the search party. The other, after a day and a night, had resorted to the universal signal of danger or distress known to almost every hunter. He fired three quick shots, waited a few minutes then fired three more. After a couple of hours he went through the same procedure and this time was heard by one of his companions.

If any man is blessed with a sense of direction, I have yet to meet him. Animals are said to have the homing instinct, but I have encountered circumstances that cause me to doubt that in unknown country they do either. Once in the northern Yukon Territory, two weeks by packstring travel from man-made trails, we hunted all day away from camp. Late in the afternoon we stalked a big bull caribou and, by the time we had made our kill, caped out the scalp and quartered and loaded the meat on our packhorse, the night was pitch black. I suggested we broil a slab of the meat and make it back to camp the next morning.

“Don’t worry about it,” the guide assured me. “These horses can go straight to camp.”

They went to camp that night but they didn’t go straight. By scent they backtracked themselves over the entire route we had taken that day, climbing ridges, following streams and hollows over the same circuitous route we had hunted. We passed areas I recognized, even in the darkness, and got back to camp only an hour or two before daylight.

Back to man’s sense of direction: Put the best woodsman you know in an insulated room, sketch a tailless donkey on the wall and give him the tail to pin in place. Blindfold him, turn out the lights, walk him in a few circles, spin him around a time or two, then noiselessly leave him in the completely dark sound-proof room to complete his mission. The odds are four to one that he won’t find the right wall and 50 to one that he won’t go directly to the derriere of the donkey.

To test your own sense of direction, leave the boat dock on a large lake where you know every shoreline and try to cross the lake in a dense fog to a spot you think you can reach with your eyes closed. Without a compass you may end up on any shore of the lake, even the one you pulled away from.

I had this experience on a wide saltwater estuary called Buttermilk Sound on the Georgia coast. We had no compass on the boat. The fog moved in, the tide was at flood and the water surface as smooth as the top of a billiard table. We thought we knew these waters well enough to ease across at slow speed but, when we began to bounce over our own wake, I suggested we drop anchor right where we were.

With the motor off we could hear a faint roar that one of our crew members identified as surf on the outer beaches and that another said was the roar of highway traffic on the mainland in the opposite direction. If we guessed wrong or continued to move in circles on an outgoing tide and if the fog persisted for a day as it sometimes did, we could have ended up on the Atlantic Ocean—out of sight of land and without a compass. We sat anchored in Buttermilk Sound for eight hours until the fog lifted. Never since have I been in a boat without a compass in my pocket or tackle box.

In the woods, even with a compass, when I have had my mind on trailing or locating game, I’ve been so badly turned around that I was inclined to dispute the compass needle. This is more likely to happen in a swamp or other flatland where every tree or clump of brush looks like every other tree or clump of brush. I have been so dead sure of my directions that I think the compass needle has gone haywire or that I’m reading the wrong end. If you’ve had that experience, you know how agonizing it is to go with the needle and against your better judgment.

Once I allowed a swamper to talk me out of using either my compass or my judgment. We had hunted until almost dark in the swamp on the Georgia side of the Savannah River between Georgia and South Carolina. We came to a trail through the swamp and I consulted my compass.

“This should lead us to high land,” I said, pointing.

“No,” he replied, indicating the opposite direction. “This is the way back to the road.”

I showed him the compass and tried to explain but he was stubborn. “I’ve lived in this swamp most of my life,” he said, “I know the way out.”

So I yielded and went with him. Half an hour later we came to the Savannah River. He stared at the rolling waters with a look of disbelief. Even then he did not concede his faulty sense of direction. “My God,” he said. “We’re in South Carolina.”

Read Next: The 11 Most Common Survival Mistakes That Will Get You Killed in the Backcountry

I watch my compass often, even when I’m in woods I know. It’s so easy to climb a ridge or go through a hollow with a different angle from the way you are traveling. And such sudden shifts of contour may turn you around.

We were 200 miles west of Anchorage, Alaska, in the expansive delta country of the Lower Kuskokwim River. The land is made up of lakes, marshes, low hills and running streams and you can get mixed up without too much effort. The guide and I had been traveling since dawn in a circle from our camp on Hewlitt Lake. I’d been watching the compass all day and late in the afternoon we waded a small stream and stood at the base of a low ridge.

“It’s getting late,” he said. “We’d better go to camp.”

I agreed and he led off in what I considered the wrong direction.

“Wait a minute,” I called. “Camp is over that way.”

“No, it’s not,” he declared emphatically. “This is the way we go.”

I showed him the compass. “I’ve been watching this all day,” I said.

“The heck with them things,” he said. “I don’t believe in all that foolishness.”

“OK, partner,” I said. “You take any direction you want. I’m going to camp.”

He hesitated a minute and then grumbled. “All right. I’ll go along. A guide is supposed to stay with his dude, no matter how crazy the guy is.”

We climbed the low hill, fought our way through a half-mile thicket of devil’s club and came out on the lake shore 100 yards above camp.

“That son of a gun was lucky to have me along,” I overheard my guide confide to the cook a little later. “Without me, him and his compass never would have found the way back here.”

If you think a map or compass is for tenderfeet or cheechakos, try being lost for a few days in the backcountry and you might change your mind.

This story was originally published in the November 1983 issue of Outdoor Life.

#8293. The Worst Part of the Trail: Shenandoah National Park

The one part of Virginia I most looked forward to was Shenandoah National Park. So many people had told me so many great things about the park before I got there. I expected breathtaking scenery; I expected it to be “cruisy;” I expected the waysides to have great blackberry milkshakes. I thought it was going to be a really wonderful time. My wife told me about her fond memories of camping there with her family, and my friend Peaks told me it had been his favorite part of the trail.

On the morning I woke up in Waynesboro at the Quality Inn, I had most of my gear ready to pack, but my clothes were hanging. I had not wanted to pay the $10 to use the coin machines, so I just scrubbed my clothes in the sink and hung them up to dry. Fortunately, everything was somehow dry by the time I woke up, and I got dressed, packed up, and went down to grab free hot breakfast, which included waffles, sausage, coffee, and orange juice. Way better than I was expecting from a budget hotel.

In the lobby, I saw BBC and Dance-On, who were going to hang around town for some extra time because BBC had a video chat for a job interview. He had shaved off his beard scruff and looked clean cut, which was unusual for most of the hikers I encountered, including myself. I wished him luck and grabbed my gear, expecting a pickup from my driver, Kevin, who had brought me in the previous day.

Kevin ran me back to the place he had picked me up at Rockfish Gap, telling me how wonderful Shenandoah National Park would be all along the way. He told me to make sure I took time to look at the signs and take pictures. My wife, wanting to relive fond memories, also wanted me to send her pictures of the park.

Can’t forget to take a picture of the map

I stepped out of the car and bid Kevin goodbye, thanking him for the ride, and I went back to the trail, stopping to look at the map and informational sign at the entrance. Shenandoah required a backwoods permit, which I had purchased online the day before in my hotel, but I had no physical copy of it, so I kept a PDF handy on my phone in case a ranger asked for it. In all my time there, none of them ever did.

The trail into Shenandoah started off with some pleasant views as I passed through sparsely wooded areas with younger trees. The weather was pleasantly cool, and spring flowers that had come and gone in the previous sections of the trail were only beginning to appear there due to cooler heights.

As midday approached, I heard a voice in the distance. It was a woman yelling, “STOP!” I became very concerned and moved ahead toward the sound, thinking I may have to intervene on some sort of abuse or phone for help. As I came closer, the periodic bursts of yelling grew louder, and I heard it again, “STOP!” followed by “Shut up!” and “We’re here for YOU!” I got closer and reached a crossing to another trail where I saw the back of a woman with a large pack and a small dog on a leash. She had turned down the side trail from the AT, periodically screaming angrily, and, as best I could tell, it was directed at her dog. As it became clear that my initial impression of her distress was mistaken, I continued on fast again, this time trying to get away from her and her outbursts.

Not long after, I crossed Skyline Drive, which was the continuation of the scenic Blue Ridge Parkway I had been criss-crossing for several days prior, reaching another scenic overlook which did not disappoint. I stopped there to have lunch and enjoy the view—a habit I had formed while passing similar overlooks in the afternoon every day. Another hiker passed by, pausing to look at the view before continuing.

View from the first overlook on Skyline Drive.

I greeted him and got his trail name, Banshee. He was a small-built young man with a lip ring and an ultralight pack. I asked if he had heard the lady shouting, and we speculated about who she was yelling at. He thought she had been walking a cat instead of a dog, but I was pretty certain I had seen a small-breed dog when I passed her.

He saw me putting a Liquid IV into my water, and asked which kind it was. He recommended the Firecracker flavor, which was his favorite, but said he also liked the lemon lime that I was using. After a few moments of chatting, he got on his way and I finished my lunch.

I hiked on for a while until I reached my goal destination of Black Rock Hut at just over 20 miles for the day. The campsites around the shelter were uneven and a lot of them were already taken. I grabbed one right across from the shelter and put my tent up right away, expecting rain that evening. I was barely set up when the rain started, but it didn’t last long. I lay on my sleeping pad for a bit before I had the motivation to get up and start making dinner at the picnic table next to the shelter.

Though there was a fire pit, the park had an ongoing fire ban. The shelter crowd picked up, and I saw my new friend Banshee along with a guy from New York City named Raja, and an older man who went by Chestnut. Someone asked him how he got his name, and he sighed. He explained that he had told another hiker some facts about the American chestnut tree, and that earned him his name. One of the other hikers made the mistake of asking him what he had told them to get the name, and we all got a full lecture on the history of the tree and how it had been destroyed by an invasive fungus, but they were trying to cross-breed it with another species of chestnut tree to get a resistant breed.

The crowd was good—a mix of section hikers with a few thru-hikers. I enjoyed the conversations and got plenty of unsolicited camping advice from Chestnut, but when the rain sprinkles picked up, I ended up going back to my tent to call it a night.

The next morning was foggy, cold, and damp. I packed up my wet tent, which had leaves and debris stuck to it, and I put my Frogg Toggs suit on before making coffee and breakfast. I accidentally burned a hole in the sleeve of the rain jacket with my stove, so I fished the duct tape out of my pack to patch it before I went on.

The fog remained for most of the morning, and the rain continued on and off throughout the day. Every time I came to a scenic view or an overlook, there wasn’t much to see but a wall of cloud. The cool weather was no fun, but at least it only bothered me when I stopped moving. Despite my best effort, my socks and shoes got wet, and my morale dropped from there.

Around midday I reached one of the Waysides with a camp store that sold food and snacks, boasting a bathroom, plumbing, and other amenities. I got there and saw someone inside, so I thought it must be open, but I was informed that they were preparing the facility to open the next day. I was able to fill up my water and throw away my trash in their bear-proof cans, so it wasn’t a total loss, but it was still unfortunate timing on an already rough day. Banshee showed up behind me and decided to hang around for a while so he could recharge his phone on the outlet that was accessible outside.

At the end of the day I reached another 20+ mile day at Hightop Hut, opting to stay in the shelter to avoid messing with my dirty, wet tent. A man hiking with his preteen child stopped by the shelter while I was eating and said hi, asking if I knew of a good place for them to set up their tent. Once they left, I didn’t hear from them for the rest of the night. The rain continued in sprinkles and picked up again during the night, leaving everything soaked when I got up in the morning.

I got ready under the shelter’s overhang as best I could, not seeing the father and young son who had camped nearby the night before. Once I got going, wearing my full rain suit, the rain continued to pick up. I had my gloves on, and they helped keep my hands warm, but they got wet along with everything else I was wearing. My Frogg Toggs rain suit kept me warm and insulated, as I’d already discovered, but it did little to keep me dry; I would either sweat from the extra heat or the rain would get through at the cuffs and neck and pool in the sleeves. I found it was usually best to wear fewer layers under it.

As the day continued, I found that most of the views were obscured by clouds and there was not much to see. I trudged through muddy ground, and between the rain and the fog, I found very little to enjoy that day, but I knew I was going to run across the Big Meadows Wayside and that drove me on. I had banked on being able to resupply there and I really wanted to try one of the famous blackberry milkshakes.

While most scenic overlooks that day were a bust, I did come to one where I had a nice view from above the clouds with the mountain peaks poking out over them. I paused to snap a pic before pushing on.

For all the complaining I did about the fog, at least this was a cool scene.

Eventually, I came to the wayside. I was drenched, so I stood outside, peeling off my layers, and I set my gear by the door, hoping it would dry out a little before I had to put it all back on. There were already wet floor signs posted, assuaging my guilt for dripping as I walked the aisles to shop.

The resupply at the Big Meadows Wayside was not as good as the FarOut comments had made it sound. Having lived in Japan and tasted good ramen for several years, I was reluctant to eat instant ramen, and it was the one popular trail food item that I had avoided. Unfortunately, it was the only carbohydrate option at the wayside. And without tuna packets, Spam singles were the lone packable protein. I loaded up with the best food items I could find and bought some postcards to send to my grandparents. I also got one for my wife, thinking if I wasn’t going to get good photos during my rainy walk through Shenandoah, then I would at least send her a postcard of a nice spring view. The older lady at the counter said they could send the postcards for me once I had them filled out.

I ordered lunch at the restaurant and filled out postcards, apologizing for all the water I dripped everywhere. My stamps had somehow gotten wet in their protective plastic bag and a few of them were ruined, but I had just enough to put on all the postcards. My food and milkshake came out, and the blackberry milkshake, though pricey, proved to be worth the stop, even if the resupply was disappointing.

When I finished my food, I went to the checkout counter and asked the clerk if she could mail my postcards. She seemed uncertain. “The other lady I spoke with earlier said it would be no problem,” I said. She went to ask her manager, and then came back out and took the postcards. I wasn’t confident that they would get sent or arrive after the younger clerk’s hesitation, but I later found out that everyone had received them.

With a heavy heart, I walked back out and started putting my wet layers back on. Nothing had dried at all. Now that it no longer had the warmth of my body heat on it, it was especially awful to put back on.

No sooner had I got situated, shivering in my cold, wet gear, than Dance-On and BBC walked up to the door of the wayside. “We got a hostel for the night,” Dance-On said.

I had not been aware that there were any good options for hostels in Shenandoah. I didn’t see any listed on FarOut at least, and I had not expected to leave the park until I walked out of it. As cold and miserable as I was, though, I considered this new information. “Do you think they have room for one more?” I asked.

Dance-On checked with the hostel and also with the shuttle driver, and before long I was no longer going to stay another cold wet night in the park.

After Dance-On and BBC got some food, I followed them to the pickup spot, where we met Nelson, their shuttle driver, and got a ride to Small Axe Farms.

The hostel was a bit of a drive from Shenandoah National Park, and the accommodations were humble. It was simply a barn, and you could hear the sheep and goats on the lower level, who got much more vocal at their feeding time. Kelly and Alec, the owners, showed us around and got us situated. I was able to set out my tent to dry, and I was hoping to brush off some of the dirt and leaf litter after it dried. Unfortunately, another rain shower hit right after I set it out.

Kelly collected laundry from all the guests, promising to return it by the following morning. I threw my gloves in with everything else, hoping to get it all dried more than washed. When it was my turn for a shower, I had been warned that the hot water was going out, but I actually got a good hot shower, which made an incredible difference.

There were several other guests I recognized at the hostel, including Raja and Chestnut. Most of them gathered at dinner, which Kelly made with heaping portions of pork chops and potatoes, allowing us all to eat our fill, and she even served dessert after.

When it was time for bed, the arrangement had been for everyone to use their own sleeping pads and blankets, so I was prepared for that, but one of the sofas was open, so I ended up sleeping on that. I missed the part where Kelly had told us to use sheets and blankets from their chest in the barn if I was going to sleep on their furniture, but one of the other guests was quick to let me know when I started putting my own sleeping quilt on the sofa. Once settled, I drifted off to sleep, warm, snug, clean, and fed, barely noticing that I was in a barn with animals and no climate control.

The next morning, I got up and checked on my tent, only to see that it was gone. I was afraid it had blown away, but I asked Alec, who told me that Kelly had brought it in because of the rain. Kelly served breakfast on her own schedule, which was much later than I liked, but, again, the meal was good and plentiful. The laundry bags began to come out, and I gathered my gear as best I could.

When Kelly gave me my tent back, it was clean and neatly folded. She had washed off all the dirt and debris for me, and dried it in her basement. I was incredibly grateful as I packed everything back into my pack and prepared to take off back to Shenandoah with my friends Dance-On and BBC.

After another bit of a drive with Nelson, we got dropped off at the same spot where he had picked us up. There, it came down to the classic debate of AT thru-hiking purity: Dance-On and BBC were already planning to road walk, which many hikers recognize as the best way to experience Shenandoah. I, however, wanted to get back to the white blazes of the official Appalachian Trail. I knew that I was going to end up skipping a small section since we had gone to the parking area to meet the driver, and I had no intention of backtracking to the wayside and finding the trail from there. The way I took ended up being about a mile shorter than if I had stayed on the trail. The way Shenandoah had been treating me, I actually didn’t mind skipping a small section of it. I didn’t even mind missing the mileage; I more than made up for it when I did the stairs of the approach trail twice back at Amicalola Falls.

The best part about getting back to Shenandoah was that the rain finally let up. I was starting to see some of the views and scenery that the park was well known for. However, it was still cool, and I realized I had forgotten to find my gloves in the laundry pile. I tried to make arrangements with Kelly to get them mailed home so I could maybe get a hold of them later. As of this writing, I still have not received them.

At the hostel, someone had told me that this would be a historic day for the park because King Charles and Camilla were going to tour the park as part of their official visit. Their schedule did not interfere with my hike, but I did run into some people whose planned day hike section was closed off.

With the rain gone, I got to see some great clear views, and there were plenty of spring flowers in bloom. I came to another wayside for lunch, meeting with Dance-On and BBC again. We planned to eat at the wayside restaurant, but it wasn’t going to open for an hour or so, so we all got coffee and sandwiches at the kiosk in the lobby.

I split from them after I finished eating, and got back on my way, planning to stop at a campsite where the AT crossed the Thornton River Trail because it was good mileage, falling between two shelters that were not far enough or too far. However, I saw from FarOut that there were some nuisance deer in the area of the campsite. The comments were actually kind of funny because there seemed to be a back-and-forth between people who favored chasing off the deer vs people who thought the deer were a delight.

Having lived in Japan for several years, I had memories of my visit to Nara Park with my wife. One of the tourist attractions at Nara Park is buying rice crackers to feed the deer, who will bow to you to get a cracker. However, as with any wild animals habituated to being fed by humans, the deer became aggressive if you weren’t giving them food, and after my wife ran out of crackers, one of the deer actually bit me because it thought I had more crackers in my pocket.

The situation at the campsite was similar, but fortunately it was a lone deer instead of hundreds of them like at Nara. However, the deer was persistent and aggressive. I set up my tent and the deer appeared shortly after. As soon as I opened my food bag, it was trying to stick its head in, so I chased it off, yelling and clapping. The deer did not go far, though, and it came back as soon as it saw that I was relaxed, hanging around and begging like an obnoxious dog.

Banshee walked by soon after, noting the deer and tsk-tsking over its obvious habituation. He went a little farther down the trail and found a campsite just out of sight of mine, but I don’t think he had the deer problem.

I finished eating and tucked in for my last night in Shenandoah. The next day I had a reservation for Mountain Home B&B, where I hoped to get a ride into town for a more suitable resupply before I started the final section of Virginia.

The deer was gone when I awoke, but it materialized, as if summoned, as soon as I started making breakfast. I got back onto the trail and ran into Dance-On and BBC again, telling them about my B&B reservation. They had been unable to reserve online because there seemed to be a shortage of bunks in the hiker room. I suggested that they come along, and we could see if they could get rooms in person.

I found my way out of Shenandoah National Park in the afternoon, reflecting that, despite how much I’d looked forward to it, I was incredibly relieved to be done with it. Between obnoxious hikers and campers, bad weather, and pesky animals, all the hype going in turned out to be a major letdown. Yet a part of me felt that maybe I had unfinished business with the park; that I would have to come back and see it all again on a better day. Reflecting on some of the cool people I met and looking through my photos of Shenandoah, I am all the more certain that it deserves another chance.

#8292. Animal Attack Roundup, Nov. 4

While they predominate the media reports, most animal attack victims are not tourists unwisely attempting to take selfies with wildlife. People who live and work every day among animals are the ones who most often face the consequences.

As expanding populations push human settlements further into wildlife habitat, we can expect to see more conflicts. Here are some recent incidents.

Photo: Wikimedia Commons/Tisha Mukherjee, CC BY-SA 4.0

In Indonesia, 24-year-old Selviana Ambu Kaka was attacked by a crocodile while washing clothes in the Bondo Kodi River. Her fiancé and his sister witnessed a large crocodile emerging from the water, biting Ambu Kaka on the leg, and dragging her into the river. They immediately alerted nearby relatives and authorities, and a search commenced.

The people of Southwest Sumba, the closest town, organized and combed the area with nets. When they found a large crocodile matching witness descriptions, they hauled it onto shore and killed it. The animal measured nearly 4.9 meters long.

Early on the morning of October 24, Ambu Kaka’s remains were found approximately 30m from the attack site. She is one of many such victims in Indonesia, which sees more saltwater crocodile attacks than any other country.

Habitat destruction is largely behind the massive number of human-crocodile conflicts. It’s an understandably hard sell, however, for conservation workers to convince locals that preventing attacks means protecting the perpetrators.

The victim had recently returned from Jakarta to become formally engaged on October 30.

Photo: Wikimedia Commons/ Rohit Gangwal, CC BY-SA 4.0

A 65-year-old farm laborer, Tulsi Rama Sawar, was killed by a leopard in state of Maharashtra, just north of Mumbai, on November 1. The noise of the attack summoned help from the locals. By the time they arrived, the leopard had fled, but Sawar was deceased. Her case comes less than a month after a leopard killed a 52-year-old woman in the same area.

Town residents are demanding immediate government action to capture the animal. If their demands for cage traps and cameras are not granted, locals threaten collective protest. The attacks represent a threat to their lives, but also their livelihoods, as farmers are unable to work the fields out of fear of attack.

Elsewhere, in Uttar Pradesh near the Nepal border, a 45-year-old farmer named Kennu fought off an attacking leopard, sustaining serious injuries. The man was working in a sugarcane field when the predator leaped out from hiding. Kennu fought back, and the animal retreated long enough for him to flee home, where family members brought him to medical care. Forestry officials have urged agricultural workers to avoid working in the fields alone.

Farm workers are not the only leopard victims, however. Early in the morning of November 4, a 15-year-old girl was dragged from her home in the Shahdol district of central India.

Saraswati Singh Gond was sleeping in bed beside her sister on their veranda, which did not have a door. A leopard entered during the night, not even waking her sister. Singh Gond’s body was found approximately 300m from the house. The search for the leopard continues.

Photo: Wikimedia Commons/Shadow Ayush, CC BY-SA 4.0

Leopards are only one of the wildlife threats that rural Indians face. A 55-year-old woman was gathering mushrooms in Utterakand in northern India on October 30 when she was attacked and killed by a wild elephant. Devaki Rana was lifted up and thrown to the ground, her son reported.

The incident occurred in one of India’s elephant corridors, which allow highly endangered Asian elephant herds to move between their fragmented habitats. The corridors are essential to conservation, but also present a concentrated area where attacks are more common.

Another fatal encounter took place in the state of Chhattisgarh in east-central India. A man of between 35 and 40 years of age, traveling by motorcycle with his nephew, came upon an elephant standing in the road. It immediately charged them, killing the uncle, while his nephew managed to hide beneath a parked truck. Eventually, the elephant left, and he was able to escape.

Locals believe that the elephant in question is one known as Kabra Kaan, which they see frequently and which has been connected with earlier incidents. The Forestry Department, however, has not confirmed this.

Elephant corridors allow them to pass between the remaining forested areas. Photo: Wildlife Trust of India

In Japan, brown bear attacks have been rising for several years. As in many places, human settlements are encroaching on brown bear territory. A decrease in farmland has left no boundary between the urban and the forested worlds. The government has responded with controversial bear culls, despite the concerns of conservation workers.

The latest incident is very different from the increasingly common attack stories. Late on the night of October 30, an express train running on Hokkaido’s Soya Line collided with a large brown bear. The body of the bear was trapped under the train, and the wheels derailed.

A brown bear became trapped beneath the wheels of Sarobetsu No 3. Photo: Hokkaido Railway Company

None of the crew or 32 passengers were injured in the crash. However, fearing more bears were in the area, officials kept everyone on the train overnight, until they could be safely extracted the following morning. Company officials have confirmed that this is the first bear-collision derailment in their nearly 40-year history.

Lou Bodenhemier holds an MA in History from the University of Limerick and a BA in Creative Writing from the University of Arizona. He’s interested in maritime and disaster history as well as criminal history, and his dissertation focused on the werewolf trials of early modern Europe. At the present moment he can most likely be found perusing records of shipboard crime and punishment during the Age of Sail, or failing that, writing historical fiction horror stories. He lives in Dublin and hates the sun.

#8290. Young Climbers Bag New Routes, Including First Ascent, in Rolwaling

An energetic foursome of young French climbers had a busy time recently in Nepal’s Rolwaling Valley, east of the Khumbu. Eric Bazon, Pierre Girot, Sophie Jacob, and Kilian Moni did two new routes, including a first ascent of a 5,205m rocky spire and one very difficult line. They then climbed another peak on a “rest” day.

As soon as the climbers reached Rolwaling, they had to change their primary goal, which was in poor condition. Their acclimatization was also progressing more slowly than expected. Instead, they focused their attention on a ridge they saw from their base camp every morning. On October 20, Bazon, Jacob, and Girot set off toward the summit, while Moni waited for them at the base.

“Before long, the climbing turned vertical, and the ridge became razor-sharp and exposed,” Bazon wrote. The climb took three days on the ridge, bivvies included, and led Bazon, Sophie Jacob, and Pierre Girot to the west summit of ChekiGo (6,128m). It took another full day and one more bivouac to reach base camp.

Cheki Go’s main summit was first climbed in 2005 by Bruce Normand of the UK and Oliver Von Rotz of Switzerland via the west face. A Spanish team led by Mikel Zabalza first reached the west summit via a direct route up the west face in 2017. The team had just returned from bagging the first ascent of Jugal II.

“It was quite an intense experience for a ‘secondary’ project: one that combined rock climbing on mediocre granite, improvised protection, and steep snow ridges, all while hauling our ropes on our backs,” said Bazon.

The ridge was technical enough to be a good start: 5c on rock and M4 on mixed terrain. In Alpine grades, the team assessed it as TD (very difficult).

Since the weather forecast looked good for another four days, the team decided to continue climbing. They split into two teams: Bazon and Girot headed for a peak previously climbed by elite American alpinists Domen Kastelic and Sam Hennessey in 2014: Chukyima Go (6,259m). Like their predecessors, the French team approached the west face from the Naa Valley in Rolwaling.

“There was this direct, narrow, and obvious couloir that simply begged to be climbed,” Bazon reported.

The climbers at an open bivy. Photo: Eric Bazon

The next morning, they found the west face in great condition, which allowed them to climb a direct route to the summit along rock cracks, steep ice, and varied mixed terrain.

It took them two days (October 27-28), with one cold bivy on the face with their feet in their backpacks, to complete the route’s 23 pitches. Their West Face Direct route is 900m long, and the team assessed it as ED (extremely difficult), with M6 on mixed sections, and an Alpine ice grade of AI5.

The photo below shows that the new French route, TchikitaMa Go, runs to the right of the previous line opened by the two Americans.

Left: the new route opened by the French team, compared, right, to the 2014 line by Domen Kastelic and Sam Hennessey. Photo: Eric Bazon/PlanetMountain

Meanwhile, Sophie Jacob and Kilian Moni went for an unclimbed peak that also rose right in front of their base camp: 5,205m Janjmu. The pair completed the first ascent on an aesthetic 600m line up the north face. They called the route The Eternal Stars (“Les etoiles eternelles”) after some friends who had recently perished.

“It felt just like being at home in the Alps, with the added challenge of high altitude,” the climbers reported. “We pushed ourselves to the limit, both physically and mentally, across demanding yet incredibly logical pitches.”

But this was still not enough for the pair. They squeezed in a final climb of Yalung Ri in what they called “a contemplative, active recovery” day. They then finished the trip by paragliding from the summit.

Kilian Moni flies from the top of Yalung Ri. Photo: Kilian Moni

#8288. Just as the Rut Kicks Off, 2 Popular Climbing Stick Companies Issued Recalls

Published Nov 5, 2026 9:55 AM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

Two hunting equipment manufacturers, Latitude Outdoors and Hunt Arsenal, have issued immediate stop-use notices following reports of potentially dangerous equipment failures. Both companies are investigating the reported issues and advising customers to discontinue use until further notice. Here’s what you need to know.

Latitude Outdoors has issued an immediate stop-use notice for its popular Carbon Synergy Climbing Sticks after receiving reports of steps moving, slipping, or detaching from the climbing stick posts. This system of climbing sticks was popular among public-land hunters and even won our review of the best climbing sticks (before these safety concerns came to light).

A company representative says the company identified the bottom step as the point of failure after several customer complaints.

Latitude acquired Treestyx LLC in late 2025 and subsequently introduced the Carbon Synergy Climbing Stick. The product retained the original Treestyx design and construction while incorporating a new knotless attachment method.

According to Latitude, earlier versions of the product met industry testing requirements, and the Carbon Synergy Climbing Sticks underwent additional testing and recertification before their release. Warranty claims involving the step-to-post connection have raised concerns about the product’s reliability, however, ultimately resulting in its recall.

Although the company said the reported failures represent a small percentage of products in use, it is advising all customers to stop using Carbon Synergy Climbing Sticks immediately.

Latitude is offering full refunds to customers, regardless of where the climbing sticks were purchased. Customers who purchased directly through Latitude can initiate a return through the company’s online portal and receive a prepaid shipping label. Refunds are also available for Carbon Synergy Illuminators and Carbon Synergy Stealth Strip Kits purchased directly from Latitude.

Customers who purchased Carbon Synergy Climbing Sticks through authorized retailers should return them to the original retailer for a refund.

Retailers have also been instructed to discontinue sales and remove affected products from inventory. For more information, visit Latitude Outdoors’ return portal and see their official recall notice.

Obviously, this poses a major problem for deer hunters who are in the field now. Some social media commenters even claimed that they were going to take the risk and use the recalled sticks anyway, since they were already on their hunting trip.

Another popular saddle hunting company, Hunt Arsenal, has also issued an immediate stop-use notice for its 2026 Maxx Step Double and Triple Aiders. According to Hunt Arsenal, the attachment cord connecting the aider to the climbing stick may fray, separate or break during use, creating a serious fall hazard. The stop-use notice advises any customer using 2026 Maxx Step Double or Triple Aiders to stop using them immediately, even if the attachment cord appears undamaged.

While the company works on a solution, Hunt Arsenal advises customers to set affected products aside and not return or discard them until further instructions are provided. Hunt Arsenal expects to provide additional information early in the week of Nov. 9, including instructions for customers who purchased directly from the company or through authorized dealers. Hunters unsure whether their aider is a 2026 model should also discontinue use until they can confirm its production year.

The company said reports received so far involve only 2026 production models, and it is investigating a possible manufacturing issue that may have damaged the cord in some units. The Maxx Step Single Aider is not affected by the notice.

Updates will be available through Hunt Arsenal’s website and social media.
