#8287. Could hiking BE any hotter ? – Stage 4 of the Hexatrek

The fourth stage of the Hexatrek takes you through gorges and valleys. With 14,389 meters (47,200 feet) of elevation gain over 500+ kilometres, it is the flattest of the six sections that make up this trail, but it is also by far the driest. Many times over the last few months, we have been warned by other hikers about the upcoming conditions. Quite a few fellow thruhikers have confided in us that they will either skip this section entirely, or flip-flop and do the Pyrenees first before (maybe) returning to complete Stage 4 in more manageable weather conditions in the autumn. We also considered this option but, after spending a week at home and having had some time to rest, we decide to continue with our straight-through SOBO hike after all.

We restart in Châteauneuf-du-Rhône, where we got off trail a week ago, and we stay at a wonderful little campground with lovely hosts. It doesn’t hurt that it is also the cheapest campground on trail so far at €13 for two people. Early on, we realise how different the hiking experience will be here compared to the Alps. The first day mostly consists of roads, wide forest paths, and rolling hills rather than lengthy climbs. Another new development is that we seem to have these routes mostly to ourselves. Well, apart from the herds of wild boars that frequently rummage around in the bushes at dusk and make us reconsider our planned sleeping places at night. Instead, we start a practice that will soon become quite normal – we nighthike. While this is not our favourite way to thruhike, it has its advantages since it is the only time of day the sun isn’t burning our skin, the air isn’t stifling, and the heat is not exhausting us.

Also early into this section we cross the Gorges de l’Ardèche, a natural reserve with a river surrounded by cliffs, forest, and scrubland. A signpost tells us that the temperature can reach 60°C here…and we can believe this easily. In general, this gorge turns out to be a surprisingly difficult part of the trail. We hadn’t anticipated the repeated technical parts along this path. It feels like the trail changes every half kilometer, from scrambling over boulders to trekking across sand, from paths that are overgrown to sheer rock faces with ladders or chains to hold on to for stability. We even had to squeeze through a tight hole in the cliffs at one point.

While most of these paths are fun and feel like doing parcour, we can’t help but feel a bit annoyed too because we didn’t anticipate our pace to slow down to 2km/h, and we certainly hadn’t planned on staying inside the reserve for the night. It’s mandatory to stay at an official campsite here and these charge €15 per person. But we don’t have another choice and at least we get to enjoy some amenities like showers and bathrooms.

When I say hiking here is always different and keeps surprising us, I do mean it. For example, we hadn’t realised that at one point we would walk right through a nudist campground, or that we would do two thigh-high river crossings in one day. This gorge keeps us on our toes. I really should mention that this particular section only took two days to cross, but those days certainly left an impression.

After the gorge, most of this stage consists of good paths and little elevation gain as promised. We are consistently able to cover 30-40km on any given day. Twice we manage to do a marathon day (42+km) which we are, given the circumstances, immensly happy and proud with. During the day,  it is usually punishingly hot. Our clothes cling to our skin, the sweat is rolling off us and burning in our eyes, and our bodies often feel sluggish and tired from heat exhaustion. But after nightfall we feel as if we are able to fly through this section.

Apart from the temperatures, some overgrown paths usually present the biggest challenge, since the water situation is thankfully easier than expected. Although we are drinking around 5 litres each per day, we get away with carrying out up to 3.5 litres per person. After some careful planning, we never get into the trouble of running out and a major concern we had prior to starting this section is resolved.

On the fun side of this stage is definitely the Gorges du Tarn. It is possible, and often recommended, to canoe on the river of this canyon. This alternate follows the trail for 21km, just on water rather than on land. The canoe rental companies have adapted to thruhikers and offer luggage transportation to the end point where they pick up the boats again. It is a gorgeous day out on the water and a fun way to make the miles. It is still strenuous muscle work and we did get stuck here and there due to low water levels and had to paddle quite a bit over the course of the journey.

Stage 4 has a multitude of suprises for us, one of which came as a bit of a shock…

Who would have thought that there are scorpions in southern France?

The natural surroundings here are truly fascinating, as are the urban areas, which I will be covering in the next post.

#8284. Duo Completes Baffin Island Circuit By Skiing, Hiking, and Packrafting

Caleb McDaniels, 25, and Henry Penfold, 22, have completed their impressive expedition around Baffin Island. The Americans combined skiing, hiking, and packrafting to almost circle the world’s fifth-largest island. McDaniels told ExplorersWeb they did about 20% skiing and the rest was evenly split between backpacking and packrafting.

The pair began and ended in Iqaluit, Nunavut’s capital. The final section of their trip was also the longest, a 1,130km stretch with no villages after Igloolik to resupply. They made light work of it, knocking it out in 40 days and bringing their total distance to 3,262km over 145 days, from their late May start to their return to Iqaluit in mid-October. By then, the oncoming Arctic winter gave them few hours of light to work with.

The pair’s completed route around Baffin Island. Photo: Caleb McDaniels

With no resupply points, the pair left Igloolik with 82kg of food. They hoped to do it in seven weeks but brought even more food, because they weren’t sure how long that giant giant section would actually take, explained Caleb McDaniels.

“With no way to carry that much weight in our packs, we loaded up our packrafts and paddled the first 400 miles [644km]. Then, for the final 300 miles [483km], we heaved on our packs to walk overland,” they explained.

The paddling portion went quickly, aided by some ingenuity. “Much of the time, we were able to sail using our trekking poles as masts and panels cut out of an old tent for sails. Speeding along at over five mph, we did some incredible downwinding, spray flying from our bows.”

Using makeshift sails. Photo: Caleb McDaniels

They also effectively halved the 480km trek by packrafting over two large lakes, including Nettilling, the world’s largest lake on an island. Yet there was no way to ease the final 160km slog into Iqaluit.

Postholing through early winter snow back to Iqaluit. Photo: Caleb McDaniels

“It was more of a postholing session — we slowly picked our way across snow-covered boulder fields and partly frozen marshlands. Constantly breaking through thin ice over the tundra marshes, we walked in our drysuits to keep our legs and feet dry. Each morning required half an hour of chipping ice and melting out our shoes, which invariably froze solid,” they said.

McDaniels and Penfold had planned a roughly circular route around the island, but “we weren’t trying to circumnavigate Baffin,” McDaniels told ExplorersWeb. Two previous parties had circumnavigated the island by dogteam, but McDaniels and Penfold’s route was driven by aesthetic considerations rather than to satisfy a catchy trip definition.

Slogging overland. Photo: Caleb McDaniels

They chose their route after looking at satellite images and enjoyed both spectacular scenery and some special wildlife sightings, including at least one that was a little too close for comfort.

“One morning, as I went to fill our water bottles, I stumbled upon a sleeping polar bear hidden behind a low rise. Only a few yards away, it lifted its massive white head and glared at me for a moment before returning to its nap in the sun,” McDaniels wrote. “I carefully retreated behind the rise and yelled over to Henry to get the shotgun and flares out just in case. We quickly packed our boats and got on the water.”

In Foxe Basin, they almost collided with a sleeping walrus, and on Nettilling Lake, they met one of the resident seals. “He was immensely curious and not at all afraid. He swam around our boats for half an hour, playing with our stern lines and swimming back and forth between us. At one point, I put my hand into the water, and he brushed it with his nose!”

Martin Walsh is a writer and editor for ExplorersWeb.

Martin spent most of the last 20 years backpacking the world on a shoestring budget. Whether it was hitchhiking through Syria, getting strangled in Kyrgyzstan, touring Cambodia’s medical facilities with an exceedingly painful giant venomous centipede bite, chewing khat in Ethiopia, or narrowly avoiding various toilet-related accidents in rural China, so far, Martin has just about survived his decision-making.

Based in Da Lat, Vietnam, Martin can be found in the jungle trying to avoid leeches while chasing monkeys.

#8283. The 10 Best Rimfire Scopes of 2026: Budget to Precision Optics Tested

Published Nov 5, 2026 10:12 AM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

A rimfire rifle used to be the next step up from a Red Ryder. You’d grab it to plink at the range, teach a new shooter, or shoot a few squirrels. But rimfire rifles have evolved, and so has the entire hobby of shooting them. It’s now completely normal to expect a rifle to shoot 1-inch groups at 100 yards and a range session to stretch from 25 to 300 yards.

Scopes have kept pace with the rifles. You might find a basic 3-9x on a stock 10/22, but you won’t find one on someone’s RimX build. Today’s rimfire shooter wants close-focusing adjustable parallax, a first-focal-plane reticle, and plenty of elevation travel to reach well beyond 100 yards.

I selected the best rimfire scopes with those demands in mind, but I haven’t forgotten the utilitarian and budget friendly scopes. Here are my top picks from my testing and our optics tests.

I use rimfires for hunting, fun shooting and occasionally competition. I’d typically need at least two scopes to cover those pastimes: a handy 3-9x for hunting and a 3-15x for shooting small targets at extended ranges. But the Nightforce NX6 2-12×42 F1 can take on all of those uses, and do them well.

We tested the entire NX6 line at Outdoor Life’s 2026 optics test, and I was thoroughly impressed with the 5-30x56mm F1’s ability to ring steel at 300 yards and focus down to 11 yards. That scope is a bit big for my typical rimfire uses. The 3-18x is a highly versatile option that Outdoor Life Editor-in-Chief, Alex Robinson, recently picked as the best high-end scope for deer hunting, but it’s still a bit heavy for my taste. The 2-12x is my pick for the ultimate rimfire scope because it’s ideally suited for small-game hunting, plinking and shooting steel beyond 100 yards. While it’s not the scope you want for hitting tiny targets at long range, it has enough magnification to hit rimfire-sized targets around 100 yards, and I routinely shoot my KYL rimfire rack with it at 50 yards.

The scope’s attributes extend beyond its versatility. It has decent glass, an incredibly easy-to-use zero stop, close focusing and excellent tracking. Some might find the FC-MRx reticle too busy, but I like it for fast holdovers and its reference points for wind holds.

I currently have the NX6 2-12×42 on a CZ 457 American with a Proof Research carbon-fiber barrel. The rifle is a hammer and very light, and the NX6 is right at home on it.

Read Next: CZ 457 American Review: Quarter-Inch Groups Right Off the Rack

If you’re looking for to compete in NRL22, there are several excellent scopes to choose from. But the Razor HD Gen III 6-36×56 is my overall best pick. It focuses down to 10 yards, has 36 MRAD of elevation adjustment, and plenty of magnification for shooting matchsticks and other tiny targets. The new VMR-5 reticle is a nice clean reticle that’s ideal for people who prefer dialing and you can still get the EBR-7 reticle if you prefer holdovers.

Here’s what optics editor, Andrew McKean, had to say about the Razor HD Gen III after our optics test:

Vortex might have been satisfied with simply upgrading the reticle inside its flagship precision scope, which has won enough PRS and NRL matches to qualify as a class leader. But with the new Gen III version of the venerable Razor HD, Vortex has created a new turret system that is precise, smart, and innovative.

The heart of the turret update is what Vortex calls its L-TEC+ zero system in which relaxing a single set screw allows users to make fast and precise turret adjustments. The system allows zeros to be established between the turrets’ .1 MRAD clicks, meaning that shooters no longer have to be satisfied with turrets set a half click above or below their true zero, a fudge factor that is more problematic the farther you shoot.

The operation takes a bit of getting used to. Tester John B. Snow, thinking the external slot on the head of the turret was designed to accept a beefy screwdriver bit, reefed on our sample, breaking the pot-metal, before reading the instructions and learning that once the retaining screw is loosened, the turret moves easily with only fingertip tension. Our other rifle-range revelation: The creepy caterpillar-looking grub that emerges from the base of the turret is not an embedded chrysalis but rather a smart revolution indicator that becomes fully emergent on the third full rotation of the elevation turret.

For the smart turret updates, the Vortex wins our Innovation Award, but that’s hardly the only update to this excellent scope. The new EBR-7D reticle is a marvel of efficient simplicity. Built around a .03 MRAD red-illuminated center dot with open aiming cross, the reticle’s elevation steps are in .2 MRAD hatches, and windage steps in .2 MRAD dots. We would like to see slightly bolder indexing, as the reticle references were hard to see below about 11-power.

The image delivered by the Razor HD is one of the best in the class, and we liked the turret indexing and smart and useful pull-to-turn illumination control. With a very close parallax adjustment and the infinitely adjustable zero, this would make an excellent rimfire competition scope.

Vortex is understandably proud of this scope, but with a retail price of around $4,000, we think it’s pretty pricey compared with its peer group. — Andrew McKean

There’s not much innovative or surprising here, just a basic duplex reticle inside a straight-ahead scope with decent turrets and a durable build. Backed by an excellent warranty.

If simplicity is the pathway to versatility, then the Vortex Crossfire II is at home on a small-game bolt rifle or a fast-shooting AR. It might not have the chops for precision work, but the duplex reticle is fast and reliable. The controls are a little mushy, but the eye relief and eye box are both forgiving and the fixed parallax makes it a great plinking scope. — Andrew McKean

Another in a long line of solid, bright Hawke scopes. This sub-$450 Vantage 30 is an upscale sibling to the Vortex Crossfire HD 6-18×50. Both sport useful second focal-plane BDC reticles with center-dot illumination. But the Hawke brings a little more sophistication to its controls, with exposed pull-to-turn turrets, immersive field of view, and a floating center-dot aiming point that lights up in either green or red.

Optics are good but not great. The illumination is good but we wish it was more intense to boost visibility in bright sunlight. And turret tracking started to slip a bit at the very end of its elevation travel.

But the Hawke impressed us with its smooth, tactile controls, and the BDC reticle is fast, with MOA-based references that correspond to the drop of standard center-fire loads. With a 50-yard zero with our standard 40-grain CCI .22 LR ammunition, we easily stretched the reticle to 300 yards by dialing 35 MOA of elevation and holding another 10 MOA. That’s impressive range for the scope-and-rimfire combo.

“It’s a simple, straightforward hunting scope that’s priced about right,” says tester Dale Manning. Enough said. — Andrew McKean

One of the surprises of the test is how testers universally fell in love with this little, versatile scope. On the surface, it seems like an oddball. Less than 10 inches long, it requires a cantilever mount to fit most rifle receivers, and it looks more like an LPVO than a serious precision scope.

But once you get behind the GPO Centuri Compact, a whole world is revealed through the excellent milling reticle. At lower magnifications with the illumination at its highest intensity, the reticle functions as a point-and-shoot red-dot sight. But at higher magnifications, starting about 10x, the reticle’s precision references become visible. A series of .1 MRAD hashes enables pinpoint aiming. For shooters who prefer to dial, the big exposed turrets pull to turn and move with authority. A smart revolution indicator pops up on the elevation turret when shooters enter the second revolution.

​If you’d rather tune the reticle to your specific load, GPO offers a free custom ballistic turret with purchase. That’s an additional value for a scope that’s already priced fairly at about $650.

Testers debated the best use cases for the Centuri Compact. Some felt it’s best suited to an AR carbine. Others wanted it on their big-woods whitetail rifle, and still others felt it would be an excellent scope for stalking elk in dark timber. That latter use is enabled with a smart illumination that lights up the floating center dot and inverted horseshoe. The red illumination is infinitely adjustable thanks to a rheostat control.

​The eyebox is stingy at higher magnifications, which forces shooters to have perfect alignment. But that’s a minor miss. The scope garnered enough pluses to finish in the top third of the field of scopes that are much more squarely configured for hunting.— Andrew McKean

The Busnell R7 won the editor’s choice award for being the best hunting scope of the year. While it’s an excellent big-game optic, it’s also right at home on a rimfire rifle. Here’s McKean’s take on this excellent piece of glass:

With this big, bright, and surprisingly sophisticated R7, Bushnell is restoring its relevance as a first-order hunting optic brand. The first focal-plane scope has an open tree-style reticle that’s anchored by an illuminated segmented circle and floating center dot that enables precision work as well as fast holdover and wind-informed shots at game.

For hunters and target shooters who would rather dial, the pull-to-turn elevation turret is nicely indexed and moves with positivity. The windage dial is capped.

Bushnell has invested heavily in the R7 line, which is the best of the Good/Better/Best product-line hierarchy that started with the R3 a couple years ago and continued with the R5 last year. The company has four different configurations of the R7, released just this month: a 1-8×24 LPVO, a 2-10×42, and a 3-15×50 in addition to the 4-20×50. The lower magnification scopes are available in second-plane reticles, but the two higher-mag versions come in either first- or second-plane reticles and either MIL or MOA, giving buyers a crazy number of variations on the platform.

We tested the second-plane MOA version of the 4-20×50, but for its versatility, performance on a wide range of targets and distances, and its flawless handling, we named the FFP R7 not only best Bushnell in the test, but the best overall hunting scope in the field of 25 excellent competitors. They include Nightforce’s new NX6, Leupold’s VX-4HD, and Zeiss’s new V3 families, along with some excellent submissions from Vortex, Trijicon, and Burris.

For its overall performance, the Bushnell R7 4-20×50 is this year’s Editor’s Choice winner as the top hunting scope of 2026.

The scope stacked points with a combination of good ED Prime glass, clear indexing on its controls, tight and positive turret and focus controls, and an illuminated Hybrid Dot Tree reticle that splits the difference between a precision competition and a hunting reticle. Its zero stop, which we’re glad to see on this type scope, is a 6-screw affair that’s a hassle to set, but works wonderfully as a solid backstop on elevation turret travel.

We worried about the durability of the R7, but it passed our inaugural drop test without skipping a beat. We dropped the scope three times from three feet on concrete covered by a 2-inch pad, and the Bushnell retained its zero.

Of course, our test teased out some deficiencies. The reticle references aren’t especially visible until about 7x, and I’d like to see one or two more intensity steps to the center-dot and segmented circle illumination to make them pop in daylight.

But if you’re looking for a rimfire or long-range competition scope that you can easily transition into a big-game hunt, this is a wonderful choice. The price, at about $950, is fair for the versatility and fine handling of this true crossover scope. — Andrew McKean

Set-it-and-forget-it hunters will appreciate this solid, honest scope for its lack of adornments. No illumination. A simple plex reticle in the second focal plane. It’s like the Fullfield mentioned above but with better glass and controls.

But hunters who are practiced at ranging a target, then dialing an aiming solution based on ballistic solvers will go crazy for this new configuration of the venerable Burris Veracity. The elevation knob is exposed, nicely indexed, and ready to dial. A little too ready, as it doesn’t lock. For some OL testers, that’s a problem, as an exposed turret can easily get pushed off zero given the hard knocks of the field.

But Burris has that figured out, too, with a zero stop that ensures a return to zero. It’s a tedious 6-screw affair to set, but once the zero stop is established, it is a rock-solid baseline for dialing.

​Given the wave of hunting scopes containing first-plane reticles with busy windage and elevation references and illumination modules, this iteration of the Veracity is refreshing. But it also forces users into either dialing for distance or sticking with the single aiming point at the crosshairs. We’d rather see the 3-15×44 Veracity with the illuminated RC-MOA (Rapid Cross) reticle that gives hunters the option of dialing or using reticle references to hold for elevation and wind.

We quibble a bit at the $1,000 price for such a stripped-down scope, but the turret tracking was among the best in the field, and Burris’s “Knob Synergy” elevation dial is tight, positive, and the low-profile build won’t hang up in the field. All in, the 3-15×44 version of the Veracity is a welcome addition to the 2.5-12×42 and 5-25×50 versions. — Andrew McKean

Combining simple controls and a modest but versatile magnification range, this durable scope is perfect for just about any .22 or .17, whether for small-game hunting, plinking, or most precision target work. It has good glass, repeatable controls, and enough holdover references on the vertical stadia that, with some practice, you can extend your range out to 100 yards and longer. At close to $300, it’s priced in the meaty middle of the market and can easily transition from a first-gun optic to just about any other rifle, whether a rimfire or not.

Here’s a rimfire scope for just about any purpose. This outwardly pedestrian optic has a lot going on between a surprisingly precise second-plane reticle, bright glass, and fun indexing on the nicely tactile turrets. The best thing you can say about any scope is that it is consistent, and the VX-Freedom delivers bullets with pleasing reliability. It’s a good rabbit and squirrel scope. Still, the MOA-based references on the vertical crosshair make it a decent option for engaging distant targets, which means you don’t have to invest in a ponderously big first-plane target scope to take titles at NRL22 competitions. Lastly, the Leupold rimfire scope brings the company’s good glass and an excellent warranty.— Andrew McKean

Tract’s 22 FIRE series has a full series of scopes for .22 and .17 shooters, but this AO model (it stands for Adjustable Objective) is the most versatile scope in the line from the direct-to-consumer brand. The duplex reticle features a fine crosshair with a .25 MOA center dot, which allows for full view of the target and precise bullet placement, which competitive bullseye target shooters will appreciate.

The adjustable objective enables precise focus for targets inside 10 yards all the way out to infinity, a feature you don’t often see on rimfire-specific scopes. The objective focus is a little clunky compared with the side parallax of most modern scopes, but it works well and further enables precise shooting. At about $275 it’s not a cheap scope, but the glass is good, the controls are some of the best in the business, and the precision it allows also makes it a killer squirrel scope. — Andrew McKean

The Burris Eliminator 6 is the easy button for long-range shooting. It ranges, calculates ballistics, and tells you where to aim. Here’s what shooting editor, John B. Snow, said about the Eliminator 6 in his precision scope buying guide:

This is the most innovative scope in this roundup. Burris has long been a category leader in scopes with integrated rangefinders, and Eliminator 6 is the newest iteration of that tech. Once the scope has been fed a ballistic profile and zeroed — neither process is overly complicated — it delivers impressive point-click-and-shoot capability.

The second focal plane reticle contains a multitude of LED illumination points. When you range your target — which is done via a large button on the left side of the scope or through a remote Bluetooth switch — one of those dots lights up indicating your hold. It is remarkably idiot-proof.

I know we live in an age of technological marvels, but the fact that you can roll through the scope’s magnification range and the aiming dot will slide up and down the crosshair continuously displaying the correct hold is remarkable.

Targets beyond 1,000 yards can become difficult to laze, and you’ll likely need to fine-tune your ballistic profile to keep the scope’s solutions spot-on. But within 800 yards this system couldn’t be quicker or easier to employ. — John B. Snow

Your first consideration if you’re in the market for a rimfire rifle scope is how well it will perform with the short-range capabilities of the caliber. You probably don’t need a ton of magnification or reticle references if all you want is to shoot tin cans or 50-meter bullseye targets. But the world of rimfire shooting is evolving to look a lot like long-distance center-fire precision shooting, with all sorts of precision rimfire competitions and games that put a premium on both short-range and long-range precision. For backyard plinkers, you probably just want a simple scope with a duplex reticle, but for the latter, you’re going to want a first-plane reticle with lots of turret adjustment. Then there are the pure small-game scopes. These are lower-magnification optics with just enough reticle references to get you on game and maybe make longer shots, head-shooting squirrels, for instance.

For small-game hunting, I want a scope that gets on target fast, has a reticle that “pops” from the background, but has enough references for me to place bullets precisely out to about 75 or 100 yards. In this collection, the standout hunting scope is Bushnell’s Trophy Quick Acquisition (QA), a 1-6×24 marvel that points quickly, has an illuminated center dot for low-light work, and enough holdover references for longer shots. Others worth a look: Vortex’s Crossfire II, and Tract’s 22 FIRE. At the other end of the spectrum is EOTECH’s expensive 1-10×24 Vudu, which doubles as a marvelous AR optic. Or consider Leupold’s VX-Freedom. Its simple duplex reticle is fast and reliable.

I like lower-power scopes for most rimfire work, whether that’s hunting or target shooting. A 2-7-power or even 1-8-power will give you all the magnification you need for most purposes. But if you’re interested in the precision rimfire competitions, then you’re going to want more magnification to really see the nuances of distant targets. For those times, I’d go with a 5-20-power or 4-16-power range, and make sure that precision target scopes also have manual focus—often called parallax—to bring targets of whatever distance into crisp focus.

The price of rimfire scopes ranges all the way from about $100 up to nearly $2,000. There are problems with both ends of that spectrum, just as there are great deals as long as you know what attributes you want and how you’ll use the scope. Starting at the lower end of the price spectrum, I’d be a little leery of super-cheap scopes, simply because they are probably made with substandard components and may not be as durable as higher-priced models. If you spend under $100 on a scope, make sure it has a good warranty that will cover any breakage or malfunctions. But you can buy a lot of scope for under $200. Scopes in this roundup include Bushnell’s Trophy QA and Vortex’s Crossfire II, and both the Leupold VX-Freedom and Tract’s 22 FIRE AO are both priced around $300 and offer excellent durability, utility, and warranties. Precision rimfire scopes can be especially expensive, largely because their precision controls and components are built to a higher standard. Still, the Sightmark Presidio, priced under $400, and the Vortex Strike Eagle are both worth looking at for budget precision options. On the other end of the spectrum, both the EOTECH Vudu and Blackhound Emerge offer tons of precision for rimfire shooters, but have all the attributes to transition once you move up to center-fire precision target shooting.

Somehow, the optics industry has squeezed all the fun out of rimfire shooting. Instead of cheap, reliable, and utilitarian rifles, we now have fancy chassis rifles with all the attributes of their big-bore brethren. And prices to match. We’ve complicated what was once the most fun and simple type of shooting into rigorous competition. That’s all great if you want to make .22 shooting into a serious thing, but don’t forget that rimfires are the gateway for most shooters and hunters into our community, and the scopes and rifles that are the best for new shooters are often the most simple and cheap. So read this review with a little bit of skepticism. There are optics for every stage in a shooter’s evolution, but maybe pay special attention to those fun, simple, gateway scopes.

Scott Einsmann is Outdoor Life’s gear editor. He oversees the gear team’s editors and writers who are subject matter experts in bows, knives, hunting, fishing, backpacking, and more. He lives in Richmond, Virginia with his wife and two bird dogs.

Andrew McKean is Outdoor Life’s hunting and conservation editor, drilling into issues that affect wildlife, wildlands, and the people who care about them. He’s also OL’s optics editor, helping readers to make informed buying decisions.

#8281. Americans Bag Major First Ascent in Pakistan

Americans Dane Steadman and Cody Winckler, awarded with a Piolet d’Or in 2025 after the first ascent of Yashkuk Sar, have done a similar monster 1,800m-long new route on the north face of Sosbun Brakk (6,414m). This time, Grant Stewart joined them for this off-season climb in the Karakoram.

This first ascent of the peak’s north face included difficulties up to M7, WI5. The climbers had to overcome several obstacles before even setting foot on the face. Like many other alpine-style teams this season, they were originally planning to climb another peak. But instead of adapting because of washed-out trails, they had bureaucratic issues. Their permit, obtained 10 months earlier, was revoked some weeks before their departure. They had to quickly find a different goal.

Meanwhile, the airline misplaced Winckler’s baggage — every adventurer’s nightmare. Somehow, the outfitter sent it to base camp some days later. Then, Steadman had to overcome serious Acute Mountain Sickness in base camp. Their acclimatization was hampered by freak spells of bad weather. Finally, the line on Sosbun Brakk they initially chose was too hard and risky because of a hanging serac they only spotted after they began.

The team’s lonely base camp. Photo: Dane Steadman

“Back at BC, it was time to rest, regroup, and contemplate a totally different line that we’d seen from on the wall, which gave us new hope,” Steadman recalled.

Off to the north face. Photo: Dane Steadman

On October 1, the three climbers set off on that potential new line. “Instead of angling left up hard mixed ground above the cone as before, we made an arcing traverse right, across an ice apron, to gain runnels on the right side of the face,” Steadman explained.

The team gained 800m on that first day and set their first bivouac on a snowy arete, just in time to be slammed by a violent storm that kept them in their tent the whole next day.

Steep mixed terrain. Photo: Dane Steadman

A tarp to protect the team’s bivouac from falling spindrift. Photo: Dane Steadman

“In the morning, we made a gamble for the top by leaving the tent and starting up a massive gully system,” Steward wrote. “At its top, we reached another dead end in a huge serac barrier. To escape this, Dane committed to a visionary pitch, casting off up a blank slab to eventually reach an ice smear.”

Chaotic, difficult rocky sections. Photo: Dane Steadman

“A huge serac to our right and smooth slabs out left posed a serious question; eight meters of sideways teetering on tiny gneissic edges and a miraculous rock thread were the answer,” said Steadman.

“We continued up the massive hanging glacier to reach the hallucinatory final headwall of steep ice/mixed climbing and mushroom-weaving lunacy,” Stewart continued. “One final traverse with 1,800m of exposure under our feet and a magically appearing, dead-vertical ice tongue led us to the summit ridge.”

A totally vertical section. Photo: Grant Stewart

“The wild terrain on the upper mountain took longer than we wanted,” Steadman admitted. By the time they finally reached the summit, it was 4 pm, the storm was coming the following day, and they still had a long way (and many rappels) down.

Summit picture on Sosbun Brakk. Left to right, Dane Steadman, Grant Stewart, and Cody Wrincker. Photo: Dane Steadman

“The sun would set around 6 pm, so we threaded the first of 35 rappels and started down. Long after dark, we finally arrived back at our bivy ledge at around 5,800m,” Steadman recalled.

The storm was not supposed to start until noon the following day, but it was already snowing at 8 am, with still 1,200 vertical meters of descent to go.

Rappelling down the route. Photo: Dane Steadman

“Before long, we were caught in a proper storm,” Stewart explained. “We committed to a faster and hopefully safer descent by rappelling down the west rib to the Sokha/Sosbun col. By the time we reached the col, we could barely communicate over the screaming southwest wind.”

After some scary rappels in high winds down the serac band, the climbers finally reached a sheltered section of the face. They still had to deal with heavy spindrift coming from above until finally, at around 4 pm, they touched down on the glacier. And yet, the adventure was not over — especially for Grant Stewart:

Following Dane, I took maybe 10 steps when I felt the ground under me crack. Instinctively, I jumped and landed on my stomach as a huge crevasse swallowed the ground behind me. Soaking wet, we began postholing into the wan light of a mesmerizing white out.

[We stuck] to the center of the glacier as avalanches rumbled down all around in the whirling snow. After a strange eternity, the ragged colors of a tent appeared and we were greeted by ecstatic dancing, big hugs, and endless cups of chai from (our BC crew) Ibrahim and Idrees.

Happy climbers and base camp crew after a safe return from the summit. Photo: Dane Steadman

The team didn’t report their success and the details of the climb until they returned home. And then, the first words of appraisal were not for the route itself, but for the mountains and people of Gilgit-Baltistan.

“It’s a unique place…where continents and cultures collide. Trips there, while often difficult, are rewarding in ways hard to describe simply,” Steadman said. This was his third trip to the Karakoram, a place he has fallen in love with.

Angela Benavides graduated university in journalism and specializes in high-altitude mountaineering and expedition news. She has been writing about climbing and mountaineering, adventure and outdoor sports for 20+ years.

Prior to that, Angela Benavides spent time at/worked at a number of local and international media. She is also experienced in outdoor-sport consultancy for sponsoring corporations, press manager and communication executive, and a published author.

#8278. Weekend Warm-Up: Assynt

Assynt, subtitled “Home is where the croft is,” is a short documentary that brings viewers to the Scottish Highland community of Assynt, where residents live on traditional crofts.

The croft is a uniquely Scottish term, describing the smaller, less fertile plots of land that poorer people were forced onto, following the infamous Highland Clearances of the 18th and 19th centuries. Crofters lived on their crofts and farmed for subsistence, grazing sheep on shared land. Unable to support themselves on the croft alone, most also worked in fishing, kelp, or peat to support themselves.

It was a very hard life. But Lewis MacAskill, whom the viewer is soon introduced to, doesn’t see it that way. He is one of just over a thousand residents of Assynt, who chose to stay and continue the crofting tradition.

“I regard the croft as an extension of who I am as a person,” MacAskill explains.

The small community of Assynt. Photo: Screenshot

MacAskill introduces us to some of the other members of the community. Anna is a sheepdog owner and trainer, whom we see herding sheep using the same techniques people here have used for centuries. Stuart is a passionate fisherman, who shares his love of Assynt’s natural landscape with his young son.

We also meet some of the creatives who have, MacAskill says, been drawn by the unique landscape and material culture. We see a potter using local materials, a fiddler, and a spinner on her spinning wheel.

The spinning wheel came to Europe from the Middle East by the 13th century, and was widely adopted by the 18th century, replacing the older drop spindle and distaff. Photo: Screenshot

MacAskill moved to the croft a decade ago, and doesn’t regret it. Having grown up visiting every summer, he has always felt drawn to the land and knows others feel the same. But a small, isolated community like Assynt is constantly in danger of depopulation. MacAskill hopes that people keep choosing to move back and stay, heeding the same call he did.

The film ends on this note, with a montage of scenes from life in Assynt and the landscape it sits in, while an elderly crofter sings a traditional Scottish song of homecoming.

Lou Bodenhemier holds an MA in History from the University of Limerick and a BA in Creative Writing from the University of Arizona. He’s interested in maritime and disaster history as well as criminal history, and his dissertation focused on the werewolf trials of early modern Europe. At the present moment he can most likely be found perusing records of shipboard crime and punishment during the Age of Sail, or failing that, writing historical fiction horror stories. He lives in Dublin and hates the sun.

#8277. My Biggest Backpacking Gear Hits and Misses of 2026

It’s time to make one of my favorite videos of the year, which is my roundup of all of my favorite and least favorite gear from the 2026 hiking season.

And this year, I put in hundreds of miles. I hiked the JMT, I hiked a large portion of the San Diego Trans County Trail, I did a large section of the Colorado Trail, so I definitely had the chance to put in plenty of miles, plenty of field time with these pieces of gear, and I’m excited to tell you guys what I loved and what I really did not like this season.

Everything from tents to backpacks to new apparel, new fleeces, new mid-layers, new base layers, new electronics, new sunglasses, all sorts of new stuff. And I have a lot of thoughts, some of them great, some of them not so great, but I’m excited to hear what you guys think, so let’s get into it.

The first piece of gear that I’m really excited to talk to you guys about today is what I’m currently wearing, and that is my Alpha 60 from SamBob.

Now, I have had experience with Alpha Direct layers in the past, but this is SamBob’s lightest Alpha Direct model, the Alpha 60. They also offer an Alpha 90, an Alpha 120.

But specifically when I picked up this layer, I was looking for a mid-season light mid-layer fleece that I wouldn’t overheat in, that I could still hike in, that was breathable, that was quick to dry, that was lightweight, that was versatile, that was comfortable enough that I could wear it during the day, at night when I went to bed, as a PJ layer, all of the above.

So ultimately, I was really happy with this piece of gear.

Alpha Direct is not the kind of thing that I tend to turn my nose at. I know that it is a controversial piece of gear just because it is a bit more on the premium side. It is not a cheap fleece by any means.

But for me, it is definitely light enough that it is worth the extra money for me. And this is actually the third piece of SamBob gear that I own. I am a SamBob diehard. I think they make great stuff.

And all of the normal pain points that you tend to see with Alpha Direct, where folks are complaining about the durability and the longevity, I have yet to have those issues.

Again, I have not brought an Alpha Direct layer on a full thru-hike yet. I’ve brought some Alpha Direct blends, and I’ll talk about that in a minute.

But largely, I’m not seeing any wear and tear, I’m not seeing any holes, it’s not overly stinky, and I think it’s fashionable enough that I can wear it in day-to-day life.

So I love this piece of gear. I take it on trail, I take it off trail.

So yeah, that’s all to say I am a huge fan of this Alpha Direct 60 from SamBob. It has not let me down. It is breathable, it is light, it is ultralight, it’s great.

Huge fan. It will continue to come out with me in the field on future trips.

Now let’s talk about a piece of technology that I am not crazy about.

I’ve complained about this piece of gear before, but it’s gonna get me complaining about it two years in a row because it once again failed me this year.

This is the Nitecore 10,000 mAh battery pack charger.

Now, there’s some obvious upsides to this piece of gear.

If you are the kind of person who is not vlogging and you just need your phone to navigate and take photos every now and then, this is probably a perfectly reasonable option for you.

But for me, I have had this battery pack not charge or lose a charge oddly fast several times on me, to the point where it put me in dangerous situations where I realized, oh my God, my battery didn’t charge last night, I’m out here for two more days, how am I going to use FarOut?

And then I would have to massively ration my battery power, which as somebody who vlogs for work is super inconvenient and kind of scary at times, especially as an often solo female hiker.

So the Nitecore has failed me enough times now that I’ve kind of become an Anker convert.

This right here is an Anker battery. They offer them in the 20,000s. It’s definitely a heavier option. This is their 10,000.

So yeah, when you compare them, you can see the obvious upsides of bringing the Nitecore.

But what I found is that when this one doesn’t charge or loses a charge oddly quickly, this one holds it.

So I think I’m reaching for ANKER more these days. But again, it’s quite possible that I’ve just had bad luck with Nitecore.

I know plenty of people that swear by them. I use their headlamp. I love Nitecore headlamps.

They make great stuff. But in this case, I’ve had this specific piece of equipment fail me enough times that I am no longer a Nitecore stan.

And if you don’t know what a stan is, it’s just a fan.

All right, this right here is the BearVault BV ONE.

This is a pretty flashy, pretty hot new item this year that a lot of folks were talking about. Very buzzy.

It is a convertible bear can that has the ability to both screw up to hold a maximum of four days’ food and to screw down to carry just one day’s food.

And this is really appealing because if you’re going to be carrying this super big, super bulky piece of gear, then you want to know that you can shrink it down into your backpack and it’ll fit comfortably, especially as those days go on.

There’s nothing worse than being out there for like four or five days. You barely have any food left in your bear can, but it’s still super heavy and still taking up so much room in your pack.

This piece of gear weighs just about two pounds. I really like how flexible it is. I can bring this out for a weekender.

I can bring this out for a longer trip. I don’t have to have, you know, every bear can in the BearVault lineup. I can just have this one for the most part and then maybe a BV500 for those much longer trips.

So yeah, shout out the BV ONE. Not really a lot to complain about beyond the fact that I’m a little dumb and sometimes I screw it the wrong way and then I’m like, ah, that’s annoying.

So seriously, not much to complain about.

It is important to note, though, that this piece of gear is not approved for every single area where a bear can is required.

While it is an approved piece of gear by the Interagency Grizzly Bear Committee as being a proven tool for keeping bears out of your food, it is not necessarily an approved piece of gear by areas like Kings Canyon and/or Sequoia National Park or Yosemite.

These areas have their own unique lists for what are approved bear food prevention methods, and this one is not on it yet.

So if you are planning to do something like the John Muir Trail, make sure you do your research and make sure that the bear can that you bring and carry with you the entire time is an approved bear can.

That is a totally hypothetical situation that I just presented to you.

Now let’s talk about a piece of gear that I both loved and hated this season.

This right here, the Mountain Hardwear Alakazam.

I wrote an entire review on the Alakazam right here on the The Trek — check it out.

I’m really excited to talk about this. This is a piece of gear that I used to love and now hate.

Now, if I was talking to me two years ago who carried a Katadyn for like 99% of the Appalachian Trail and I was saying, I hate this filter, she heard me saying that, she’d be like, girl, you’re crazy.

I brought this water filter out for four days on the Colorado Trail and by day two, it was completely clogged.

I ran some water through it that looked like it was likely some very silty water, but you know, nothing that a fresh water filter shouldn’t be able to tackle.

It was the primary water source in this area. Plenty of folks had used it.

But the major issue with this filter is that you can’t backflush it. So if it gets all clogged up, you’re kind of screwed. You can unscrew it and you can rinse it in the water and do your best to get all that gunk out of there.

But it sort of felt like the second I ran that silty water through, I was going to be dealing with the worst, most embarrassing water flow for the rest of the trip.

I was filtering water in front of my friend and he was like, yo, that is pitiful. That’s embarrassing.

So yeah, after that trip, I became a staunch Sawyer conversionist. I love a Sawyer now. I understand the appeal of having a backflushable water filter. It runs super fast. It’s like new every time I backflush it. I’m a huge fan.

Again, I think that the Katadyn BeFree served me well on the AT when I was not dealing with super silty water.

But out here, where you’re going to be getting some more glacial flows that you’re filtering from, it is super inconvenient to be out in the backcountry for two days and now your water filter is totally busted and the next two days that you’re on trail are miserable.

So I am no longer a fan of Katadyn, I am sorry to say. Shout out Sawyer.

Another piece of apparel that I’m really excited to talk about, and if you’ve already watched my other video where I talk about all the gear that I tested this year, then this isn’t a surprise to you.

But this right here is my Jolly Gear button down.

This was actually a collaboration with Sawyer.

I wore this for all 200 miles of my John Muir Trail thru-hike this summer, and this is by far one of my favorite pieces of gear that I tested this year.

And that’s really saying something because prior to trying it on for myself, I was a massive hater of the button down.

For me, I just never thought that it was a flattering layer just for my body type.

I understood why people liked them because you could button them down to get more ventilation if you needed it on a hot day, but for me, I just didn’t think that they were very flattering.

But ultimately, on the JMT, I was looking for a performance layer.

I wanted a piece of gear that would keep the sun off my arms, and this is a UPF of 30, which is great, so you get a little bit of sun protection.

I knew that mosquitoes were going to be a risk, so I really wanted something that had sleeves, but also sleeves that I could roll up no problem and still be comfortable.

I wanted a sun hood because I knew it was going to be super duper sunny out in the Sierra, and I wanted a ponytail hole because I like to wear my high pony, especially when I haven’t washed my hair in a few days, and I want to keep it off of my neck.

So yeah, there were a lot of reasons that I decided to test this piece of gear beyond the fact that I love both Jolly Gear and Sawyer as companies.

Now that is all to say that while I love this piece of gear and I think you’ll be hard-pressed to find someone who wears Jolly Gear button downs that isn’t just like a total fanatic for them, that I did have a couple of gripes.

And Jolly, if you’re watching this, this is probably a me problem and I’m sorry in advance, but this is a washed layer.

It is real dirty. It is real dirty. I washed this. I’ve washed this several times since I wore it on the JMT.

So I don’t know if it’s just this specific colorway or maybe I’m just filthier than the average hiker, but for me what I noticed is that this layer really held on to dirt. And it’s not like the stinkiest layer, but you know, it doesn’t smell the freshest.

So yeah, that’s all to say that chances are that if I were to run this through like a power washer or something or, I don’t know, use some sort of scrubbing apparatus to really get the dirt out of the sleeves, I could, but I don’t really feel a need to do that.

I mean, this is ultimately a hiking layer for me, so if it’s a little bit dirty, like who cares?

But for folks out there that are more concerned with looking crisp and clean and sharp when they’re out on the trail, and that might sound like an oxymoron, but I know there are some of you out there because I’ve seen you and you guys look fresh as hell every time I see you, then this ultimately might not be for you.

Or you might want to get a white Jolly Gear button down that you can bleach every time you get to the trail.

So that’s a really petty criticism, honestly, not a huge deal. This is an awesome piece of gear. I love, love, love, love my Jolly Gear. I already bought a new one when I was at PCT Trail Days. I cannot wait to bring that with me next season.

Huge fan of the Jolly Gears. Shout out Jolly Gear.

Another piece of gear. Maybe not a piece of gear, but I’m going to call this a piece of gear.

Another thing that I tried this year that I was so excited to have discovered was Blue Lizard sunscreen. And funny story, how I found this, it was on the JMT. Someone left it on the ground. So it must have fallen out of somebody’s pack. I could have sat there and waited to see if somebody came back for it. But as far as I knew, if I walked away from this, I would have been leaving trash on the ground. And I just so happened to be running out of sunscreen at that point in time. So in my opinion, I was left no choice but to pick this up.

So after I picked this up, as my hike continued and my sunburn started to go away and I was able to wear shorts again, I started putting on this Blue Lizard sunscreen and I did not burn again for the rest of the trail. This stuff is the real deal.

So if you have sensitive skin, you’re prone to burning, you don’t want to wear pants all day, you’re a big shorts-hiking girly like me, then I would consider Blue Lizard, especially if you’re worried about skin cancer, which if you are outside as much as everybody watching this is, you should probably be worried about skin cancer.

So yeah, protect your skin. This is a great option.

If you put it on your face, you’re going to look a little bit goofy. Who cares?

This is great sunscreen, high quality, sport, sweat-resistant, all that stuff. I’m not sponsored. I just am an evangelist for this stuff now.

Three more pieces of gear. Thanks for hanging in there.

And I promise you if you wait for the last one, you won’t be disappointed.

Now I would like to talk to you about the tent I used on the JMT, the Big Agnes String Ridge VST 1.5. Now this is Big Agnes’s very first trekking pole tent, which was particularly exciting and intriguing to me. So I was super stoked to bring this out onto the trails and give it a try.

Especially as somebody who hiked the AT in the Copper Spur. I loved my Copper Spur. I’m a huge fan of Big Agnes.

And some major upsides for this tent are that it has a huge vestibule, a huge mesh door, lots of ventilation. It is the condensation killer, which if you hike with a trekking pole tent, which is single-wall, you know how bad that condensation can be. Additionally, I love the colorway.

It is a well-constructed, seam-sealed tent. I was in this tent in an absolutely torrential downpour to the point where it was flooding under my tent. And I stayed dry as a bone. It was basically a swimming pool under my tent and I was completely dry.

It is well-constructed. I didn’t notice any sort of tears or anything. It is roomy. It is that 1.5 sizing.

So it would be very comfortable for one person and, say, a dog, but if you had to shove two people in there, you could.

A couple of complaints about this tent, and some of them I believe are universal, is with the trekking pole tents, as you probably know, it is a bit of a learning curve to get that perfect pitch.

So occasionally I would absolutely nail the pitch. It would be taut as steel and rain would bead right off it and I’d be so proud of myself and it’d be so comfortable.

And then occasionally I would have not so great a pitch. Maybe I was on granite and I wasn’t able to get my tent stakes into the ground effectively and I had to use rocks.

And occasionally I would put one trekking pole up on the front side and then that one would fall the second I got to the back to put up the second trekking pole. That was really annoying. So a little bit of a learning curve.

I think that with enough time anybody could master this tent.

So if you’re looking for a trekking pole tent and you’re a big fan of Big Agnes, you like the stuff that they make, you like that they’re based in Steamboat here in Colorado, I like that fact very much.

And say that maybe you’re not interested in the offset pitch of the Durston X-Mid or maybe you’ve tried the Zpacks, been there, done that, you’re looking for something new, I think that this is an awesome new option.

I’m excited to see more and more hikers using this tent. I like the String Ridge. It’s definitely going to come out with me on future hikes.

The other trekking pole tent that I use is the Gossamer Gear The One and I also love that tent, so I have a feeling that both of these will be making it into my rotation.

With the caveat being that I think that I would use this specific tent more if I was hiking more out east and it was easier to get non-rocky pitches.

That’s the Big Agnes String Ridge VST 1.5.

Another piece of gear that I really loved this year was the Therm-a-Rest NeoAir.

Again, I talked about this piece of gear in my gear I tested this year, so if you haven’t watched that, go check it out. A couple of highlights about this pad that I really, really like.

It is ultralight. It is very comfy. It is about a three-inch inflation cushion so you’re well off the ground. The R-value is just above four, so it is a perfect three-season sleeping pad. It is well-insulated. It is comfortable. It is not so loud as the XTherm, which is the sleeping pad that I was coming from.

There are a lot of upsides to this sleeping pad.

It also has that awesome proprietary twist-nozzle sleeping pad inflation system that Therm-a-Rest uses. I’m a huge fan of that. I love using it.

It works great with my sleeping pad pump, so that’s always going to be a plus for me as someone who hates blowing up sleeping pads, you know, especially after hiking 20 miles in a day or whatever.

And if you leave a comment and you’re like, you’re carrying a sleeping pad pump? Yeah, come take it from my cold dead hands.

It packs down super small so I don’t worry about this being too bulky in my pack. It’ll just shove in wherever I want it to.

I haven’t had any issues with holes or leaks or anything like that and it’s probably close to 400, maybe 450 miles at this point. So yeah, this was an awesome addition to my gear closet this year. I love this sleeping pad.

Shout out to NeoAir, Therm-a-Rest. Yeah, yeah, yeah. It’s dope.

People like this sleeping pad for a reason. Like, if you look up the sleeping pad, this is going to be one of the top recommended sleeping pads for thru-hikers.

I don’t have to make the case for you. It’s great. Shout out.

All right, y’all. Last but not least, and the thing I am very, very excited to talk to you about today and overshare about, is the Backcountry Bidet. Now, this is a Backcountry Bidet. This is definitely new for me.

For context, I used to be the kind of person that would carry around 400 wet wipes and a billion toilet paper rolls and I would use them because I hated being dirty on trail.

And I would carry out like a pound of toilet paper and wet wipes and honestly, that was gross and way more unsanitary than if I had just used one of these.

You put it into a water bottle and you do your business and then you spray downwards on your behind and then you scrub, scrub, scrub with some sticks or rocks or your hand.

And then when you’re done with your business, you use soap and you wash the ever-living hell out of your hands to get them so, so, so, so clean and then you’re done. I am never going to go back after using the Backcountry Bidet.

And the looks I get when I tell my friends and people on trail that I use this is usually something like, ugh, disgusting. What’s wrong with you? And like, yeah, fair.

It’s gross to tell people that you wipe your butt with your hand.

However, I would say that since using this, I am the cleanest I have ever felt on backpacking trips. I really truly feel as though I’m taking a shower once a day, maybe sometimes twice a day. That’s definitely an overshare but I am a huge fan of the Backcountry Bidet.

If you don’t use one, just give one a try. Just give one a try.

If you hate it, you bring toilet paper too. I don’t care what you do but it’s definitely worth testing it out just so you can experience how awesome it is to get totally, totally funk-free in the backcountry.

Just don’t make the mistake of not carrying enough water to use it because the very first time I went to use this, I realized that all of my water had electrolytes in it and you do not want to wipe your butt with lemonade electrolytes.

I feel like that’s probably a common mistake, right?

All right, y’all. That is all of my favorite and least favorite gear this year that I tested in 2026.

Is there any gear that you tested this year that you really enjoyed? Do you disagree with any of my assessments of the gear that I used this year? Do you think any of it’s underrated, overrated, perfectly rated?

And then maybe recommend to me some gear that you think I might like or maybe some gear that I should test in the new year.

The plan is to hike the Colorado Trail next year, soft launch.

So if I’m able to do that, I definitely want to hear what you guys think I should bring with me because I’m definitely going to do a lot of shakedown hikes before then too. Maybe some time on the AZT. Maybe some time on the Florida Trail.

You never know. You never know. But that’s it. Thank you guys so much for watching.

And finally, if you are a big fan of Backpacker Radio or Andrew Skurka, please be sure to head down to the description and check out the live podcast that we are holding at the Skylark Lounge here in Denver on December 5th.

Thank you so much for watching and happy hiking.

#8276. Best Ammo for Deer Hunting, Tested for Accuracy

Published Nov 5, 2026 1:02 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

The latest for gun hunters and competitive shooters.

Every major ammunition company has a specific product line dedicated to whitetail hunters. Ideally, this ammo will provide good accuracy, function reliably, be widely available, and deliver consistent terminal performance – all at a wallet-friendly price.

I tested six popular whitetail loads to compare their precision at the bench, how they fed and cycled, and the consistency of their velocities in an effort to determine which shot best and whether any should be avoided. This video shows all the results in real time and gives details on their relative performance.

All the loads were chambered in 6.5 Creedmoor. I chose the 6.5 Creed because it is today’s most popular big-game centerfire rifle cartridge; it is stocked everywhere from Alabama to Alaska; and, as the poster child of Modern Cartridge Design, it is inherently accurate and I wanted the ammo in this test to perform as well as possible.

I put each load through two different rifles. One is the Seekins SIC Short Action, a high-end precision rifle that I’ve been using extensively for the last year and is slated to be released to the public in 2027. The other is a Ruger American Rifle Gen II, one of the best all-around hunting rifles for those on a budget. We’ve been big fans of the Ruger American since it was introduced – it won an Editor’s Choice in our annual gun test when it debuted – and the platform continues to impress us with its combination of accuracy-enhancing features, good stock ergonomics, and smooth-cycling action.

I put 20 rounds of each whitetail ammo through each rifle for a total of 40 rounds per offering. I measured those 5-shot groups on my E.A.T.S. targets to come up with an average group size by rifle and then calculated the combined average group size of all eight groups through both rifles.

I captured velocity data on a Garmin Xero C2 Chronograph. The Garmin’s ability to stop and restart sessions allowed me to gather 20 shots of data with each gun and ammo combo for the velocity averages, extreme spreads (ES), and standard deviations (SD). With factory ammo, any 20-shot SD in the teens is very good and there’s nothing wrong with values in the 20s either, especially for the center-of-mass deer hunting ammo we’re showcasing here.

The results of the test were fascinating. The Winchester Deer Season XP and Barnes Harvest performed extremely well, Federal’s Fusion Tipped delivered very good precision, the Nosler Whitetail Country and Hornady American Whitetail loads were solid all around, and the Remington Core-Lokt Tipped gave mixed results that serve as a cautionary tale when selecting hunting ammo.

This data is based on the average of four 5-shot groups with each rifle and ammo combination. The combined value is the average of how the ammunition did in both the Seekins SIC SA and the Ruger American Rifle Gen II.

The muzzle velocity and standard deviation data is also based on 20 shots, except for the Federal 140-grain Fusion Tipped, which is based on 30 shots of data.

This is the most visually distinctive ammo in the test with Winchester’s oversized polymer tip that’s designed to produce violent and quick bullet upset upon impact.

This ammunition delivered the best groups overall, with a 5-shot average of .700 inches. The 20 shots through the Seekins averaged .652 inches, while the Ruger’s groups averaged .749 inches.

You can find it online for about $35 for a box of 20, but it is currently hard to find a vendor that has it in stock. The 125-grain version is available but wasn’t the load we tested so we can’t assume it will perform at the same level.

The Harvest Collection is the love child that resulted from the union of Barnes Bullets and Sierra Bullets, which were joined in corporate matrimony back in 2020. I’ve had excellent results with this ammunition, which was officially unveiled in April 2025, both in terms of its accuracy at the bench and its performance in the field.

The idea behind the Harvest Collection is simple. Barnes took Sierra’s well-regarded Tipped Game King bullet and loaded it in their brass on their machinery, which has a reputation for holding tight tolerances.

With an overall average 5-shot group size of .704 inches, it finished just behind Winchester in this evaluation. That said, I’ve had even better results with this ammunition in other rifles, such as my Sako TRG 22-A1. My groups through that rifle averaged .491 inches at 2692 fps with a 15.7 fps SD.

I’ve used this load on a few whitetails at this point, and the terminal results have been excellent too.

You can find the 6.5 Creedmoor load online for about $40 per box of 20.

The Fusion Tipped bullet has become a go-to of mine in the last couple of years not only for whitetails, but also antelope, elk and mule deer.

In terms of its construction, it falls between traditional cup-and-core projectiles and true bonded bullets with respect to its toughness. It’ll retain weight better than a non-bonded bullet but is cheaper to produce than a chemically bonded bullet and has the added benefit of being more inherently accurate than one, too.

In truth, the Fusion Tipped strikes a beautiful balance between accuracy, terminal performance, and economy. During this test the 140-grain Fusion Tipped averaged .989 inches in group size, with the Seekins turning in .784-inch groups and the Ruger delivering 1.194-inch groups.

I’ve found the 6.5 Creedmoor online for $46 to $50 per box, which makes it one of the more expensive whitetail-oriented ammo offerings. If that’s a bit rich for your blood, consider the traditional Fusion line, which can usually be found for a few dollars less per box.

The Nosler Solid Base bullet was first introduced more than half a century ago, but it never caught on like the company’s iconic Partition and Ballistic Tipped projectiles and there were years where the company halted production altogether.

But this cup-and-core soft point, with its tapered jacket, makes for a dandy hunting bullet for whitetails and other big game at moderate distances and it is enjoying a revival of sorts in Nosler’s Whitetail Country lineup.

The bullet’s accuracy in this test was solid. With 5-shot groups averaging 1.167 inches it is more than capable of taking deer at distances to 300 yards or more. Interestingly, this ammunition was the only one in the test where the budget-oriented Ruger American Rifle outshot my fancy-pants Seekins SIC. My four 5-shot groups from the Ruger averaged 1.131 inches, besting the Seekins which averaged 1.202 inches.

The 140-grain 6.5 Creed load goes for $33 to $40 per box of 20 online, making it one of the more affordable selections in the test.

Inside the jacket of this bullet is a raised ring that helps keep the lead core in place as it expands and penetrates within the target. That “locking” element gave the InterLock its name and it’s been part of the American hunting landscape for half a century now.

Loaded in the American Whitetail line, it is one of the most affordable bread-and-butter offerings for big-game hunters. The price per box hovers around $33 currently.

Its attractive price tag and its reasonable performance — through the two test rifles its average 5-shot group average measured 1.375 inches — earned it a Great Buy award in this round up.

This ammunition delivered the largest overall groups in the test, with a 5-shot average of 1.519 inches. On the surface, that’s mediocre performance, but it comes with a significant caveat.

The Ruger American Rifle Gen II did not care for this ammunition. The four 5-shot groups measured 2.065, 2.699, 2.392, and 2.143 inches, for an average of 2.325 inches. That isn’t a result I’d feel confident hunting with, and I doubt many of you would be satisfied with it either.

But through the Seekins SIC SA, the ammo hammered. Those four groups came in at 1.039, .595, .589, and .630 inches, averaging .713 inches overall. Across the 12 rifle and ammo combinations in the test that was third only to how well the Seekins shot the Barnes Harvest ammo at .642 inches and Winchester ammo at .652 inches.

The lessons here are that there’s no reason for you to go afield with substandard precision from a modern hunting rifle shooting quality modern ammunition, and that it pays to test out different loads when preparing for firearms season.

The Core-Lokt Tipped offering in 6.5 Creed runs around $43 online currently.

Investing in a few boxes of ammunition is all it takes to help your deer rifle reach its precision potential. Four 5-shot groups will yield more reliable data than three, but even 15 well-placed deliberate shots on target will give you a good feel for the performance of your system.

In any event, there’s no reason to head to your favorite stand or block of public ground with a nagging sense of uncertainty about how your rifle will shoot when that big buck steps into the clear.

As you can see from this evaluation, even with a budget-minded rig like the Ruger, you can have a true sub-MOA rifle if you take the time to figure out what your hunting rig likes.

John B. Snow is Shooting Editor of Outdoor Life, where he oversees the publication’s firearms and shooting coverage. This includes gear reviews, features on technical innovations, stories on shooting techniques and general hunting coverage with the occasional fishing story thrown into the mix.

#8273. Florida Man Finishes Four Corners Walk Across America

After over three years of trekking 20,000km back and forth across the continental United States, endurance athlete Kyndal Ray Edwards has completed his ambitious Four Corners Walk. His route took him from coast to coast, then corner to corner, starting in Florida and ending in Maine, where a crowd of supporters met him last week.

Kyndal Ray Edwards, 33, is originally from Orange Park, Florida. After struggling with drug addiction, mental illness, and the justice system during his early adulthood, he decided to become an endurance athlete and mental health advocate. On January 1, 2022, he began his walking project from the beach in Jacksonville.

Over the next 15 months, Edwards walked to Long Beach, Washington, traveling 5,298km from the Atlantic to the Pacific. His plans expanded, and he undertook the challenge of walking to all four corners of the contiguous United States. From Long Beach, he headed to the northwesternmost point, Cape Flattery, also in Washington. After trekking south to San Diego, the next corner he headed for was all the way back in Florida, the southeast extremity.

Along the way, Edwards posted frequently on social media about his journey and his recovery from mental illness.

On October 25, Edwards reached West Quoddy Head Lighthouse in Lubec, Maine. This is the northeast corner of the U.S., and the finish line for Edwards. He walked a total of 19,544 kilometers in 1,022 days, averaging nearly 20km per day.

Edwards and supporters at the finish line. Photo: Kyndal Ray Edwards

A cross-country walking journey, Edwards says, has been his dream since 2013. But with the end of his Walking Across America project, Edwards is already ruminating on future challenges. Online, he has proposed going on an adventure with a stranger in all 50 states, running more ultra marathons, and undertaking endurance challenges on every continent. However, he has yet to commit to one.

The end of Kyndal Ray Edwards’s journey came only days before Karl Bushby, another long-distance trekker, completed his 28-year Goliath Expedition. The pair also happen, Edwards pointed out, to share a birthday.

Lou Bodenhemier holds an MA in History from the University of Limerick and a BA in Creative Writing from the University of Arizona. He’s interested in maritime and disaster history as well as criminal history, and his dissertation focused on the werewolf trials of early modern Europe. At the present moment he can most likely be found perusing records of shipboard crime and punishment during the Age of Sail, or failing that, writing historical fiction horror stories. He lives in Dublin and hates the sun.
