You’ll find plenty of places to refuel in style, whether you’re settling in for a leisurely lunch or just warming up between laps. “Everything is sublime!” said one happy Snowbasin skier. “The bathrooms are top-tier and the food is scrumptious, great gluten-free options compared to other resorts.”

There is one notable trade-off: No lodging at the base means Snowbasin isn’t a true destination resort in the traditional sense. And if you’re looking for a lively après scene right outside the lifts, you’ll need to look elsewhere. Luckily, nearby Ogden offers a range of places to stay, eat, and unwind, while Salt Lake City puts even more options within reach.

The bigger challenge these days is that the secret is decidedly out. Snowbasin has become a popular alternative when Little Cottonwood Canyon closes. With the resort slated to host alpine racing at the 2034 Winter Olympics, that spotlight will only grow brighter. The upside for skiers? Continued investment in lifts, terrain, and infrastructure that should make an already excellent mountain even better. “They’ve invested heavily in the lift infrastructure—the new Becker lift this season was a tremendous improvement and makes getting over to Strawberry so easy,” shared one survey respondent.

“Even in a low-snow winter, Snowbasin shined with a great experience. Their staff is the best in the industry, and the amenities are unbeatable. If you’re stuck on groomed trails, there really isn’t a better place. But on a powder day, this place really performs.”

Big-mountain terrain, jaw-dropping scenery, and a ski trip that won’t break the bank. What’s not to love?

A jump from No. 15 to No. 2 is no small feat, but Lake Louise has plenty going for it. Start with the value: Thanks to the favorable Canadian dollar, your ski-trip budget goes further here. Then there’s the skiing. Set within the spectacular wilderness of Banff National Park, Lake Louise serves up 4,200 acres of terrain with a distinctly Canadian Rockies flavor. Fast, confidence-building groomers? Check. Steep, rugged lines on the backside? Absolutely. Wide-open bowls, tree skiing, and enough variety to keep even seasoned skiers exploring? You bet. The scenery is almost unfairly good, too. As one reader put it, “Fantastic steep and deep chute skiing. No lines and amazing snow. Can’t be beat.”

The resort’s latest terrain additions make an already sprawling mountain even easier to explore. New connections link key areas of the mountain, while expanded glades give intermediate and advanced skiers more options in the trees. Snowmaking improvements on Richardson’s Ridge should also help deliver more consistent conditions when Mother Nature needs a little backup.

All of that said, you won’t find slopeside lodging or much in the way of après at the ski area itself. For that, head to Banff, a lively mountain town about 35 miles away with plenty of restaurants, bars, shops, and places to stay. Free, regular shuttles connect the town to the resort, so a rental car isn’t a must. And while Lake Louise may not have the buzzy village scene of some destination resorts, that’s part of its appeal: You come here for the mountain, the wilderness, and the kind of big-skiing experience that still feels refreshingly unpretentious. As one aficionado summed it up: “Lake Louise is simply the greatest. Love the mountain. Love Banff.”

“Lots of snow this year. I had some amazing powder days at Louise. The back bowls are some of my favorite areas to ski as well as the West Bowl. Even on non powder days, I enjoyed cruising in the alpine on the frontside.”

The resort adds Grove Glade, a groomed green run linking Merlin’s directly to the new Richardson’s Ridge chairlift, while Pikaboo and Prunepicker improve connections between key zones. Expanded intermediate and advanced glades offer even more tree-skiing options.

The resort is also upgrading the Top of the World chairlift to improve loading capacity, speed, and reliability, and expanding snowmaking coverage on Richardson’s Ridge for more consistent conditions.

A high-alpine playground with naturally reliable snow, fast lifts, and jaw-dropping Canadian Rockies views. Now, for the first time, it’s North America’s favorite ski resort.

There’s a reason skiers keep coming back to Banff Sunshine. Actually, there are several: big-mountain scenery, reliably good snow, a long season, and terrain that ranges from mellow groomers to legitimately intimidating steeps. “High elevation means great quality and plentiful snow throughout the very long season,” wrote one Sunshine fan. “Always finding new fun spots even though I’ve been skiing here for years.”

And then there’s the setting. Just 15 minutes from the lively town of Banff, Sunshine feels like a world apart once you’re riding the gondola up through the trees toward its sprawling, above-treeline playground. It’s the kind of place that reminds you why you ski in the first place.

This year, our readers put Banff Sunshine at the top of North America’s 50 best resorts for the first time ever, bumping it up from last year’s No. 2 ranking. It makes sense. Sunshine has invested in its lift system in recent years, making it easier to explore the mountain and a whole lot more comfortable to ride on blustery days. Bubble enclosures on select lifts are a particularly welcome touch at a resort where exposed alpine terrain is part of the appeal—and where the weather can be as big as the views.

The skiing itself offers plenty of ways to spend a day. Cruise rolling groomers, roam across wide-open bowls, or work your way toward the steeper, more technical terrain. For experts, Delirium Dive is talked up a lot, but don’t overlook some other sleepers, including Stampede and Saddledome on Goat’s Eye Mountain. Sunshine may not have the sheer variety of some larger North American resorts, but its mix of approachable laps and high-alpine challenges makes it an easy place for a group with different abilities to enjoy skiing together.

Then there’s the snow. With a summit just shy of 9,000 feet and no snowmaking, Sunshine depends entirely on Mother Nature—and has the elevation and climate to make the most of it. Its season regularly stretches into late May, giving skiers a shot at spring turns long after many other resorts have called it a year. That extended season, combined with the big-mountain setting, is a pretty compelling argument for making the trip. “Banff is my favorite place to ski,” opined one survey respondent. “The mountain is beautiful, the terrain is varied, and it’s not overcrowded. The town of Banff is perfect. Like a postcard. Most beautiful place in North America.”

The one catch? You can’t exactly roll out of bed and onto the lifts from a sprawling slopeside resort village. Sunshine Mountain Lodge is the ski area’s only overnight accommodation, and scoring a room means waking up to a rare kind of quiet, with first tracks practically on your doorstep. Everyone else can stay in Banff, where free shuttles make getting to the mountain refreshingly simple. The town has everything from affordable hotels to more upscale digs, plus enough restaurants, bars, bowling alleys, and other diversions to fill an evening—or several. The combination of wild alpine skiing by day and a proper mountain town by night is hard to beat.

What’s New The ski area is amping up its après offerings this season. The GOAT Club returns to Goat’s Eye Lodge for a second season of live music, DJs, and après parties, and the new Coco Lounge, on the deck of the Centennial Lodge, will serve cocktails and food with fireside seating and slope views. If you need a warm-up between laps,  Coco Lab Coffee & Hot Chocolate Bar is now at Goat’s Eye Lodge serving hot drinks. There’s also a new cocktail bar if you want something a little stronger.

#8209. These Popular Bass Fishing Myths Were Debunked Decades Ago

Published Nov 9, 2026 5:04 PM EST

The hottest fishing news, tips, and tactics

“Missed him,” I said and groaned as I reeled in a slack line. Setting the hook after I had felt a gentle tap had produced nothing but a mangled plastic worm.

“Rerig and toss it back in there,” Ralph Manns directed me. “Another one might hit it.”

Manns was right. The next time I set the hook I was rewarded with a pleasantly bowed rod. After a short fight, a five-pound largemouth bass thrashed in the landing net.

“Now, you get one,” I said and grinned as my bass splashed in the live well.

Manns complied with a cast that dropped his worm beside the same rotted stump. The line twitched, the rod arched and he quickly landed a twin to the first bass. Not a bad start for our first look at Texas’ Lake Livingston—especially after my traumatic and almost sleepless night.

It had begun innocently enough with my arrival at Livingston’s Penwaugh Marina the previous evening for a meeting of the Texas Outdoor Writers Association. Luck of the draw had placed me in the same room with fisheries biologist Ralph Manns, a pleasant mild-mannered gentleman I was meeting for the first time. I had no idea that our meeting would alter the course of my fishing life.

An insatiable appetite for more facts about bass behavior had prompted Manns to become a full-time student at Southwest Texas State University after retiring from active duty in the Air Force where he had spent 20 years as an intelligence officer and a political scientist. At the time of his retirement he was a lieutenant colonel.

En route to a masters of science degree in aquatic biology, which he earned in 1981, Manns conducted a study of black bass in Lake Travis in 1977 and 1978. The study team used electronic transmitter tags and receivers to track 14 bass while divers recorded the behavior of another 935 bass. Manns’ team also used angling techniques to obtain detailed reports on an additional 289 bass. Data on more than 20 different types of behavior and the environmental conditions that might influence the fish were fed into a computer to compile and analyze the results.

Manns’ exhaustive studies of scientific literature on bass and his extensive two-year study have led to rather innovative and sometimes controversial conclusions. During my first few hours with him, he crumbled the foundation of my bass fishing knowledge with solid scientific evidence that contradicted many generally accepted fishing theories.

Those first two bass we caught from Lake Livingston, for example, were taken from classic bass structure—a stump on the upper edge of a submerged creek bed. The bass probably had not migrated from the depths, however, to feed in the shallower water as a popular myth would have us believe.

The hypothesis that bass live in deep water, migrate to shallow water on a daily basis to feed and then return to deep water along established migration routes is generally credited to Buck Perry, the gentleman rightfully recognized as the father of structure fishing. His methods of catching bass have been so successful that other anglers and writers have perpetuated his migration theories.

Ralph Manns agreed that such structures are good places in which to fish but the analytically minded biologist could find no scientific literature to substantiate a deep-water migration theory. Manns wanted a better explanation for the appearance of bass at certain underwater structure.

“Sure enough,” Manns related, “our tracking studies verified data available in at least 15 other studies that showed the predominant movements of black bass are parallel to the shorelines and contour lines and not perpendicular to them. The movement, moreover, usually is at a nearly constant depth.”

A national magazine recently published a story entitled “When the Sun is High, the Bass Go Deep”. The author surmised that because more bass are caught in deep water during midday hours, bass obviously migrate from shallow to deep water as the sun brightens. And that’s how myths get started.

Manns’ study of Lake Travis bass showed no such tendency.

“Our research showed some bass at shallow depths, some at medium depths and some in deep water at all times,” he revealed. “And they tended to remain at that particular depth whether active or inactive. Bass do move vertically but not routinely. A deep fish might pop to the surface to run through a school of shad, but it will grab two or three and almost immediately dive to its original depth because that’s where it has established its equilibrium and can suspend without effort.”

A bass can hover effortlessly at a particular depth because its air bladder is balanced at that depth and it gets out of balance if it varies much from that point. According to Manns, it takes hours for the air bladder to adjust to a major depth change. The more out of balance a bass gets, the harder it has to swim to maintain its stability.

Manns noted that black bass usually move along contour lines for only short distances and tend to stop at any bisecting lines of structure that obstruct their movement, such as a fence, stump or rock. By casting to a fence, an angler increases his odds simply because moving bass are likely to pause there.

Most anglers will catch more bass, Manns maintained, if they fish on the better bisecting structures for several minutes during activity periods. Additional schools often stop at the same structure long enough for the anglers to catch more fish.

Some fishermen consider schools of black bass a rarity. Limit catches might be rare but, according to Manns’ underwater observations, most bass are in either a school or an aggregation.

“There are almost no loner bass,” Manns says. “The few single fish we observed underwater were either very sick, very large or totally inactive. The sick ones obviously couldn’t keep up and the larger bass were probably unable to find compatible partners in their size range.

“Rule one,” he continued, “if you catch a bass, assume it is not alone. As a minimum, it is in a group of two to five fish. Actively striking bass are usually feeding and moving bass. They tighten up their aggregations and move in small schools.”

During activity periods, of course, almost anyone can catch bass by tossing an edible-looking lure in the path of a feeding school. It’s the inactive periods that separate expert from novice bass fishermen.

“Fishermen should remember that bass are inactive most of the time, even if their stomachs are empty,” Manns claimed. “Unlike humans who have a predictable three square meals a day, a bass may be forced to exist for days without eating. That little bit of minnow it ate three days ago must last the bass a long time and it does not waste it!”

The fact that a fish is inactive doesn’t mean that it won’t eat, Manns admitted. If something passes closely and in front of a bass’ mouth, it will usually eat because bass are opportunists. But an inactive bass probably won’t move more than a few inches to hit a lure. An angler who is fishing a spot that holds inactive bass may have to cast 15 or more times before the lure passes through that tiny strike zone in front of an inactive bass.

A fast-moving crankbait offers good odds of getting a lure to an active bass. Because active fish may chase lures for 10 feet or more, each cast effectively covers a wide path on each side of the bait’s track. The same lure retrieved past inactive bass, however, may pass by many fish without eliciting a strike.

The success of an angler’s technique, then, depends on how active the bass are. Anglers who cast and crank at wide intervals over inactive bass will usually get few strikes. Fishermen who flip worms or jigs to the base of cover objects where inactive bass may hold, however, get close enough to take a few fish. If the same anglers continue to flip slow lures while bass are in an active state, though, they cannot hope to hook as many as those with fast lures. Thus, an angler must match his lure and his technique to the activity level of the bass.

One widely accepted myth claims that bass avoid sunlight because they have no eyelids. Manns’ underwater observations indicate otherwise.

“It was clear to us that bass have no requirement to live in shade,” Manns declared. “Moving bass were as likely to stop at a sunny spot as a shaded one. Although bass have no eyelids, their eyes have pigment mechanisms that compensate for excessive light. Water is an excellent light filter, too. Unless a bass is in very shallow, calm and clear water, the water serves it well as a pair of sunglasses.”

Bass that anglers catch from beneath piers, boat houses and docks are probably there for cover or food rather than for shade. In fact, even slightly colored water refracts sunlight sufficiently to destroy any distinct shade line within a few feet. Even in moderately clear lakes, bass down more than 10 feet experience little or no shading from objects at the surface.

This means that bass a fisherman finds beneath floating structures will probably hold tightly to the bottom of the structure—unless, of course, there are other attractive structural elements on the bottom. Lures retrieved just beneath floating structures, then, will probably be more effective than lures retrieved along the bottom.

Although bass do not need to avoid sunlight, Manns’ records indicate that more bass are caught from shaded areas than from sunny ones. He stressed that this statistic is not contradictory because inactive bass may suspend in either shade or in sunny open water. But for an angler to cast his lure near enough to inactive bass to make them strike, he usually must find bass that are suspended close to an identifiable target. While the target creates shade, the shade itself is incidental and not the reason the bass are there.

Another concern of bass anglers is that bass will move when they hear noise coming from above them. Manns’ study, however, clearly showed that bass learn to ignore any sounds that don’t represent a threat. Bass frequently swam beneath docks where workers were pounding with hammers or sailors were stomping in boats. Bass also ignored outboard motor noises in Lake Travis, which is heavily used by recreational boaters. Surprisingly, however, some of the lake’s bass had learned to move away from boats with electric fishing motors and it was difficult to approach such bass unless they were pushed against cover objects.

Manns suggests that a great myth of angling literature is that bass seek out preferred temperatures, water clarity, structure and so on. He stressed that the part of a bass’ brain that processes every piece of visual or physical information is about the size of a thumbnail. A bass simply does not have the ability to be intuitive.

“A bass will not run across a lake to an area that has a better temperature level,” Manns claimed, “because it doesn’t know it’s there. Now if a bass is wandering around and finds a more comfortable area, it might think, ‘Wow! Isn’t this temperature nice?’ And if it can stay there without getting hungry, it may hang around long enough for the angler with a temperature meter to catch it.”

In Manns’ study, bass did not move to deeper water to avoid surface temperatures in the 84° to 88° range. In fact, when all other factors were equal, black bass (including smallmouths) preferred the water temperature to be between 78° and 86°, not the 72° that is popularized in most fishing literature. Manns’ findings are corroborated by at least 20 other scientific studies published during a 40-year period. Bass found in cooler water are there because of a better food supply or because they are unable to compete with larger predators present in warmer water.

Manns admits that there are optimum chemical environments for bass but in most lakes the fish must be satisfied with less. They merely move into someplace tolerable, adapt to it and once they’ve adapted to that condition, any change is a negative change to those fish.

“Most people don’t realize that a bass is constantly adapting to its environment,” Manns declared. “The chemistry of its body adapts to temperature and water conditions and, if any factors change, the fish is temporarily out of balance. When cold fronts go through, for example, sudden drops in temperature disturb the fish’s equilibrium and it becomes slightly sick until it adapts to the new condition. That helps explain why bass normally don’t bite as well after a cold front.”

A common dream of anglers is catching bass on almost every cast from a “hotspot” where hungry largemouths eagerly await the next cast. The nearest thing I ever found to that fabled “hotspot” was on Lake Sam Rayburn back in 1968. My partner and I found a timbered flat near a river channel where every cast with our crankbaits hooked a chunky bass. We tied the boat line to a limb and promptly caught 60 largemouth bass from an area no larger than the average living room. In that era of 15-bass limits it was the first chance I had to cull bass to improve a stringer.

Our hopes for a repeat performance the next day were short lived. Our first few casts hooked bass, but the action ceased and we never relocated the bass. Nor did any of our friends ever find fish there on many subsequent trips. Manns offered an explanation for the phenomenon.

“They were probably transient bass, which is a major cause of confusion to anglers. Bass are generally thought of as having one type of behavior pattern. Actually, though, there are two types of black bass: transient bass and home-range bass. The concept is an old one that shows up in scientific literature as far back as 30 years ago.”

Manns theorized that the fish’s health or its ability to catch prey determines whether it is a home-range or transient bass. Healthy fish establish territories and hold them, moving as little as possible. They conserve energy by feeding quickly and remain in the same general location unless there is a major change in water conditions or the food supply.

Large bass populations or shortages of prey create competition for food, however. Those bass that feed less efficiently must feed longer and move often to find forage. A transient is one because it is a loser.

There are many transient bass in our better bass lakes and they almost always school. An angler who finds such a concentration can catch great numbers of them at one time but he should not necessarily label the area as a great fishing hole. Such catches can be the result of chance meetings with transients.

Manns says that an angler should not spend much time returning to the site of a big catch unless he has reason to believe, such as repeated success, that the place is a home-range area. An angler can more consistently catch bass by returning to locations where he has taken one or two fish over and over again. Those are probably spots that have enough food to hold home-range fish day after day.

Manns stressed that bass reactions vary according to how hungry they are. A very hungry fish will probably strike at any lure it can get in its mouth. A bass that has been feeding on shad for 20 minutes, however, will probably only take something that is similar to the shad.

Although bass can see colors, anglers should remember that bass do not perceive them as a human would. Manns recalled a day when he and his partner followed a large school of bass feeding heavily on shad. The two cast all of the traditional shad-color lures without a strike. As soon as Manns put on a gold lure, though, he caught fish on almost every cast.

The bass obviously responded to some flash of gold from the shad caused, perhaps, by the angle of sunlight. The bass had enough color discrimination that they triggered to the tiny variation. Manns, therefore, suggests that anglers who are unsuccessful in catching obviously active bass should change lure colors, sizes and actions until they find one that triggers the fish. Bass are not ambush predators as are halibut, angler fish and sculpin; nor are they chase predators such as tuna or striped bass. A black bass is a compromise fish designed to do a lot of things—none of them perfectly but all of them well. The bass is a seeker with a short sprint. It enters cover for protection and to rest, not to ambush prey. Cover actually limits and hinders a bass’ ability to strike and that is why prey fish hide in such areas.

The standard hunting pattern of a bass is to move around structure objects to see if anything strays far enough from cover to become vulnerable. It assesses its ability to catch individuals of prey and strikes only at those it thinks can be caught. The bass ignores prey that are likely to dodge and thus escape. A bass will ignore a lure that looks like a healthy bluegill just as it would ignore a real bluegill under the same circumstances.

“Bass fishing is very mathematical, very predictable,” Manns claimed. “It is a problem to be solved. Most of the false concepts arise because writers intellectualize about bass. The reaction mechanism of bass is actually very very basic: a reaction to a stimulus and a response, nothing more.

Read Next: Old-School Tips for Catching Big Bass Right Now

“A bass can’t outsmart you. All you have to do is find something that will stimulate it, put it where it will stimulate it and you will catch a bass. There’s really nothing more to fishing than that.”

Manns makes it sound simple and it looks simple enough when you watch him in action. He merely works the odds, covering as much favorable water as possible with a wide variety of lures. But he seems to catch many more bass than the average fisherman. The years he spent in their living quarters are paying off.

This story was originally published in the November 1983 issue of Outdoor Life.

#8208. Traversing the Saiga Silk Road

As we skidded off the main road and onto a mud path maintained only by tire treads, lines began to blur.

Flanking our two-track trail were a series of parallel lanes no more than a foot wide, which forked, merged, and crisscrossed our own. In the distance, I saw what looked like a ghost train, faintly visible and thrust forward by howling Siberian winds.

Through borrowed binoculars, I soon got my first glimpse of an ancient tableau, seemingly untouched since Neanderthals roamed the earth. On the far horizon, hundreds of nomadic travelers pierced the frigid air with their ringed horns, inhaling the brittle shards through Snuffleupagus snouts as they sprinted across the desolate steppe.

Watching them charge through the treeless plain at full bore, I was reminded of a saying I’d heard shortly before arriving in this remote corner of Kazakhstan: “The saiga is a freedom-loving animal.”

Since time immemorial, saiga antelope have blazed trails across Central Asia while other civilizations rose and fell around them. They once inhabited a world dominated by woolly mammoths, saber-toothed cats, and giant deer with antlers 12 feet across—and outlived them all. When pioneering human caravans first attempted to navigate this unforgiving land, they considered the saigas to be their guides.

Ahead of my arrival, seasonal rains transformed once-green grasslands into sludge punctuated by tufts of withering brush. Driving through such muck is, I would soon discover, akin to controlled hydroplaning. The steering wheel bucked wildly as our tires swerved, shredding deep into the gunk and desperately gripping anything remotely solid enough to push off from.

In the front seats were Alexandr and Albert, two team members from the Association for the Conservation of Biodiversity of Kazakhstan, or ACBK. Between them, they have more than twenty-five years of experience following saigas across the steppe, and I’d arranged to join them for the western leg of one of their field audits.

Our visit was timed to coincide with the rutting season, a critical part of the year for saigas. This is a gathering time, when antelope from across the region sprint together in massive single-file lines, before congregating for a series of competitive battles and subsequent mating rituals.

For males, it’s a time for strutting and headbutting to demonstrate one’s physical prowess to female onlookers—an activity so energy-intensive that many will forget to eat and keel over from extreme physical exhaustion. For females, this is a time of choosing. In addition to assessing fitness, they pay particular attention to one distinctive feature: a potential mate’s floppy, elongated nose. The saigas’ sniffers are essential for filtering out dust in the semidesert plains and for warming frigid winter air before it reaches their lungs. A large nose is the ultimate sign of virility, so as the males marched into these annual gatherings, they were doing everything they could to accentuate their schnozzes.

Because of the saigas’ preference for large-scale migrations across a landscape almost entirely devoid of trees, they have long been a favorite of global wildlife trackers. The isolation and starkness of the saiga world is a strength when it comes to GPS collars, which deliver a reliable stream of daily pings without risk of visual obstruction. Prior to such breakthroughs, conservationists would sometimes spend weeks roaming the boundless steppe unsuccessfully trying to locate the nomadic herds.

The wildlife sanctuary we were traveling through was created only a year prior, with its boundaries informed by tracking data that Albert and his team personally collected. He seemed pleased that the animals were continuing to use the newly designated space as intended. Standing along the roadside, Alexandr spotted a stream of the famously skittish ungulates wrapping around the contours of the earth. As he did, ripping wind and snow started blowing in sideways—the outer ring of an encroaching storm.

These were no fluffy flakes. This was the harsh, crunchy ice of a walk-in freezer, which instantly hardened our truck’s caked-on mud like liquid nitrogen.

Seemingly unperturbed by the dropping barometer, Albert chirped, “Who’s hungry?” Setting up an impromptu picnic, he and Alexandr dug into a prepared meal of fresh bread, tea, and dried meats of unknown provenance. In a muted attempt to thaw my face, I opted to guzzle spicy instant noodles.

A tradition of nomadism has loomed large in this corner of the world since at least the Early Iron Age. The very word kazakh is thought to be derived from the Turkic word qaz, which means “wanderer” or “vagabond.” For millennia, small human groups routinely migrated to higher altitudes in the hot summer months, where melting snow made for abundant water and greenery, before returning to sheltered valleys ahead of winter’s whipping winds. At various times of the year, disparate nomads would also congregate for formal meetings and large cultural festivals, complete with physical challenges like wrestling and tug-of-war. When the gatherings were finished, the nomads dispersed once again.

Historical analysis has shown that nomads’ seasonal migrations and time-honed transit corridors may have helped pave the way for portions of the Great Silk Road, which was less a singular route than an ever-evolving web of pathways and bypasses that linked together reliable stopovers. At the Silk Road’s peak, this corner of western Kazakhstan along the fertile banks of the Ural River became a vital transcontinental crossroads. To this day, the river still serves as a natural boundary between Asia and Europe, meaning this part of Kazakhstan is, quite literally, where East meets West.

The land above the Caspian Sea also served as a main artery that linked together key transit points. Strategic settlements along the riverbank allowed weary caravans to rest their heads, unwind in large public baths, exchange knowledge, stock up on essential supplies, and regroup before moving onward.

Among overland voyagers traversing the continental divide, saigas have long been spoken of with an almost mythical reverence. Cave paintings of the antelope created as far back as the seventh century BCE depict them as resilient, elusive, and charismatic. Expert navigators who embody the true spirit of a most inhospitable terrain.

In human society, traditional nomadic practices persisted even as the land itself was variously claimed and reclaimed by Turkic tribes, Genghis Khan, and the Russian Empire. Only with the rise of the Soviet Union in the twentieth century did mandatory sedentarization efforts successfully manage to lock nomadic people in place, force them to farm, and extinguish a cultural flame that had burned brightly for millennia. Denied the ability to live in perpetual motion, people’s navigational muscles began to atrophy.

This transition was viewed by many as an inevitable shift toward “modernization,” but it also represented a significant diversion from our own history as a species. Of the roughly 300,000 years that Homo sapiens have existed, we spent the first 288,000 of them living in small, mobile groups that followed the migratory patterns of other animals. Forcing nomads into agricultural plots was also a colossal failure because much of the steppe soil was unsuitable for growing crops, which is why so many people were nomadic in the first place. Iconic filmmaker Werner Herzog once remarked that “whatever went wrong and makes our civilization something doomed is the departure from the nomadic life.”

Whether by choice or necessity, most Kazakh people now lead stationary lives in urban centers. The world that nomads once freely roamed has also been feverishly transformed, not only by agriculture but through the construction of new roads and railways.

For the saigas, whose nomadic days never ceased, these new layers now represent an existential threat.

With the weather taking a turn for the worse, Albert and Alexandr ultimately decided to call it a day and start fresh in the morning. After a blistering drive through whiteout conditions, we hunkered down in a tiny village less than 10 miles from the Russian border, where Albert pulled out his laptop and showed me how saiga movements have changed over the years.

“They would routinely trek hundreds of miles as part of an expansive migratory route across the Eurasian steppe,” he said. “Saigas could be found from the Caucasus Mountains to Mongolia, and everywhere in between.”

For millennia, they lived with few barriers and obstructions on the landscape. Then, seemingly overnight, rattling railways and roaring roads began to crisscross the region, fragmenting the saigas into smaller, more isolated groups. As the interior steppe got more accessible to vehicles and passengers, development begat more development.

On his screen, Albert clicked open a recent map that showed how a population of GPS-collared saigas once routinely traveled deep into Uzbekistan before being unceremoniously clipped off by a new rail line in 2014. The data from the years prior to the railway’s construction showed a flurry of squiggly lines representing individual animals zipping back and forth with the seasons. The post-construction slide showed those same animals spinning around despondently on the northern side of the tracks, while the fresh grasses and water they had come to rely on withered away to the south.

Such interruptions can lead to a complete collapse in spatial knowledge—a loss that science writer Ben Goldfarb once wrote is “as thorough as the erasure of a language.” Just as human nomads forced to stay in one place eventually lost connection to the physical landmarks of their ancestors’ journeys, young saigas learn where they can reliably find food and shelter, as well as places to stay away from, through active participation and observation. This cultural exchange keeps their world in orbit and is one of the reasons they have been successful at navigating a terrain fatal to so many before them. As the land they know is cleaved and partitioned, whole stretches of the Saiga Silk Road begin to fade from memory.

To unwind this damage, Albert’s team has partnered with the Kazakh government to construct dozens of saiga-friendly crossing points, where slightly sloping dirt ramps rise up to match the height of the train tracks, making it appear from a distance as though there’s a natural gap in the rail line. Cattle-guard fences positioned far away from the crossings ensure that trains and saigas never actually run into each other at these intersections, which would shatter the illusion of safety.

ACBK has also worked with the Uzbek government to reshape its border fences from a barbed-wire wall to an X-shaped barricade that blocks vehicles from driving through but leaves just enough space for saigas to pass. Over time, Albert hopes such efforts can rebuild the trust necessary for them to confidently return to a plateau they once relied on.

The next morning, I was astonished by how austere the steppe looked compared with the day before. Gone was the slippery muck and browning grasses of shifting seasons, replaced by a blanket of crunchy snow. Against this stark black-and-white backdrop, the fresh crystals functioned like fingerprint dust, illuminating the only remaining pops of color: the rust-red streaks of human and nonhuman pathways in the dirt.

Parked in an otherwise empty tract of prairie land, we watched in stunned silence as thousands of saigas seized the day, flying like banshees across the periphery, their hooves gouging the frozen crust and stamping pigment into an earthen canvas.

As I gazed east toward the colorless horizon, I tried to envision how it might have looked in the thirteenth century, when this corner of the world boasted a vast network of caravanserai, or road inns, where exhausted travelers could rest and recover before continuing onward into the great unknown.

I pondered what it must have felt like for an intrepid merchant to know that they would not see another human being for many days, maybe weeks. To be fearful of what you may soon encounter, but take solace that the space between is not wholly empty. For there is life beyond humanity’s margins, and among nonhuman communities, that in-between space is the center of everything. That, I imagined, must have offered some measure of assurance that the road ahead, perilous though it may be, is well traveled.

This essay was adapted from the new nonfiction travelogue The Hidden Nations of Animals and is published here exclusively for Adventure Journal, with permission from Penguin Random House.

#8207. To Win the Backyard Ultra World Team Championship, Try Being … Vulnerable?

Author Dan England spoke with five members of Team USA after they won the 2026 Big’s Backyard Ultra World Team Championship on October 22. A rough start forced the team to abandon the fundamentals of competition and ask for help, be honest about their problems, and sacrifice for others. It paid off: the U.S. came from behind to defeat Australia and Belgium, who took second and third, respectively.

Early into the second night of the 2026 Big’s Backyard Ultra World Team Championship, Mark Dowdle turned to U.S. teammate Levi Yoder and admitted that he was so tired he might fall asleep and into the nearby ditch. Yoder replied that he was so tired he was hallucinating and might wind up in that same ditch.

Before the start, Harvey Lewis, a two-time individual backyard ultra world champion whom many on the U.S. squad thought of as their de facto captain, told his teammates to lean on one another. But Dowdle hesitated the first day, and so, he thought, did many others. It made sense: Backyard ultras are usually individual events predicated on you staying strong while others give up.

For the uninitiated, backyard ultra rules are pretty simple: Run a 4.167-mile loop on the hour, every hour, until only one remains. (That runner must complete one final loop, also called a yard, to be declared the winner.) At the Backyard Ultra World Team Championship, which alternates every other year with the individual championship, each participating country simultaneously hosts its own backyard ultra with 15 runners. The team with the most cumulative laps wins.

Typically at backyard ultras, competitors are wolves looking for the elk with a limp. No one wants to look weak. No one demonstrated this formidable exterior better than Dowdle in the Last Soul Ultra this April, when his gamesmanship created the event’s most talked-about moment. But his competitive side was ubiquitous among the 15 elite backyard runners on Team USA. They each won backyard ultras to qualify; they were wolves, not elk.

Yet Team USA struggled from the start. With daytime temperatures in the 70s Fahrenheit, it felt warmer than they thought it would. The course was hilly, with over 400 feet of climbing per loop, costing them a minute or two per loop in a format where extra seconds are precious. Indeed, over the first 40 laps when all runners from all 67 countries were still in the race, the U.S. had the slowest average lap speed of 52:21—nearly seven minutes slower than the fastest country, Slovakia.

Struggling through that second night, the U.S. decided to try a different tactic. They decided to be vulnerable.

Lewis urged the team to be honest about how they were feeling because there was a good chance others could help. It took Dowdle a bit to believe, even after watching how others supported each other.

“It did take encouragement from my team to even be more of a teammate,” Dowdle told Trail Runner.

But Dowdle was enthused when, after his admission that he was struggling, Yoder suggested that they look out for each other over the next 3 miles they had to complete to keep going. Dowdle got the message: This would be a different backyard than he’d ever run before. They talked to each other through the loop and by the end they had caught up to their teammates.

“That turned the corner for me,” Dowdle said. “In a normal race, I would never say that I was falling asleep to another runner. You just would never give up that information. But that opened the door for me to be more vocal about how I was doing.”

Several other members of the U.S. squad admitted that being honest with each other and asking for help when they needed it was key to them winning the world title. Instead of acting like individuals in a last-man-standing race, they were a unit. That helped many of them run farther than they ever had before—eight Americans ran over 80 yards, or 333.3 miles—when it looked like Australia might literally run away with victory.

“When some were feeling strong, we would help those who were not feeling OK,” said Megan Smyth, who set a PR with 82 yards and was the last woman standing. “I’m pretty sure that’s how so many of us got over 80 yards.”

The backyard, despite its do-or-die nature, lends itself to camaraderie because of the way runners all start the next 4.167-mile loop together on the hour, every hour. Jon Noll qualified for Team USA by running over 440 miles at the individual world championship last year. Even there most competitors congratulated each other after each lap. “The ultra community, in general, is not exactly a cutthroat environment for the most part,” Noll said. He especially felt that sense of camaraderie this time as the miles piled up.

This is why Smyth loves the backyard format.

“There’s no incentive to win a lap, so you really do wind up cheering for each other,” Smyth said.

Still, Team USA had to get comfortable with each other in a hurry. Even with seven returning members from the third-place 2024 team it was a little awkward at first: Some had previously competed against each other, and some called each other friends. Some were rivals. Other first-timers felt a sense of awe: Smyth had imposter syndrome, which doesn’t make it easy to talk about, say, a sore ankle.

But she also welcomed the unique race set up. If a typical backyard ultra can feel crowded and chaotic, the team race with its 15 competitors feels sparse, even intimate. Smyth got her wish right away.

“I haven’t gotten to do true team running since my cross-country days,” she said. “It was just a magical experience.”

A couple team meetings over Zoom, as well as an in-person meeting before the race, helped shoo away some of the awkwardness, Lewis thought. But Smyth said Lewis helped bring the team together during the event, too, with little (even corny) things like running in a fighter jet formation and chanting “U.S.A!” for a lap.

Smyth remembers walking at night and nearly falling asleep before the Ron Express came up behind her. Ron Wireman, competing in his second team championship, struggled early in the race and needed help from others. That first night, he was eager to pay his teammates back and named himself after a train to help them through the dark.

“He said, ‘MEGAN ARE YOU AWAKE?,’” Smyth said.

Smyth, just like Dowdle, learned how to ask for help. Later in the race, as the prospect of doing another lap on the steep trail, she requested a “hill sherpa.”

The team cohesion would be tested right away as Lewis insisted they answer a question democratically: Should they run the road or the trail?

Team USA competes on the original Big’s Backyard Ultra course in mastermind Gary “Lazarus Lake” Cantrell’s literal backyard in Bell Buckle, Tennessee. On odd years during the individual championship, racers run a trail loop during the day and a road loop at night. This time it was runners’ choice throughout the race.

The road was flatter and easier, but the hard, smooth surface can be problematic for trail runners. Smyth, for instance, said she didn’t bring many pairs of road shoes. But Laz recently made “improvements” to the trail loop that made it steeper, tougher, and slower. The precious minutes saved on the road loop could be the difference between having time to recover, fuel, sleep, and even go to the bathroom, and to DNF.

“There isn’t a lot of wiggle room in a backyard,” Lewis said.

Communication was key as the team tried to accommodate runners struggling with the trail by adding more laps on the road.

“We were changing things as the race went on,” Noll said. “Sometimes you didn’t know what course you were doing [on the next lap]. Mentally that can be hard.”

Ultimately, the back and forth paid off. Eventually emphasizing the road over the trail helped the team squeeze yards from people who may not have been able to continue otherwise.

“If we hadn’t moved to the road, I don’t know if we would have won the race,” Lewis said.

As the third day burned off its final few hours, Australia had a commanding lead of 58 yards over the U.S. The Aussies still had 11 runners in the race; the U.S. was down to 9. Nicholas Steel kept announcing to his U.S. teammates just how far behind they were. More than one American admitted later that they found these updates annoying. Dowdle told himself he didn’t care and tried to enjoy the experience.

But backyard veterans will tell you that the race doesn’t end at hour 70; that’s really when it starts. One Aussie dropped at yard 70, another at 72, two at 73, and two more at 75. By yard 80, nine Aussies had dropped. They had only two runners left—a precarious place to be, given the final runner can only complete one additional lap after the penultimate runner drops. Sure enough, Australia was out by yard 88. We’re not being judgy about this: They were on their third day of running without sleep. But that brutal attrition gave the U.S. a shot.

Suddenly Steel’s updates were inspiring. They would need Dowdle and Noll, the workhorses, to keep doing their magic. But the Americans realized that they could win if they got at least half their runners to yard 75 and several past yard 80.

“The possibility that we could catch up lit a fire under my belly,” Dowdle said, “and I remember thinking, ‘Oh, maybe I do care.’”

Even the Americans who dropped relatively early decided to stay at the campsite to cheer. This was big: Dowdle finished one lap with 15 seconds to go, riding the wave of exhortation to get him across the line in time.

Lewis did what he could to keep as many runners out there as possible. He ran with those who were close to dropping, even to his detriment. At times he finished the lap with less than three minutes to go. Lewis, famously, sleeps for a few minutes after every loop, but running with others meant he wasn’t able to do that. Ultimately, he went out for yard 84 but didn’t finish it, a result that Lewis found disappointing.

“I didn’t have my own rhythm because I was helping others,” Lewis said. “My ultimate goal was to be there for the team, so I sacrificed myself and my own best race for that.”

That kind of support from teammates, along with the competitive boost the Americans got chasing down Australia, helped push some to their backyard ultra PRs. Nick Petterson made it to 84 yards, 19 more than his previous best. That’s nearly a full day more of running.

“The team needed you, and that was a really easy thing to grab onto,” Petterson said. “We needed everyone to crank up the numbers. That motivation outside of just myself was really helpful.”

Petterson thrives off that external focus anyway. During backyards, he enjoys asking others how they’re doing, even though it’s not always reciprocated.

“The team factor was a major driver when times got hard for me,” he said. “I might have gone out earlier if it wasn’t for that.”

Yoder made it 86 yards, 11 more than his qualifying mark. Ryan Snickles went 69 yards after qualifying with 55. Smyth set a PR by five yards and quit only after her ankle swelled like a balloon. Jeff Walker got 75 yards, 30 more than his qualifier. Even Steel seemed inspired by his own updates. He went 94 yards—177% of his 53-yard qualifier.

Ultimately the U.S. won by a landslide with 1,120 yards to Australia’s 1,069.

It’s the second world title for Team USA in this rapidly developing sub-sport. When the U.S. won in 2022, it was with only 860 yards. Belgium, which has won the other two team titles, took third this year—although two of their runners set the individual backyard ultra world record of 124 yards, or 516.7 miles over five days of running.

“When other runners are hanging on longer,” Lewis said, “it impacts everyone to hang on longer.”

Ultimately, Dowdle was the last American standing with 107 yards—a personal best by 13 yards, or 54 miles. Noll got the assist with 106 yards. Despite his initial reticence, Dowdle says he values moments with his teammates more than his individual national title.

“There was one lap where I broke down crying,” Dowdle said, “and Nick Petterson saw me and put his arm around me and was just with me during that time.”

Dowdle wouldn’t want the backyard format to be flooded with team events, but he wants to go back:

“I’m bummed that you have to wait two years for it again.”

#8205. The Best Ski Packs of 2027, Tested in the Backcountry

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Our 14 testers ran 18 packs through a season of fast transitions, steep bootpacks, and long days to find the best of 2027. (Photo: Rick Sorensen)

Overview: The best backcountry ski packs of 2027 include the Ortovox Venet 30 ($170) for most skiers, the Raide EX55 ($599) for expeditions, the Dynafit Radical 30 Snow Pack ($190), and the Rab Descendor 40 Ski Pack ($200) for ski mountaineering. Our 14 testers—men and women—evaluated 18 packs over a full season in Colorado, Utah, Alaska, the Alps, and more, judging fit, weight distribution, access, and durability.

When traveling in the backcountry, it’s not just what you bring but how you carry it. Intuitive access points make finding and stashing items easy, and externally fastened gear needs to stay secure without blocking pockets. But making the most of capacity is arguably the most critical feature. As our testers make tracks farther out in the mountains and become more self-reliant, they tend to reach for higher-volume packs that can fit everything they need without overloading them to the point of a skin track gear explosion. We factored comfort into all of it while testing 18 packs, narrowing the field to the best backcountry ski packs of 2027 for every type of ski adventure.

Pros and Cons + Triple-zipper access + Huge hipbelt pocket – A-frame carry blocks pack access and the diagonal carry strap was a little tricky to access

Ski packs work best when you can avoid taking them all the way off and rooting through the main compartment when you need to pull out gear. That means shorter stops in the skin track—if you stop at all—which helps you keep momentum and body temperature up on cold days. The Venet 30 features triple-zipper access to the main compartment, which let our tester quickly grab his water flask while skinning around Hemavan, Sweden, and Helgeland, Norway. The large hipbelt was also a tester favorite. “While I loved the elastic waist on the Ortovox Freerider, the normal hip strap with the pocket on the Venet was a huge plus for general touring,” said one. “On longer days I kept snacks in it and on more freeride days I kept a GoPro, for which easy access allowed me to actually remember to pull my cam out before descents.”

Testers called this the most ergonomic and versatile pack they’ve used from Ortovox, thanks to its simplicity, the comfortable adjustability of its straps, and its full-contact back panel. The mini top pocket was well sized—not too deep and easy to access—and the hidden mini pocket in the avalanche tool compartment was useful for carrying an emergency bivy and small med kit, keeping them “out of the way” of the rest of your gear.

This pack’s ideal use is general touring with the occasional bootpack, but it’s capable as a more technical bag when ropes may be required. It performs well as a freeride sidecountry bag or on longer tours—comfortable for mellow days and functional for technical ones.

Features that would make this pack even more user-friendly: a small zip on the right back side to mirror the bottom zipper for water access, the ability to carry two ice axes (the elastic cord holds only one), and easier access to the pack when using side ski-carry.

Pros and Cons + Modular volume + Rolltop closure – No external helmet carry

Schlepping all your gear on a big hut trip or expedition-style endeavor has long presented a dilemma: how to carry a pack big enough for everything at basecamp while also having a daypack small enough for lighter missions. Bringing two packs is inefficient, but skiing with a few items jiggling loose in a giant frame pack feels cumbersome. The Raide EX55 expands to 75L and carries enormous loads, then cinches down once you’ve emptied most items out, so it skis like a little daypack. “During our big four-day ski traverse out of Bishop in the Eastern Sierra, I’d get to the base of a couloir, fill a bivy sack with all our junk, cinch the pack down, and boot up like I had a regular ski pack on,” said our Mammoth-based tester. “It skis incredibly well given how much gear it can swallow.”

Raide accounts for the added weight with thicker shoulder and hip straps and better load lifters than its smaller counterparts, the LF30 and LF40. All of it is ideal for heavier hauls. The EX55 doesn’t just turn into a giant sack and skimp on key features. You can still deploy your probe without taking off your pack—ideal for glacier travel of any kind—and the same goes for the shovel with the pack on one shoulder. Testers called the ski carry systems excellent, and being able to grab an ice tool without removing the pack is invaluable in steep bootpacks. “This pack strips backcountry skiing down to its absolute essentials but lets you do it on a bigger scale,” said one.

The one complaint we heard was that the EX55 lacks the external drop sleeve found in the LF30 and LF40 for carrying helmets and skins, so when the pack is loaded for overnight carries, it’s tough to stuff skins in and out of the front zip pocket. It also makes the pack very tall when fully loaded with a helmet inside.

Weight: 2.31 lbs Size: Women’s, Universal

Pros and Cons + Thick back panel padding + Easy-access diagonal-carry bungee cord strap – Not ideal for those who pack extra gear

When you’re banging out hot laps, your pack should feel like part of your body. This one holds tight to smaller female torsos and disappeared on the back of another Sierra tester last spring as she skied 1,500- to 7,000-foot days on Mount Shasta, in the Eastern Sierra and at Lake Tahoe’s Rubicon Peak. “This pack skied really well, and gear that’s good enough to disappear is my favorite,” she said  after testing other packs with hipbelts that didn’t curve as ergonomically as this one.

Testers appreciated the top, rear-panel, and side zips, which made it easy to organize their stuff inside and keep things like crampons and water readily accessible. The avy gear gets its own pocket with a wide zipper, and an ice axe can be removed without taking the pack off, as can skis with a skimo-style diagonal carry bungee strap.

At 30 liters, it’s right on the edge of fitting everything you might want to carry on a day tour. “When I went out to the Norman Clyde Couloir, conditions were cold and windy, so I wanted to carry more than I usually do for a day tour,” said our tester. “The pack fit snacks, 1 liter of water, a hardshell, a puffy, ski and boot crampons, an ice axe, a helmet, a slender rescue sled, avy gear, a small first aid kit, and two pairs of gloves. I was definitely worried about busting the zipper, but it held all day.” The load lifters worked well to support this weight, and the thick back panel kept hard items like water bottles from poking into her back. If you prefer to bring this much stuff or more on most outings, you may find this pack a little too small.

Pros and Cons + Spot-on fit + Long side zipper accesses items of any size – Wobbly elastic diagonal ski carry

Spring ski mountaineering missions can mean longer days, longer approaches, and extra gear—crampons, more water, sometimes ropes—so you need a pack that carries it all in an efficient, functional arrangement. Loading it up is one thing; accessing it is another. The Descendor 40 balances both with a few key features. Our Colorado-based tester was a big fan of the side-access zipper, which is functionally useless if it isn’t long enough. This one is plenty long, and it was the only access point he needed while touring. He could easily pull out anything inside, including a large DSLR camera, skins, and a food bag, and he opened the rolltop closure only during full transitions.

The pack also has the best integration of hydration features. “On the right strap, there is a perfect pocket to carry a soft flask, including a strap to secure the flask against jostling,” our tester said. “I have lost soft flasks while skiing in other packs and am not worried about that on this pack. On the left shoulder strap, there is a small zippered pocket that is an appropriate size to carry items like gels, sunscreen, lip balm, etc. Overall, these features made it easy to stay hydrated and sunscreened on a fast and light ski tour.”

Testers lauded the comfortable back panel, wide hip straps, padded shoulder straps, and load lifters when needed. The pack carries weight well and fits true to size.

This pack is designed for long, efficient ski tours and glaciated summit pushes where ropes and technical gear are needed. It has features for ski mountaineering and carries additional gear like ice tools, with a gear loop for carabiners and a system for quickly strapping skis to the pack. The rolltop is an attempt to make the pack more versatile—a 40L pack that can act as a 25L—but it needs some refinement to better accommodate smaller volumes. Our tester also found the elastic strap for diagonal ski carry too long, and his skis bounced around while bootpacking couloirs.

Built for fast pow laps and and slackcountry days, the Dakine Heli 2.0 is everything you need to stay well equipped on your next mountain adventure. From diagonal ski and splitboard carry to vertical or horizontal snowboard carry, it doesn’t matter your style—it can get your gear wherever you need to go. The pack’s fleece-lined pockets keep your goggles smudge-free, and the snow tool sleeves keep your smaller items organized and accessible. And maybe most importantly, RECCO Technology helps keep you searchable in case of an avalanche or rescue.

Weight: 2.1 lbs (35L, S/M) Sizes: S/M, M/L

Pros and Cons + Easy access to inside storage + Removable snowboard carry straps – Avalanche tool pocket is too large

It’s a bold move to update a classic product, but Black Diamond took a leap on the tried-and-true Cirque by making several big changes. The brand added a side zipper to access the main compartment and more durable materials, including a PFC-free 210D nylon fabric and Dynex grid that’s stronger than the older version and more water repellent. Testers loved these new features and didn’t encounter any durability issues during the whole season of slamming the pack on and off in quick transitions with sharp ski edges and tools rubbing on the outside.

The new Cirque 35 excels on spring missions in the alpine, where quick access to crampons, an ice axe, and other gear is key. “I love a roll-top pack, and this is one feature that I really appreciate,” says one tester who toured it during winter and spring days around Aspen, Colorado. “I was able to throw in an extra layer for tours without hesitation because of the space it offered and how easy it was to get in and out, especially with the large side zipper.” The diagonal ski carry system with a bottom loop and top webbing strap with a hook was quick and easy to deploy in transition, and the ice-axe bungees were a breeze to unfasten on unexpected sections of steep terrain.

Our 6’1″ tester thought the pack was a bit short, and some disliked the hassle of opening both the webbing hook and roll-top buckle to get inside. Snowboard straps are sturdy but removable when you don’t need to carry a board on your pack.

Pros and Cons + Excellent freedom of movement + Compact fit – Limited carrying capacity

Skiing or snowboarding with too much extra space in a backpack allows the contents to rattle around inside, which can be an annoying distraction. Our Montana tester didn’t have that problem when hiking the ridge at Bridger Bowl, their local ski resort, with this compact, 15-liter pack with clever pocket placement and internal organization. Thanks to the low profile, it was comfortable enough to wear on the chairlift, and the fit felt snug while riding, too, with padding in all the right spots on the upper back, hips, and shoulder straps.

“It didn’t flop around at all like bigger packs do when empty, nor did it limit my movement in bumps or when really laying down carves,” another Montana tester said after securing the pack’s wide, sturdy hipbelt. They rode with this pack at Bridger Bowl in sub-freezing temperatures, requiring extra fuel and layers, and didn’t feel that it was too bulky. He also appreciated the glove-friendly A-frame and vertical ski carry options on short sidecountry hikes and bootpacks, along with snowboard straps and an internal avalanche tool compartment for sidecountry missions.

Overall, this is a small, space-efficient pack with smart pockets (fleece-lined goggle and external side zip) for short missions just beyond the gates or for fully-supplied resort laps.

Packs come in various sizes to fit different torso lengths, so measure your spine from the base of your neck to the top of your hips and choose your size accordingly. Torso lengths generally range from 15 inches, or size XS, to 20-plus inches, or size L. Because fit is the single most significant factor in pack comfort and carry, we recommend going to your local gear shop wearing the layers you plan to tour in and trying packs on. The hipbelt should securely wrap your iliac crest, and the back panel shouldn’t hit the back of your head when you’re wearing a helmet.

If half-day backcountry tours are your norm, choose a lower-volume pack, 20 to 30 liters, that fits just the essentials—shovel, probe, water, extra layers, snacks. If you typically spend full days in the backcountry, you’ll want a higher-volume pack, 30 to 40 liters, with room for the extra supplies you’ll need out in the elements. For overnight trips and expeditions, look for a 50-plus-liter pack.

Also make sure your avalanche shovel and probe slip easily in and out of the dedicated avy pouch in an emergency, and that the pack is big enough and organized enough for how you tour. Don’t be afraid to size up if you’re unsure how much space you’ll need—a few extra liters of empty space won’t weigh you down much. If you want to secure your skis to your pack, look for an A-frame or diagonal ski-carry strap system and back-panel suspension that can support the extra weight. The same goes for your helmet: most packs have integrated helmet carry, but not all do, so double-check if it’s essential to you.

Always carry avalanche safety equipment when traveling in the backcountry. That means wearing a beacon and carrying a shovel and probe in your pack. You’ll also need extra layers, a helmet, sufficient hydration—including something hot in an insulated bottle on longer backcountry days—snacks, a first-aid kit, and a basic repair kit.

To nail down the best ski packs of 2027, we seeded 18 products with 14 different testers. Each tester was matched to packs according to their planned objectives, body type, ability level, and testing environments. Then we set testers loose in the mountains, mainly in Colorado, Utah, Wyoming, Montana, Washington, California, and Alaska, with a few trips to Scandinavia and the Alps. Testers jammed gear into packs, stuffed them shut, and pushed them to their limits on both rugged and mellow ski ascents and descents.

We focused on newly designed packs with practical, ski-specific features that make traveling on snow easier, safer, and more enjoyable. We also brought tried-and-true, unchanged models into the mix so you’re seeing the best of what’s available. Comfort is a must, even for packs meant to carry smaller, lighter loads, as is durability, so we asked testers to evaluate straps, back panels, and hipbelt carry alongside the quality of materials.

Every time a pack went out, testers filled out feedback forms assessing fit, weight distribution, ease of access, and even pocket size and placement. Testers noted how easy it was to find what they needed, transition in the skin track, and carry their skis and boards on their backs while climbing steep couloirs. After a full season of rigorous testing, we selected the cream of the crop and reviewed those packs here.

Scott Yorko is a former gear editor for Backpacker, SKI, TransWorld SNOWboarding, and Outside. He lives in Colorado, where he splits his ski time between the world-class resorts around Aspen and the backcountry terrain of the West Elk Mountains. He loves to chase storms and visit pow-shredding friends, many of whom tested this year’s crop of ski packs in places like Alaska, Jackson Hole, the Sierra, Utah, and the Colorado Rockies.

#8204. After Testing 122 Pieces of Gear, We Found the Best Climbing Gear of Fall 2026

Gear testing above 12,000 feet on the golden granite of Chamonix's Aiguille du Midi. It's a hard job, but someone's got to do it. (Photo: Anthony Walsh)

Rock climbing season doesn’t end when snow hits the high country. Some of the best conditions of the year are right around the corner: cool temps, ample shade, and just the right amount of humidity in the air. Unless you’re sharpening your ice tools, don’t give up on the rock (or plastic) season just yet—with the right gear, you’re in for the best season of your life.

Climbing’s gear-testing team has spent all summer sweating it out with the latest and greatest so you don’t have to. We tested 28 harnesses, 27 pairs of climbing shoes, 30 pairs of approach shoes, 9 ropes, and 28 backpacks—a healthy mix of new items and longtime favorites. Some of the gear was good, some was great, and a lot of it missed the mark: bruised hips, sore feet, exploding packs—it’s all part of the gear-testing game.

2026 was the year of the hyper-specific shoe. Although notable all-arounders made it onto our list, the real highlights were the shoes who didn’t try to do too much. One shoe felt about as stiff as a crampon, with its new-age carbon insert, and powered us up numerous vert testpieces; another had about as much support as a woolen sock (but, like, in a good way!); and the best shoe I’ve ever used for offwidths is absolutely terrible for finger cracks. Perhaps 2026 is the year of the shoe quiver.

The harness is the one piece of gear that will make or break your day on the wall. In an effort to find the best climbing harness available, we put everything from fast-and-light alpine G-strings to beefy big-wallers to the test this year, taking them on trips from the cold Canadian alpine to the steep walls of Devil’s Tower to overhung sport routes at The Red.

Unlike this year’s crop of rock shoes, my favorite climbing packs worked hard to serve multiple niches. One versatile alpine-climbing pack carried anywhere from one to four days of mountain kit with ease. And a new haul bag might just be the last pack (and airplane carry on) a rock climber will ever need.

The best climbing ropes are a tough category of gear to review because, these days, almost all are well made and perform great right out of the package. It’s only after hard wear—climbing pitch after pitch in rain, snow, and ice, coiling and uncoiling on dirt and sand, and taking some big whippers—that a rope reveals its true colors.

Helmets are our best defense against rockfall and weird whippers while climbing outdoors. And after years of writing accident reports—often of climbers who took a seemingly benign fall, before something weird happened—I regularly note how fortunate the climber was to be wearing one. When shopping for a helmet, take the time to find one that’s comfortable, lightweight, breathable, and fits properly—because actually liking your helmet makes you far more likely to wear it.
