#8161. 4 Speed Records and Free Solos That Went Down in the Last 2 Weeks

Becca Droz (left) and Kate Kelleghan (right) set a new female speed record on the classic 'Naked Edge' in Boulder's Eldorado Canyon on October 26. (Photo: Jon and Jess Glassberg / Courtesy COROS)

Maybe it’s the erratic weather pressures of El Niño, or perhaps there’s just a particularly competitive spirit in the air right now. In the past two weeks, several climbers have broken records, made improbable repeats, and soloed terrain that would make many of us squirm.

Last week, we looked into the culture of free solo speed climbing in Boulder, Colorado, speaking with several athletes about the risks and influences they carry in their high-stakes sport. On the heels of this deep dive, two of the athletes who spoke to us went on to break additional records of their own within the past few days. This includes a new FKT on Half Dome and a fresh women’s speed record on Eldorado’s most famous route.

More broadly, we’ve seen a few historic achievements in the past couple weeks by free soloists and speed athletes alike. Here are four record-breakers we’ve been watching lately, in chronological order.

Just a few weeks ago, Alex Honnold told Adrian Ballinger that he thought someone would likely repeat his free solo of El Capitan before anyone dared to repeat his insanely hard linkup of peaks and scrambles in Red Rock. Back in 2022, he dubbed that linkup the Honnold Ultimate Red Rock Traverse (aka the HURT).

Honnold will have to eat his words, because on October 19, Nevada climbing guide Nik Mirhashemi put down the world’s second HURT, with slight modifications. Friends have been calling his revised route the NURT: Nik’s Ultimate Red Rock Traverse.

For the NURT, the 36-year-old skipped four non-technical summits, including Goodman, Buffalo Wall, Sandstone North, and Limestone North. Instead he traversed from White Rock Peak to ascend the seven-pitch Frigid Air Buttress (5.9+; 800ft). He then continued to the top of Icebox Peak. “Basically, I had to choose between adding Frigid Air or sticking with the OG route, where those nontechnical peaks are,” Mirhashemi said. “I didn’t want to skip Frigid Air as it is quite classic.” He also called the section he swapped in one of the traverse’s “routefinding cruxes.”

Despite the variations, Mirhashemi doesn’t think there’s a significant difference in effort level. He said that though his traverse is slightly shorter, he added more technical terrain, making the difference essentially a wash. “Nice to add a little personal flair to these things I suppose,” Mirhashemi said.

“I wanted to try the HURT for similar reasons to Alex,” Mirhashemi told Climbing. “Super long days of soloing moderate terrain is one of my favorite things to do. I’ve been coming out to Red Rock for many years and just moved here a year ago. I’m always looking for new ways to challenge myself and it just made sense as a goal right in my backyard.”

Last spring, Mirhashemi made his first HURT attempt, then completed several “scoping missions”  to prepare for his fall go. “I was never sure if I could pull it off,” he said. “Stoked it’s not haunting me anymore!”

Kate Kelleghan has been busy breaking her own record again, shaving minutes and seconds off the female fastest known time on The Naked Edge (5.11b), a classic multi-pitch in Colorado’s Eldorado Canyon.

Kelleghan, along with her French partner Laura Pineau, already held the record for the route’s women’s speed record of 37 minutes and eight seconds, which was 32 seconds faster than Kelleghan’s previous go in 2021 with Becca Droz, a Boulder-based climbing guide.

In late October, Kelleghan began working the route again with Droz. And on October 26, the athletes set a new record of 36 minutes, 26 seconds, shaving 42 seconds off the previous record.

“Becca and I were the team that started the women’s record, so taking it back together feels full circle for our friendship and our community,” Kelleghan said. Droz added that being able to track splits, as well as time out the approach, actual climb, and descent with their COROS watches “was a game changer”; both women are COROS athletes.

The men’s record is held by John Ebers and Ben Wilbur at 24 minutes and 14 seconds.

Just a couple months after smashing the speed record on the First Flatiron in Boulder, 32-year-old American climber Michael Reese established a fastest known time on Yosemite’s Half Dome on October 28. In so doing, he broke an 11-year FKT set by the late Dean Potter. Reese climbed the 2,000-foot batholith from the Mist Trailhead to its summit in 1 hour, 12 minutes, and 58 seconds. He followed Potter’s original line up Grizzly Gully, then free soloed Snake Dike (5.7 R; 800ft). He broke Potter’s previous record set on May 3, 2015 by about six minutes.

A few days after his Half Dome lap, our reporter Holly Chen, who also reported on his Flatiron speed record, caught up with Reese.

“In 2021, one of Dean Potter’s good friends told me about this as a potential record to try. He became one of my main climbing partners,” Reese told Chen. Since then, Reese has made 16 attempts and several scouting missions before his record-breaking attempt in late October.

“Records are made to be broken. I’m not gonna be surprised if it’s broken one day,” Reese said.

In the second-hardest free solo by a woman, Aleksandra “Ola” Taistra climbed a seven-pitch, 720-foot route in Sardinia, Italy on October 29. The line in question is Margarites (7a+/5.12a) up the limestone cliffs of Monte Oddeu. Established in 1998 by Andrea Calvo and Lorenzo Nadali, the route has become one of Sardinia’s “most sought-after lines,” according to Taistra. It includes a bouldery 7a+/5.12a crux pitch high off the deck; two 7a/5.11d pitches; and four additional pitches graded 6c+/5.11c, 6b+/5.11a, 6a+/5.10c, and 5c/5.10a, in order of descending difficulty.

“Climbing Margarites for the first time I thought that climbing it without a rope was impossible for me,” Taistra shared with Climbing, “and that’s exactly how the plan was born—first get to know the route, and then properly assess my skills.” Taistra says that when she finished free soloing Margarites, she thought: “Oh, that’s it?”

Taistra already put down one of the hardest female free solos in history in May, when she climbed Alfredo Alfredo (5.11d/7a) ropeless. Now, the only known harder female free solo belongs to French legend Catherine Destivelle, who climbed an unnamed route in Mali without a rope that she said maxed out at 7b or 5.12a/b.

In May, 44-year-old Taistra told Climbing that free soloing gives her “so much peace” and feels less stressful than climbing with a rope. The 44-year-old climber rehearses her routes on toprope until she feels confident in the moves.

#8160. Three Ground Rules for Getting Outside

Getting outside is for everyone. That’s what Sierra is all about, finding top active and outdoor brands at prices that make it accessible to try a bunch of new adventures. That’s the spirit behind Sierra in the Sierras, in which Dylan Efron (Emmy-winning co-producer of Netflix’s Down to Earth with Zac Efron) hits the trail with a friend to try something completely new.

With gear and apparel from Sierra and guidance from Outside editors, in episode one Dylan explores the Sierra Nevada with Danielle Fishel, Boy Meets World icon and Dancing With the Stars co-star. Along with new adventures, they learn some fundamental principles for having fun outside. Ones you can use yourself.

Whether it’s your first hike or just your first hike today, no one likes to be uncomfortable. The right gear helps. If you’re like Danielle, a self-proclaimed “indoor person,” or simply trying a new activity, you’ll want to focus on comfort and versatility above all else. The aim is to A) feel good while enjoying your new hobby and B) have the freedom to explore further as you progress. The gear choices at Sierra make this easy, thanks to a combo of trusted brands, great prices, and an ever evolving inventory of fresh finds in-store and online.

Like most things in life, getting outside is better with friends. In the first episode of Sierra in the Sierras, Dylan recruits Outside’s Climbing Editor, Anthony Walsh, to give Danielle a lesson in bouldering. And that’s just the start. Next up is slacklining and then a highlining adventure.

If you’re nervous about trying a new sport, having a friend or guide to show you the ropes (literally or figuratively) can make a big difference. But the most important thing is trying something new—it can be just as fun to be complete beginners together.

Dylan and Danielle got the chance to explore the stunning terrain in the Sierra Nevada around Lake Tahoe, but you don’t have to wait for your next big trip to take an adventure outside. Wherever you live, there are more natural playgrounds in your area than you think. Use apps like Trailforks and Gaia GPS to plan your next outing, and discover the outdoors in your own backyard.

The world says to go harder, faster, stronger—but Sierra says, “go however you want.” From hiking up mountains to strolling down the block, Sierra loves it all. Whether you’re athletic or more athletish, Sierra has tons of active & outdoor essentials like top-brand gear, footwear, apparel & more for everything you’re into, all at unexpectedly low prices.

The weather outside may be frightful but there’s nothing like some rolling laughter and hilarious Christmas jokes to warm you right up (except, maybe cocoa). If you’re looking for the funniest Christmas jokes for kids, you’ve come to the right place. We’ve got Santa jokes, elf jokes, snowman jokes, and when you’re done, be sure to get them giggling with our ultimate list of jokes for kids, funny dad jokes, and birthday jokes.

1. What should you give your parents at Christmas?A list of what you want.

#8158. Colorado Trail and Continental Divide Trail ‘Extensively Damaged’ After Severe Flooding: Here’s What We Know

In just over a week, two massive flooding events hit southwestern Colorado, destroying homes, businesses, and infrastructure across numerous mountain towns. But property is not all that the floods affected. Parts of both the Continental Divide Trail (CDT) and the Colorado Trail (CT) suffered damage that locals and trail organizations are calling “extensive” and “severe”, and which could take a very long time to repair.

“Rebuilding these damaged sections will not be quick, easy, or cheap,” Paul Talley, executive director of the Colorado Trail Foundation (CTF), said in a November 5 update on the floods. “But we are committed to rebuilding.”

As many of these areas are still inaccessible, there is very little confirmed information on their current state. Videos circulating online show missing bridges at key river crossings, and reports from the USFS and other agencies indicate that trailheads are damaged, and “heavy debris” is blocking some sections. But there has yet to be a full, official report on damage to these trails.

Here is what we know so far based on official updates, local reports, and videos.

Junction Creek is the CT’s southernmost section. Its trailhead, just outside of Durango, is also the CT’s southern terminus. Junction Creek Trail crosses multiple footbridges over the creek along its 19-mile stretch. A conditions report on the U.S. Forest Service webpage says that a “Huge rock and heavy debris” is currently blocking the trail about a half-mile from the trailhead. One video claims shows an area along Junction Creek Trail near Gudy’s Rest, where a footbridge has been washed away completely. The USFS posted its own video of the road to Junction Creek to Facebook, showing a new “20-foot waterfall” over the edge of the destroyed road.

“There is no doubt that trails across the forest have suffered severe damage,” the San Juan National Forest wrote. “For example, we know that the Colorado Trail along Junction Creek has largely been obliterated and that the trail bridge is gone. In some sections the trail is buried underneath riverflow that was re-routed during the flooding.”

Authorities said that recovery work would likely not begin until spring and summer 2027 due to weather, and discouraged hikers from even attempting to set out on the area’s trails.

“Record flooding across Southwest Colorado has left San Juan National Forest roads, trails, and other infrastructure inaccessible, severely damaged, and, in many cases, impassable,” another post reads. “Don’t become a statistic — rescue will not be readily available due to the current demand for search and rescue services.”

Another video posted to Instagram shows the sign that many hikers use for their CT terminus photo now standing directly at the edge of a tall wash filled with flood debris.

The CTF said that it will be working over the winter with USFS, local partners, and volunteers to determine timelines and project budgets for the restoration efforts.

“It will be months before we can better understand what the next steps need to be on the sections damaged by climate events this season,” wrote Talley in his November 5 update.

There is even less information regarding damage to the CDT, which also passes through the flood-affected areas of Southwestern Colorado.

The Continental Divide Trail Coalition (CDTC) posted on Facebook on October 23, warning hikers that flooding had made “travel to and from the CDT trailhead at Wolf Creek Pass impossible,” and that “hikers may need to make alternate plans to avoid the area.”

On November 2, the CDTC posted another update for CDT travelers. “The extent of damage to the CDT, access roads, and CDT communities is still unknown,” it said. While the interactive map on its website shows no current closures of the trail due to flooding, the CDTC advised hikers to use “extreme caution and check with local authorities before visiting.”

Backpacker reached out to the CDTC for comment, but did not receive a response by the time of publication.

While the full extent of the damage to these trails remains to be seen, what’s certain is that the CTF, CDTC, USFS, and other state agencies have a great deal of restoration work to do next summer. Volunteers will be in high demand, and Talley, of the CTF, promised to be open about how hikers can help.

“While we do not yet know what it will take to rebuild, we do know what we will need,” Talley wrote. “We will need our supporters, we will need our dedicated volunteers, and we will need that community spirit that makes the CT so special.”

#8152. New Climbing Gym in Massachusetts Plans to Give Away All Its Profits

Berkshire Boulders General Manager Austen McNulty (left) and founder Nick Friedman (right) inside the gym. (Photo: Courtesy Nick Friedman)

The United States has become known for corporate climbing gyms and nationwide chains fraught with labor issues that charge high dollar. A recent analysis by an adventure travel company, which leverages 2026 data as well as the Climbing Business Journal’s 2025 trends report, declared that “the United States is the industry’s laboratory” when it comes to mega-gyms backed by private equity. As climbing becomes more popular, and thus more profitable, one may question whether these gyms will inevitably become the norm.

But in Great Barrington, a small town of a little more than 7,000 residents in Western Massachusetts, entrepreneur Nick Friedman is moving in the opposite direction: starting a new, independent gym that gives away all its profits.

You can trace the 38-year-old’s vision for an altruistic gym back to his childhood, when his dad put his career on hold to demand that General Electric clean up the river that ran through town—and Friedman’s property. In the 1970s, General Electric dumped polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs) into the Housatonic River, so Friedman’s dad fought to hold the company liable. GE settled, paying $250 million.

In the process, Friedman learned the importance of activism. The cause close to Friedman’s heart is climbing access, which is not exactly easy to come by in Great Barrington or the Berkshires—but not for a lack of rock. While he calls the climbing in Great Barrington world-class, he says that privately owned land and conservation organizations that don’t understand the value of climbing make access a problem.

“Great Barrington is this unique case study in incredible climbing that is barred from true public domain due to land access challenges,” said Friedman, who has been deeply involved in local access work. In 2023, Friedman, who also serves on the board of the Western Massachusetts Climbers’ Coalition (WMCC), purchased a 70-acre parcel in the Farley Ledges climbing area. This bought WMCC time to organize the permits and funding to purchase it from Friedman earlier this year. While Farley Ledges currently remains closed due to an access issue involving a private landowner, WMCC is raising funds to construct a new parking lot and trail to reopen climbing.

Making these land purchases and forging the agreements necessary to maintain and expand access in Western Massachusetts takes a lot of resources, Friedman explains. That’s where his new gym, Berkshire Boulders, which opens on November 6, comes in. He plans to donate 100% of his profits to community organizations, including WMCC and Access Fund.

“The WMCC is very excited about the opening of Berkshire Boulders and the potential it has to positively impact climbing access in Western Massachusetts,” said Regina Madden, a WMCC board member and chair of its communications committee. Protecting and maintaining access requires ongoing resources, so a local business committed to supporting that mission creates an excellent opportunity. In addition, Berkshire Boulders can serve to bridge the gap between indoor and outdoor climbing, helping to foster a stronger sense of stewardship and community.

While Friedman may pursue nonprofit status down the line, he says it was faster to get the gym off the ground as a business that gave away its profits, rather than a 501(c)3 nonprofit. And as someone who has specialized professionally in startups, he adds that he’s always been “intrigued” by hybrid models that blend for-profit business models with nonprofit values.

Currently, the organizations Berkshire Boulders plans to support include WMCC and Access Fund, as well as non-climbing local organizations including the Railroad Street Youth Project and Greenagers, which fosters sustainability work among youth.

“I felt that a climbing gym could play a central role in that effort and become this anchor and the starting point for a broader vision of bringing outdoor recreation more front and center in this small town,” Friedman said.

Friedman doesn’t see accessibility as a binary, “indoors or outdoors” issue; he views it holistically. This is why he’s made it the gym’s mission to improve climbing access indoors and out. He envisions a gym as a place where you can learn the sport, meet partners, and find people to help you make the gym-to-crag transition. In Friedman’s view, that gym-to-crag transition is the end game. That’s why he decorated Berkshire Boulders’ walls with photographs of Great Barrington rock, and rents out crashpads to climbers who want to try bouldering outside, but lack the gear.

But the other end game is community, which he says is hard to foster when you’re answering to private equity investors. Berkshire Boulders’ KPIs will instead revolve “around community impact.”

One way he’s doing that is by offering hardship memberships. Each month, Berkshire Boulders will award free memberships to low-income individuals through a lottery system. This addresses the known problem of affordability in the gym industry—one so notable that the American Alpine Club declared it an access issue in 2024. Friedman says he’s already approved one hardship membership application, but doesn’t have a monthly quota in mind yet. “We do expect to expand that program significantly over the next several months,” Friedman said.

A focus on community KPIs, however, will not come at the expense of a high-quality bouldering facility. Friedman insists that he is committed to a top-tier facility. He is partnering with local hold-maker Decoy and plans to change the setting across the 15-foot-high walls every two weeks. The gym also features a custom-built, “artistically created” adjustable spray wall. Using the Clift app, climbers will be able to set sequences, replicate local outdoor problems, and track leaderboards.

Currently, for Friedman, Berkshire Boulders is a passion project. His personal endgame is not to make a living off the gym—he still works full-time as the chief strategy officer at a small-batch cannabis startup. He also hired an experienced general manager to run the gym. Rather, that Friedman hopes to ultimately do is drive positive change in his local climbing community.

“Personally, I would love to see the Great Barrington climbing become a published resource for the public,” Friedman said. It’s a long game, but a worthy one, in his view, to turn the local climbing from an underground, tricky access dance to a veritable destination with routes documented on Mountain Project, a guidebook, and formal parking and approach trails.

Beyond local impact, could Berkshire Boulders, if successful, inspire a rising tide of small, mission-driven gyms in this era of indoor climbing corporatization? Friedman believes smaller gyms with a focus on community have a better shot at bringing together passionate climbers than the larger conglomerate gyms. “I would love to see an expansion of smaller independent gyms regionally,” he says.

#8150. Calling Washington Backpackers: This $5,000 Grant Could Fund Your PCT Thru-Hike

Walking may be free, but a thru-hike is decidedly expensive: Some Pacific Crest Trail trekkers run up a bill north of $10,000 during a months-long hike. That cost, plus the need to take off work for half a year, presents massive barriers to many would-be thru-hikers.

Seattleite Geoff Burg knows this—and he wants to help. With fellow Washington hikers Keya Gillenwater and Madelyn Scherrer, Burg launched the Pacific Crest Trail Grant in 2025 to award $5,000 to a Washington-based hiker with dreams of completing the trail.

Burg’s connection to the PCT goes back a decade. The attorney was hiking with his kids near Stevens Pass in 2016 when he came across some hikers in distress. Burg volunteered to drive the duo, a pair of PCT thru-hikers in their 60s, into town for medical supplies, then offered them a place to stay in his family’s home. The couple told Burg all about their thru-hike and ultralight philosophy—and the encounter stuck with him.

Over the next several years, Burg chipped away at a section hike of the Washington segment of the PCT. He fell in love with being on the trail, alone or with his kids, and with the greater hiking community around it. Several years later, a conversation with his massage therapist sparked the idea of a scholarship. Well established in his career, and with experience as an advisor for a youth outdoor leadership program, Burg was in a position to help others achieve their long trail dreams.

“We give scholarships for football and baseball and everything else,” he says. “Why not for hiking?”

So he connected with former mentees Gillenwater and Scherrer, a PCT alum, and formed a committee. The grant would offer financial support to a young Washingtonian hoping to complete the long trail.

Burg especially wanted to support young hikers with a financial need; applicants must be between the ages of 18 and 33, with strong ties to Washington state. They should also be able to demonstrate past backpacking experience, which Burg hopes will improve the recipient’s chances of succeeding on a thru-hike and paying the experience forward through volunteer projects like youth outreach or LNT education. Grant recipients who meet that criteria are chosen via a lottery, and must stay in touch with the grant committee during their hikes. Burg emphasizes that the process is not merit-based.

“We already have a community of people that can do this or who want to do this, but within that broader community, there’s so many people that can’t afford it,” he says.

Thirty-two-year-old Seattleite Kayla Provost was the grant’s first recipient. She completed her trek in September 2026, and says she couldn’t have finished the thru-hike without the financial support.

Provost had previously worked as a naturalist guide and, as a Washington resident, felt deeply connected to the Cascades. After losing her mom a few years prior, Provost felt compelled to change her lifestyle. She felt called to the PCT, but financial hurdles posed challenges. After searching “grants for thru-hiking” online, Provost stumbled across a Reddit post about the PCT Grant.

“The grant was truly a lifeline for me,” she says. “Beyond the financial support, the monthly check-ins with the grant committee gave me a sense of accountability and reminded me I had people cheering me on.”

She says the experience redoubled her desire to facilitate outdoor experiences for other people.

“It is incredibly powerful to make a choice, trust yourself enough to follow through, and learn to be comfortable with the uncomfortable,” she says. “The trail offered me a deep sense of confidence, gratitude, and trust in my own ability to navigate the unknown.”

The grant will fund its second thru-hiker in 2027. Through donations, Burg hopes to grow the program into a self-sustaining fund to support more hikers on more trails.

Applications for prospective 2027 PCT thru-hikers are currently open. Washingtonians who meet the criteria can apply by January 31.

#8149. What to Expect at Boulder’s First Sundance Film Festival Coming January 2027

Sundance Film Festival is coming to Boulder, Colorado, in 2027. (Photo: Hyoung Chang/The Denver Post)

Since 1985, the Sundance Film Festival has been showcasing independent films and drawing thousands of cinema-loving travelers to Park City, Utah. But starting in 2027, Sundance has a new home—the largest independent film festival in the country will be landing in Boulder, Colorado, from January 21 to 31.

Boulderites should brace themselves for a massive influx of visitors; last year, Park City saw 85,472 in-person festival attendees. “The Sundance Film Festival outgrew Park City, maybe 10 or 15 years ago,” Boulder film commissioner Bruce Borowski says. “At some point they had to move just to accommodate the crowds and the success of the festival.”

As a local, I’ve been able to witness the mounting anticipation firsthand. I was present at the celebratory press conference at Boulder Theater in March 2025 when Governor Jared Polis stated, “What excites me the most is that we are opening the door in Colorado for artists from across the world to showcase their stories and to become part of our story.” It’s a big win for the city both culturally and economically, but it’s also an opportunity for visitors to experience the all-around appeal of Boulder. Between attending film screenings and rubbing elbows with the filmmakers and actors in town, there are award-winning restaurants to enjoy, mountainous terrain to hike and ski, and can’t-miss tourist hot spots to explore.

The decision to bring Sundance to Boulder was based largely on the city’s natural beauty and creative community, which align with the original vision of the festival. Aside from being home to Sundance founder Robert Redford’s alma mater, CU Boulder, the city’s walkable downtown and convenient location make it a great fit for the event.

“Being located near an international airport, Boulder is really easy to get to,” explains Cris Jones, director of strategic partnerships for the city of Boulder “It’s right up against the mountains, and you get to have a mountain experience—without having to go over any mountain passes to get here.”

Unlike the festival experience in Park City, where film screenings and activations were more spread out, the Boulder experience will be more centralized; all venues—which include Boulder Theater, Chautauqua Auditorium, and eTown Hall—will be within about a two-mile radius.

“It’s more connected and accessible,” Paula DuPré Pesmen, managing director of festival and institute operations at Sundance Institute says. “It will be easy to get around from venue to venue, from panels to films, from restaurants to shops.” People can take advantage of dedicated Sundance Film Festival shuttles, along with free HOP bus service, shared e-bike passes, and free Regional Transportation District (RTD) transportation to and from Boulder. Once you’re downtown, most venues and activities are within walking distance of each other, and bus routes will encompass  the hotels in Boulder to pick up and drop off festivalgoers.

Along with the perks of having Sundance in Boulder, there are challenges expected as well, such as increased traffic and larger crowds at restaurants and businesses. And while Boulder has proven its capacity to host large events, the issue of lodging has come up. “The Boulder Creek Fest brings in over 90,000 people in one day, and the audience expected for Sundance is around 90,000 people over 11 days,”  Charlene Hoffman, CEO of Visit Boulder, says. “The challenge that we’ve had, and that we’ve worked through for the most part, is the lodging component, because housing that many people over 11 days is new for us.”

Hoffman shares that the city has helped residents in the community get their short-term rental licenses in order to rent out their homes. These listings can be found on Airbnb, Vrbo, and other home rental sites. Travelers are encouraged to look into lodging beyond Boulder County as well, such as Denver and Estes Park, both of which will be running free shuttles to Boulder.

Whether you plan to attend screenings or not, there’s plenty to eat, drink, and do in Boulder as the inaugural festival kicks off.

In between film screenings, recaffeinate at one of the many cafes in town, like Boulder-founded Ozo Coffee Roasters (located on both the east and west sides of Pearl Street). Or pop by my favorite coffee shop with a view, Spruce Confections on Pearl’s west end, and mingle with festivalgoers over fresh-baked pastries. “That’s always been the magic for me when going to the festival,” Pesmen says. “You find yourself in conversations with people in lines at coffee shops and restaurants, and you talk about things that you heard or a film that you saw.”

With over 400 restaurants in Boulder, options range from gourmet dining to fast-casual, depending on how you’re feeling after a day of watching films. For upscale Northern Italian fare, make reservations at the Michelin-starred, James Beard Award-winning Frasca. Or grab a bite at The Sink, the more than 100-year-old institution on College Hill. Not only does it have the best burger in Boulder (I can vouch for this), but it was once the workplace of Sundance founder Robert Redford. In 1955, he was a CU Boulder student working as the restaurant’s janitor.

Finally, cap off the night with cocktails at License No. 1, a speakeasy-themed lounge beneath the historic Hotel Boulderado. For creative tiki drinks and tropical decor, duck into Jungle and feel winter’s chill melt away.

Boulder’s natural scenery—particularly the iconic Flatirons formations jutting from the foothills—is even more breathtaking when dusted in glittering snow. Play in the snow at Nederland’s Eldora Mountain Resort, just 21 miles from downtown Boulder. Catch the hourly Ski-n-Ride shuttle (a day pass costs $5.50) from Downtown Boulder Station to ski the slopes or snowshoe the Nordic Center’s groomed trails. Discuss film screenings on a crisp, invigorating hike through pine-scented air at Chautauqua Park (I’m partial to the Bluebell Mesa Trail). For a mellow walk with rewarding views of white-frosted peaks, meander along the Bobolink Trail on the south side of town.

When you’re ready to head indoors, warm up with a hot beverage at the Dushanbe Teahouse and take in the beautifully intricate interior, which was crafted by artisans in Tajikistan, then shipped and assembled here in Boulder. Another tea attraction not to be missed: a tour of the Celestial Seasonings factory. Busy festival attendees in need of some relaxation can book a massage or facial at the St. Julien Spa. And of course, your time in Boulder isn’t complete without strolling the four-block outdoor pedestrian mall on Pearl Street, which will still be glowing with holiday lights. “Just being around during Sundance, even without a ticket, is a really great experience,” Hoffman says. “There’s so much energy.”

Paige Triola has been a Boulder enthusiast since moving to the city in 2019. She wrote an exhaustive guide on Boulder for U.S. News & World Report, and is eager to see the Sundance Film Festival thrive in its new setting.

#8147. 10 Simple Ways to Raise Kids Who Make Good Decisions

Ask any parent what it’s like to raise a kid today, and we’d likely tell you modern childhood seems much more complex—and perilous—than when we were young. Thanks to increased peer pressure, massive technological advances, and on-demand access to virtually anything via click or tap, kids today face a wider array of choices and decision-making opportunities than we did when we were their age.

As parents, we hope we’ve instilled strong values and resilience in our children so they’re always able to make good decisions. But how can we be sure they’ll do the right thing, especially when we’re not around? While there’s no magic formula, here are 10 tips to help your kid make smart decisions—even when you’re not there.

The earlier parents initiate conversations about how to make good decisions with their kids, the better. Explaining to your child what it means to make a good decision and why it’s important can set them up for future success. Kevin Zoromski, a psychologist and early childhood development expert says, “Give children choices as part of their day and as part of their typical routine. They will look forward to having some say over what they get to do in the household and you will establish their sense of responsibility as important decision-makers.”

Kids learn through observation and patterning the behaviors of people in their lives, especially their parents. Modeling good decision-making behavior will help reinforce your life lessons. Show your kid that you are honest, responsible, and accountable for your choices. “You are your child’s first and most important role model,” said mental health expert Ketsupa Jirakarn. “[Kids] are always observing and learning from you every day—even when you are unaware of it. So, make sure you practice what you preach.”

Let your kids know what you expect from them in terms of making smart decisions. For older kids, this could include things like always telling you where they are going, not using illicit substances like drugs and alcohol, and staying away from dangerous situations. “Children are more likely to accept the limits you set and are more likely to want to meet your expectations (i.e., be responsible) when you provide a warm, caring, and supportive relationship that underlies the discipline you impose,” according to a report from The Center for Parenting Education.

Give your child opportunities to practice smart decision-making. This could involve giving them small choices, such as what to wear to school or what to eat for dinner. It also could involve giving them bigger choices, such as whether to join a sports team or what to do with their allowance. By empowering your child to learn about the consequences of their choices through smaller actions, they will feel more empowered when making bigger decisions on their own.

When your kid makes a mistake, don’t immediately swoop in to fix the problem or resort immediately to punishment. Help them understand why a misstep was a consequence of not making the best decision, and then talk about how they can make a better choice next time. According to a report from the Harvard Graduate School of Education, “Reframing mistakes as opportunities from which we can learn—rather than failures alone—can help us feel like we are capable and in control. Reframing can also help us handle future mistakes more effectively.”

Learning how to think critically and independently requires self-awareness (i.e., knowing strengths, weaknesses, and values) as well as problem-solving skills. Encouraging your child to think through a decision and come up with a solution can further nurture and develop their critical thinking skills. “In childhood and adolescence, the body goes through many physical changes, but there are also many changes in how we think, feel, and behave, and in our motivations,” according to a report from Frontiers for Young Minds. It’s through repeated trial and error that kids develop the necessary skills to thrive into adulthood.

Some decisions have few consequences, while other decisions are highly consequential. Teaching your child the difference between big and small choices, and understanding the risks associated with some decisions will mitigate the chances of bad outcomes. For example, teach young kids about the risks of eating too much junk food or overdoing it with screen time, and teach older kids about the risks of cyberbullying and underage drinking.

Talk to your child about the choices they’re facing and help them understand the different options and the potential consequences of each choice. Teaching them how to evaluate information, identify biases, and make informed decisions as well as helping your child understand and manage their emotions and how to make decisions that are in line with their values will serve them well. “Emotional literacy starts at birth when babies can just bond with [their parents] and connect on just that level. And it continues to evolve,” said Dr. Michele Borba, parenting expert and author of Building Moral Intelligence: The Seven Essential Virtues that Teach Kids to Do the Right Thing.

As parents, being supportive and consistent with our reactions to our children’s choices will help ensure they make smart ones, even when we’re not present. If you sometimes let your child get away with making a bad decision, they will be less likely to take you seriously when you expect them to make good choices without you. Additionally, when your kid makes a good decision, be sure to praise and validate them. “Youth who experience more positive interactions with parents are better adjusted. Indeed, consistency in parenting—primarily consistency in discipline—has been linked to more positive youth outcomes,” according to a report from the National Institutes of Health.

It takes time for kids to learn how to make smart decisions. Don’t get discouraged if they don’t always and immediately make the right choices. Even when your kids are old enough to make decisions themselves, they still need your patience and understanding. Be there to talk to them, offer advice, and help them deal with the consequences of their decisions.

Bringing a little more joy to parenthood.

#8146. How Useful Is An Alpine Climbing Award, Really?

The Ultar Sar team, of Sebastian Pelletti, Ethan Berman, and Maarten Van Haeren, accept their Piolet d'Or in Saint-Christophe-En-Oisans, France, in October 2026. (Photo: Piotr Drożdż)

When I learned I’d be attending a gala for the “Oscars of Alpinism,” I made a note to pack formal clothes. The Piolets d’Or, or Golden Ice Axes, is a big deal; a rare career-building opportunity in a professional alpinist’s life. Earning this award can transform a strong amateur into a full-fledged member of global alpinism’s elite. This year, I joined the recipients who’d been coaxed out of their humble mountain hideouts to partake in alpinism’s biggest award ceremony.

Established in 1992, the Piolets have a respectable mission: to promote difficult, alpine-style new routes on the world’s great mountains. But the award has weathered plenty of criticism over the years. After rejecting his Piolet nomination in 2006, U.K. legend Ian Parnell later wrote in Alpinist: “Is it possible to choose a winner in an inherently unquantifiable pursuit [like alpinism]?” Others decry the Piolets d’Or for awarding climbers who recently died in the mountains, as well as for holding a subjective line of what counts as good climbing style.

I’ve been critical of the Piolets at times myself, especially after hearing one well-known alpinist talk longingly of wanting to climb something worthy of the award. I winced thinking about anyone tackling runout mixed terrain at high altitude with a golden ice axe taunting them overhead.

I thought of these critics, and my own biases, during my transatlantic flight a few weeks ago to this year’s ceremony in Saint-Christophe-en-Oisans, France. The award clearly has a dark side. But it has also become increasingly important in the year 2026. Lately, I’ve watched the professional climbing landscape bend to the pressures of sponsorship and social-media engagement—physical performance is but one metric to make a modern-day alpinist’s career.

In this new landscape, we see some climbers eager to make a quick buck. Others orient ascents around appeasing future sponsors or gaining attention online. In some instances, this materializes as full-scale fraud. In others, imaginative white lies of what constitutes a “summit.”

Through this lens, the Piolets d’Or represents an institution that is slowly becoming necessary. Nearly every year for the last 34 years, a varied, rotating cast of legendary alpinists sifts through the reams of new climbing achievements. Tossing aside marketing fluff and half-baked route attempts, they present to the world the year’s genuine highpoints of alpinism.

I wanted to know: Does the good of the Piolets d’Or outweigh the bad?

The singular Piolet d’Or first launched with the aim of recognizing the greatest alpine ascent of the previous year. In true Oscars’ fashion, at the early Piolet, all of the potential candidates were invited to an in-person ceremony, where the sole winner was read out, for the first time, in front of a couple thousand people.

“It was a mess,” British alpinist Paul Ramsden, one of this year’s jury members, told me of the Piolet’s early days. He and countryman Mick Fowler had been invited to the ceremony in Paris in 2003, when their ascent of Siguniang (6,250m) in China was in the running. “We all got up onto the stage, and they read my and Mick’s names out, and a French team beside us burst into tears,” Ramsden said.

American Dean Potter was on stage too, in the running for his solo ascents of the Patagonian spires Cerro Torre and Fitz Roy. When he got snubbed, he was livid, Ramsden remembered. Potter screamed at the organizers, asking why they’d told him to fly all the way to Europe to stand on stage for an award they knew he’d never receive.

Later that evening, in a sign of the early Piolet d’Or attitude, a special party took place offsite to celebrate Ramsden and Fowler’s win. With his golden ice axe in hand, Ramsden remembered ambling over to the afterparty, only to be stopped by a bouncer. The club had a dress code, and Ramsden was wearing sneakers. “So we weren’t allowed into our own party,” Ramsden laughed.

The Piolet d’Or ran uninterrupted from 1992 to 2007, when mounting criticism came to a head. Most notable was from the Slovenian alpinist Marko Prezelj, who was invited to that year’s event after his ascent of Chomo Lhari (7,326m), on the border of Tibet. He walked slowly onto the stage, took a long pause, then refused to accept his award, explaining why he thought the Piolet was antithetical to his view of alpinism. “Comparing different climbs is not possible without some kind of personal involvement and even then it is difficult,” Prezelj later wrote. “Last year I climbed in Alaska, Patagonia, and Tibet. I cannot decide which expedition was the most… the ‘most what’ in fact?”

Prezelj and others had become increasingly uneasy with how the Piolet d’Or pitted alpinists against each other. With only one winner, everyone else, in their eyes, became a loser. Such was not the spirit of alpinism.

The organizers cancelled the ceremony in 2008 and took a beat to reimagine it. A year later, after personnel changes and plenty of disagreements, a new version of the Piolet emerged, complete with an updated charter. The now-plural Piolets rewarded a climb’s lightweight style, self-sufficiency, technical difficulty, and management of objective hazards. Most importantly, though, the Piolets adopted a more community-based attitude. Everyone who was nominated for the award was given a Piolet d’Or.

This year’s ceremony was devoid of the drama that tainted the Piolet’s past. No one walked onto the stage just to reject the award. There was no French team in tears, and—as far as I could tell—no leery feeling of one-upsmanship among the award recipients. It was a bunch of climbers, wearing sneakers and duct-taped down jackets, drinking a bit too much red wine.

Paul Ramsden, who is 57, has been to a number of these week-long parties over the years, five times as a recipient—the most of any climber—and multiple times again as a jury member. Despite the criticism it’s received over the years, and his own jarring experience in 2003, he is now a proud supporter of the Piolets d’Or.

“I see awful style from climbers in some parts of the world,” he told me, citing large teams with bolt kits and hundreds of meters of fixed ropes, all but assured to succeed with enough dogged, industrial determination. “By rewarding alpine-style climbs, we’re not really rewarding the recipients. We’re signalling to the rest of the climbing community what ‘good’ style is.” In practice, that means that if a climber doesn’t have the skill to scale an unclimbed face with the same hardware they might take to a crag, they should leave the objective for a future generation of climbers who can.

One alpinist, who wished to remain anonymous, but has been nominated for a Piolet before, emphasized how flimsy and subjective any notion of “good” climbing style is. In a phone call with me, they noted how the Piolets jury considers climbing in insulated boots and ultralight crampons with Google-Earth reconnaissance as “good” climbing style, but considered carrying a few extra ropes to fix sections of the route poor form. The jury considers climbing in a lightweight team of two an enviable expression of alpine self sufficiency, yet a team of five or six is antiquated and ungainly.

Even understated, minimalist climbing expeditions to the Himalaya these days require a cottage-industry of resources: international flights, bus rides, porters, cook tents, tens of thousands of dollars of equipment—the list goes on. Deciding what the “correct” amount of resources an expedition should use is an inexact science, and one which the Piolets jury is still figuring out.

“I think it’s cool that we have a pretty objective governing body deciding what is actually good for alpine climbing,” Australian-Argentine climber Sebastian Pelletti, a recipient of a Piolet this year, told me. Like me, Pelletti has noticed professional alpinists erroneously claiming a “new” route to their sponsors and the world.

Last year, I wrote about one of those so-called new routes on Jirishanca (6,094m), in Peru’s Cordillera Huayhuash. Three very famous European alpinists climbed about a thousand meters of new terrain to the mountain’s summit ridge. Above, a spine of unconsolidated snow—the crux of the mountain—proved too difficult for the team. They bailed. A few days later, the climbers and their sponsors plastered a topo for this new route far and wide, drawing a bright red line that stopped on Jirishanca’s “east summit.” The east summit does not exist, nor has it ever been considered a final destination on the mountain. It is a brief bump in an otherwise vertical landscape, at least six pitches below Jirishanca’s actual summit.

When I wrote that article, some people called it a hit piece; I thought I was going light on the climbers. So when the Piolets d’Or announced their “long list” of notable ascents of 2025 earlier this year, I combed through it, seeing which routes made the cut. (Not all long-listed ascents are short-listed for the Piolets d’Or. The long list aims to recognize all new alpine climbs accomplished in good style.)

The Jirishanca “east summit” team was absent in the Peru section; the jury had not even considered their effort a route. But also within Peru’s long list, in the very same Huayhuash range, was a route on a mountain I had not heard much about, by climbers far less famous than their peers down valley. It was about the same length as the Jirishanca route, and just as difficult, but it went to the summit of Yerupajá Grande (6,635 m) and down the opposite side of the mountain. The climbers called it The Essence of Commitment, and they were being awarded the highest prize in alpinism.

#8145. 7 Ways to Stretch Your Days Between Showers Without Becoming a Walking Biohazard

The pages of Backpacker are a safe space for those of us whose on-trail routines fall outside the normal boundaries of hygiene. But I’ll be the first to admit I’ve pushed those limits, even by the backpacking community’s loose standards. I’ve taken my hair out of a 10-day ponytail and had it stay in the shape of a ponytail, gotten a comb so stuck I had to break the teeth to get it out, and watched in wonder as my socks, coated in several days of sweat and grime, stood up unsupported after I took them off.

We might not follow the standard showering protocol when we’re living in the woods, but there are a few ways to mitigate the horror that those around you endure during your next extended stretch between town days without packing a four-pound hygiene kit.

Your hair isn’t greasy, but your scalp sure is. If you’re planning on going a long time between hair washes, do everything in your power to keep scalp oil from dragging through your hair. This is where a Buff, headband, or hat comes in handy. The less your hair is falling in your face, the less you’re going to keep swiping at it, moving the oils and grime from your hands and scalp through the strands.

It seems counterintuitive, but if your goal is being Less Gross, you should brush your hair less frequently, not more. You can do this by braiding long hair, or pulling it back into a combination ponytail/braid. This pulls double duty, preventing (some) tangles while keeping your hands away from it. I opt for a tight French braid to tame flyaways, then throw a headband or Buff over the top to keep it in place. I’ve kept this braid in place for more than a week at a time, and while it wasn’t pretty when I finally brushed it, I was less greasy than I would have been if I’d been messing with it every day.

Wet wipes are a luxury item for discerning ultralighters, but for the rest of us, they’re the next best thing to a shower. Choose your variety based on your needs. Standard wet wipes will do the trick for most hikers thanks to their combination of cleanser, moisturizer, and antibacterial agents.

You can also choose a backcountry-specific option like Pact—each wipe is the size of a bottle cap and hydrates with a few drops of water. Sea to Summit’s outdoor wipes are also gentler on your face than standard Wet Wipes. (Caveat: If you have sensitive skin, disregard everything I just said and ask your dermatologist for the best option for avoiding backcountry breakouts.)

For most people, the strongest odor buildup is under the arms and around the groin area. Both places have a high concentration of sweat glands, folds of skin that stay warm and trap moisture, and natural bacteria (healthy ones!) that help break down oils. Keeping these body parts wiped down and freshened up at the end of each day will help prevent dirty skin from chafing and keep those stronger odors at bay.

Just be careful not to upset your body’s natural pH, and if you have concerns about scented wipes or their ingredients, err on the side of caution and keep them away from truly sensitive body parts. I’m a huge fan of the antimicrobial Kula Cloth instead of the drip-dry method, and I probably don’t have to explain why that’s a good hygiene choice.

Slapping a frozen burrito onto the gas station counter with dirt-blackened fingernails is pretty gross, but the space under those unkempt nails doesn’t just look yucky: It’s a prime spot for dead skin cells, dirt, and oil to stay trapped. None of us are washing our hands in the woods as frequently as we do at home, and limiting the chance for bacteria by keeping your nails short makes a huge difference. Toes are the same story, but add in an increased risk of fungal infections and ingrown nails.

There are plenty of valid points on both sides of the synthetic-versus-natural-fibers argument, but when it comes to odor resistance, natural fibers are the runaway winner. Synthetic materials like nylon or polyester bind to skin oils, creating a breeding-and-feeding ground for bacteria, which turn trapped sweat into clinging, stinky odors. Natural fibers, on the other hand, regulate your microclimate (the space between your skin and clothes) better and release moisture rather than trapping it in the fibers.

Both materials are wicking, but natural fibers have antimicrobial properties that greatly reduce the growth of those stinky microorganisms. If odor prevention is your goal, opt for a lightweight merino/bamboo blend for your hiking top, natural fibers for your undergarments, and merino or alpaca for hiking midlayers. Avoid clothes made primarily from polyester or nylon, though almost everything will have some percentage of synthetic fibers for durability.

On a shorter trip or cold-weather outing where I’m trying to save pack weight, I’ll occasionally wear my camp pants for chilly early-morning miles, or wear my hiking midlayer to sleep in. But for longer trips where your hiking clothes (and yourself) are going to be fighting the biohazard warning sign, keep your camp clothes for camp and your hiking clothes for your daily miles.

You can keep those camp clothes even cleaner by using your wet wipe ration to wipe your body and feet thoroughly before putting them on, which will also help keep oils and grime out of your sleeping bag liner.

#8144. Is Your Sodium Intake Impacting Your Hiking Performance? A Dietitian Explains Why It Matters.

Take a look at the nutrition label on a freeze-dried backpacking meal, and you might be surprised by how much sodium it contains. Some meals pack more than 1,500 mg into a single pouch, roughly two-thirds of the recommended daily limit of 2,300 mg for most adults. That’s a lot for one dinner, but when you’re spending hours sweating your way up steep climbs, you’re also losing sodium along with water.

Sodium helps regulate fluid balance and supports normal nerve and muscle function. Yet there’s a contradiction in how you might think about it on the trail: you question the sodium in your freeze-dried dinner while adding electrolyte powder to your water bottle and snacking on pretzels, jerky, and cheese.

So, are you consuming too much sodium or not enough? The answer depends on what’s already in your food, how much you’re sweating, and how you’re replacing fluids.

You can pack nearly identical amounts of food and end up with dramatically different sodium intakes. I compared two realistic days of backpacking food, each containing commercial meals, protein bars, snacks, and other familiar trail staples. Both provide roughly 3,150 calories and weigh about 23 ounces dry, yet one contains 5,465 mg of sodium while the other contains just 1,975 mg.

That’s nearly 3,500 mg of difference before you add a single electrolyte packet. Some of the variation comes down to individual products: Mountain House Beef Lasagna contains 1,180 mg of sodium, compared with 340 mg in Good To-Go Pad Thai. Even switching pretzel flavors or protein bar brands can make a noticeable difference. Neither food bag is automatically better, but the comparison shows why it’s worth checking what you’re already carrying before deciding to supplement.

Health experts recommend limiting sodium for a reason. Consistently consuming more than your body needs can raise blood pressure, increasing your risk of heart disease and stroke over time. A particularly salty meal can also leave you thirsty or temporarily bloated as your body regulates its fluid balance. If you’ve been advised to limit sodium because of high blood pressure, kidney disease, or another medical condition, those recommendations still matter when you’re backpacking.

But eating a high-sodium diet day after day isn’t necessarily the same as eating salty meals during a strenuous backpacking trip. When you’re sweating heavily, you lose sodium you wouldn’t lose while sitting at a desk. That doesn’t mean every milligram of sodium in your food is necessary, or that you should add electrolytes without thinking about what you’re already eating. It simply means your activity and conditions matter when interpreting those numbers on the label.

Even if you’re hiking alongside someone on the same trail, you may be losing very different amounts of sodium. Sweat losses depend on two things: how much you sweat and how concentrated that sweat is. Research has found sweat sodium concentrations ranging from roughly 230 to 1,600 mg per liter. Temperature, exertion, clothing, heat acclimatization, and individual physiology all affect your losses, which means mileage alone tells you very little about how much sodium you’ve lost.

Here’s another wrinkle: losing 800 mg of sodium through sweat doesn’t automatically mean you need to consume 800 mg to replace it. Your body regulates sodium and water balance, and research suggests targeted sodium replacement matters more under certain combinations of prolonged exercise, substantial sweat losses, and fluid replacement. That’s why taking an electrolyte packet every hour isn’t necessarily appropriate. A packet doesn’t account for how much you’re sweating, how much you’re drinking, or how much sodium you’re getting from food.

Sodium doesn’t have to come from an electrolyte supplement to count. Salty snacks, meals, and electrolyte drinks all contribute to your intake, although when you consume that sodium can matter during long, sweaty days. Imagine spending ten hours hiking in warm weather, sweating heavily and drinking water but eating very little. At camp, you prepare a freeze-dried dinner containing 1,500 mg of sodium. That sodium helps replace losses and retain fluids during recovery, but it wasn’t available during the preceding hours of hiking.

Eating salty snacks throughout a prolonged, sweaty hike provides some sodium along the way instead of waiting until dinner. That doesn’t mean you need electrolyte powder in every water bottle. If you’re regularly eating pretzels, cheese, jerky, or other salty foods, you’re already consuming sodium during the day. On the other hand, if your trail menu contains relatively little sodium or you struggle to eat while hiking, an electrolyte drink may be a convenient alternative. What matters isn’t whether the sodium comes from a packet or a snack, but whether you’re adding something your food isn’t already providing.

It’s easy to assume that replacing the sodium you lose through sweat will protect you from exercise-associated hyponatremia (EAH), a potentially dangerous drop in blood sodium. But according to the Wilderness Medical Society, most cases occur primarily because you drink too much fluid relative to your losses, often combined with your body’s tendency to retain water during prolonged exercise. Sweat sodium losses can contribute under some circumstances, but taking electrolyte supplements won’t prevent hyponatremia if you’re overdrinking.

The guidelines recommend avoiding overdrinking, generally by drinking according to thirst or using fluid needs you’ve estimated from experience in similar conditions. They also recommend having salty foods or drinks available during long, hot activities. Headaches, fatigue, nausea, and muscle cramps aren’t reliable indicators that you need more sodium because they can have several causes. If you or a hiking partner develops worsening confusion, repeated vomiting, seizures, or collapses during or after prolonged exertion, seek urgent medical help rather than assuming more water or electrolytes will solve the problem.

There’s no simple answer. Your sweat losses vary with the conditions and your individual physiology. Even knowing exactly how much sodium you lose wouldn’t tell you how much to replace. For context, 1,500 mg per day is considered an adequate intake for most adults under ordinary conditions, while 2,300 mg is the general recommended daily limit. Neither is a backpacking-specific target. A food bag containing 5,465 mg isn’t automatically excessive for a strenuous hiking day, just as one containing 1,975 mg isn’t necessarily inadequate. And since research hasn’t consistently shown that extra sodium improves endurance performance, there’s little reason to chase a precise replacement target.

The bottom line? Hike your own hike. If you’re curious about your sodium intake, track what you eat and drink, the conditions you’re hiking in, and how you feel during and afterward. You might notice patterns that help you plan future trips, without getting caught up in replacing every milligram of sodium you sweat out.

Want more Outside health stories? Sign up for the Bodywork newsletter. And for tips on how to train, fuel, and recover better, sign up for the Sweat Science 101 newsletter.

#8143. 11 Early Holiday Deals for Hikers Our Editors Would Actually Buy

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

If it feels too early to start thinking about holiday shopping, well, I agree. Halloween is just behind us, Thanksgiving is still weeks away, and yet every store has already decked their halls with fairy lights, Christmas trees, and giant faux candy canes. But, setting aside my Scroogey (and maybe slightly Boomer) complaints for a minute, there are some real advantages to getting your holiday shopping early. For one, you don’t need to worry about shipping times. For another, you can browse the season’s best deals at your leisure. While not all brands have officially started their Black Friday or winter sales yet—REI’s doesn’t begin until the 13th—eager bargain hunters can find heavy discounts on everything from tents to boots already. These 11 Backpacker-tested and -approved shelters, bags, trail runners, and other assorted goodies are on sale for 25 percent or more off right now.

For beginners and anyone who prefers to linger in camp, a tent’s weight matters less than its durability and livability. The Marmot Limelight has both in spades: With 34.4 square feet of floor space for the 2 (42.5 for the 3), double doors and vestibules, and additional gear storage space in the included wings, the tents have enough room for even tall backpackers to spread out comfortably.

A legit backpacking tent for less than $200 is a steal in this economy. Like the Limelights, the Tungsten is a solid option for anyone who prefers to live a little larger in the backcountry. The freestanding tent features an 8.72-square-foot vestibule and a 38.2-inch peak height, making it comfortable for long nights or waiting out a storm. Bonus: The color-coded clips make setup easy.

Swapping to a trekking pole tent is an easy upgrade for anyone who wants to cut their pack weight. While the REI Co-op Flash Air 2 lost out to models from Durston, Zpacks, and Six Moon in this year’s ultralight tent test, at this price, it’s still a legit option for anyone searching for an upgrade. The 2 lb, 6.5 oz tent pitches with a pair of adjustable trekking poles, while two additional small poles at the feet and crossbar create extra room.

The Copper Spur line is a perennial favorite of our testers; we’ve tested it in almost every kind of conditions, from South American rainstorms to clear desert nights. The HV UL1 Bikepack features 20 square feet of floor space; at 2 lb, 5 oz, it’s light for a freestanding tent, too.

From thin sleeping pads to inconveniently-placed zippers, we side sleepers have a lot stacked against us in the backcountry. The Sidewinder is specifically made for those of us who prefer to curl up, with a center zip that you won’t end up laying on when you toss and turn.

The REI Co-op Magma 30 doesn’t have any gimmicks: It’s just a down-the-middle, well-made sleeping bag suitable for 3 season use. The 850-fill-power down lets it compress handily, with a long taking up just slightly more room than two 2-liter Nalgenes.

The Aspire was our testers’ favorite women’s rain jacket of 2026 (the Foray is the men’s version), so at half off it’s an easy buy. Our testers praised the breathability of the 3-layer Ascentshell construction, while the 40D, 100-percent recycled nylon face fabric shrugged off close encounters with trailside foliage.

We named Black Diamond’s Fineline the best-value rainshell for women in our 2026 test. But value isn’t all this lightweight shell has going for it. The 2.5-layer shell’s light stretch made it comfortable to wear on everything from high-tempo hikes to mountain bike rides, and we appreciated the helmet-compatible hood and hand pockets.

With their wide, splay-friendly toebox and zero-drop design, Altra’s shoes are popular enough on hiking trails that they need no introduction. With its 33mm stack height, the Olympus 6 is an excellent pick for backpackers who want a little more cushion than the popular Lone Peak provides.

I’m personally a big fan of Adidas’ Terrex Free series, which I’ve taken everywhere from the Panamanian jungle to the Appalachian Trail. Testers who tried this speedy shoe out agreed. A Gore-Tex bootie shuts out slop, while the DreamStrike+ EVA midsole kept them feeling bouncy underfoot.

Don’t be fooled by the space-age looks: Our testers reported that these kicks from Merrell were at home on the trail, with a “ridiculously thick” EVA foam midsole that absorbed shock on rough treadpath without ever feeling unstable.

#8141. The Supreme Court Just Gave Trump Approval to Build a Border Wall in Big Bend National Park

Construction crews tear into Big Bend National Park to build the border wall (Photo: RONALDO SCHEMIDT / Getty Images)

Bulldozers may soon tear into the rock cliffs and desert sand in Big Bend National Park to erect parts of the Trump Administration’s controversial border barrier.

On November 9, the U.S. Supreme Court gave the federal government the green light to resume construction on barriers, fences, and surveillance equipment along the U.S.-Mexico border in a remote corner of Texas that includes Big Bend National Park.

In an unsigned opinion, the court ruled that Congress has expressed “clear preference for expeditious border construction.” The government’s desire to limit immigration overrules any “aesthetic, recreational, and environmental harm,” the court added.

The court ruled 8-1. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson dissented with the decision.

The Center for Biological Diversity, one of the plaintiffs in a lawsuit that challenged the construction, blasted the decision in a statement.

“The Trump Administration and its contractors are hellbent on destroying one of America’s greatest national parks, and the Supreme Court just gave them the green light,” Laiken Jordahl, national public lands advocate at the Center for Biological Diversity, said on Facebook.

The ruling marks a groundbreaking decision in a months-long game of political football between the Trump Administration and a growing number of advocates, Texas locals, and lawmakers who opposed the construction.

Officials with the U.S. Customs and Border Protection and the Department of Homeland Security have said that the barriers along stretches of the Rio Grande and Big Bend National Park are needed to curb illegal immigrants from entering the U.S. from Mexico.

Advocates and local property owners in Texas have argued that the number of illegal crossings in the Big Bend region is negligible, and that construction would irreparably damage the pristine landscape, hurt local flora and fauna, and destroy local businesses that rely on the landscape for tourism and agriculture. In April, a coalition of opponents to the project filed suit to block the construction.

In August, construction crews arrived in the Big Bend region and began clearing swaths of desert for bollards and fencing. But construction ground to a halt after state politicians put pressure on Trump administration officials. And on October 2, a federal judge overseeing the legal case ruled that the construction should stop because it threatened to harm a group of plaintiffs who had sued to stop it.

The border wall plan drew ire from officials on both sides of the political spectrum. On November 9, Texas Senator John Cornyn, a Republican, published an op-ed in the San Antonio Express-News titled “The Case Against the Big Bend Border Wall.”

“Texans should not have to bear another unnecessary financial burden caused by building a 30-foot wall atop a 1,000-foot riverbank cliff,” Cornyn wrote.

After the Supreme Court decision on November 9, environmental groups and other opponents voiced their disapproval on social media.

“We are outraged by the Supreme Court’s decision allowing Trump’s border wall construction to resume in Big Bend National Park,” the Sierra Club posted on X. “This destructive project threatens irreplaceable wildlife habitat, sacred cultural sites, and one of America’s most treasured landscapes.”

In a statement, Cary Dupuy, Texas Regional Director for the National Parks Conservation Association (NPCA), said the decision would have “profound consequences.”

“Our national parks are meant to be set aside from harmful development and safeguarded under the highest standard possible under American law,” Dupy said. “Regardless of the court’s decision, we urge the administration to implement alternatives to damaging border barriers and other heavy infrastructure in this wild place. There is still a chance for us to save Big Bend, and there is still an opportunity for the administration to change course.”

Meghan Riley, senior attorney with the environmental advocacy group Earthjustice, called Big Bend a “national treasure.”

“allowing the administration to bulldoze through these fragile and protected ecosystems puts irreplaceable land at risk,” Riley said in a statement. “Once this damage is done, there is no simply putting Big Bend back together.”

Dave Cortez, director of the Sierra Club’s Lone Star chapter, pointed out the bipartisan anger at the border construction within Texas.

“Millions of Texans turned out to vote for change last week, and Republicans, Democrats, and Independents alike have spoken out against the Trump administration’s reckless and destructive plans to bulldoze the treasured borderlands of Far West Texas and the greater Big Bend region,” Cortez said in a statement. “This Supreme Court decision ignores the bipartisan opposition to a project that threatens some of Texas’s most cherished landscapes.”

#8139. “These Aren’t Victimless Crimes.” Vandals Deface Ancient Petroglyphs Near Moab.

Vandals scratched graffiti above ancient animal petroglyphs at the Bear Panel along Highway 279 near Moab, Utah. (Photo: BLM Utah)

The Bureau of Land Management (BLM) announced on November 6 that it was investigating vandalism at two ancient rock-art sites near Moab, Utah, where someone carved names into petroglyphs, leaving damage that may be impossible to remove.

The incidents occurred at the Bear Panel, a rock-art site along Highway 279 near the Colorado River, and another panel near Hell’s Revenge, a popular four-wheel-drive trail in the Sand Flats Recreation Area.

“These images are a physical expression of the past, their connection to their ancestors and to that landscape,” Chris Merritt, Utah’s state historic preservation officer, told Outside. “They will now forever be scarred by someone’s thoughtlessness, and that hurts the continuation of culture.”

The BLM has not publicly identified any suspects in the two latest incidents. An agency spokesperson told the Moab newspaper The Times-Independent that the agency planned to treat the graffiti in the days following its November 6 announcement, although some damage may be permanent.

Under the federal Archaeological Resources Protection Act, vandalizing protected archaeological sites can carry fines of up to $20,000 and two years in prison.

Photos show the name “Meru” scratched beside ancient carvings depicting a bear and a bighorn sheep at the Bear Panel. At the second site, near Hell’s Revenge, someone carved “Craig W” across several petroglyph figures.

Merritt said much of the artwork at the two sites dates back roughly 1,500 years and reflects Ancestral Puebloan and Fremont traditions, along with those of more recent Indigenous communities. The panels are part of a larger cultural landscape around Moab, where Indigenous peoples once lived, farmed, and traveled, he said.

Restoring the damaged petroglyphs presents different challenges at each site, Merritt said.

At the site near Hell’s Revenge, vandals scratched graffiti directly across ancient carvings. Merritt noted that typical fixes, such as scrubbing the stone or trying to conceal the marks with pigments, risk damaging the original artwork underneath.

The Bear Panel presents a different problem. A crack in the sandstone just below the graffiti means that scraping the rock could create openings for rainwater, weakening the structure through freeze-thaw cycles.

“Five minutes of damage could take weeks of repair to do carefully to preserve the subsurface imagery and the rock face,” Merritt said, emphasizing that any remediation must involve consultation with descendant tribal communities.

Merritt said rock-art vandalism has become more widespread in Utah in recent years, a problem he believes is partly connected to growing visitation on public lands.

“We’ve always had folks going back to the 19th century scraping their initials on the panels, but what we’re seeing within five or six years is a pretty significant increase in the scale and distribution, hitting archaeological panels that have never had graffiti before,” Merritt said.

The latest incidents follow another case in March 2026, when the Grand County Sheriff’s Office investigated graffiti carved into petroglyphs near Tusher Tunnel, along an off-highway vehicle route northwest of Moab.

To combat the problem, Merritt said Utah is using its Protect Our Past education campaign and a statewide network of volunteer site stewards who monitor archaeological sites. Signage and fencing can also help discourage vandalism, he said.

In November 2025, a Utah woman who vandalized petroglyphs on BLM land near Wire Pass was sentenced to 12 months of probation and ordered to pay $14,853 in fines and restitution, according to a U.S. Department of Justice news release. She was also prohibited from entering BLM land during her probation.

“These aren’t victimless crimes,” Merritt said. “We need to find ways to catch, prosecute, and convict these folks, so it sends a message to future visitors that this is not acceptable in Utah or anywhere you visit heritage sites.”

Anyone with information is asked to contact Moab BLM Law Enforcement at 435-259-2131.
